title: Acoustics & Audio Signal Fundamentals
subtitle: The physics, mathematics and psychoacoustics every audio engineer is assumed to know
tagline: Sound is a pressure wave, hearing is a filter bank, and every decision downstream is a number you can compute.
author: Oboros
certificateDesc: has completed a rigorous, collegiate-level foundation in acoustics and audio signal theory, and can compute wavelengths, decibel relationships, room modes, reverberation times, comb-filter geometry, Nyquist limits and dynamic-range budgets, read equal-loudness and masking data, and design and audit a disciplined gain structure from acoustic source to delivered file.

modules.title: Sound as a Pressure Wave
modules.tagline: Frequency, wavelength, amplitude and propagation speed — the four physical quantities every later chapter reduces to.
objectives: Able to describe sound as a longitudinal pressure disturbance and distinguish sound pressure, particle velocity, intensity and power.
Able to compute wavelength, period and frequency from one another, and adjust the speed of sound for air temperature.
Able to predict level change with distance in a free field and explain why real rooms violate the prediction.
Able to reason about when a wave will reflect, diffract or pass through an obstacle using the ratio of wavelength to object size.
Able to justify why the audible band is roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz in terms of both physics and physiology.

lessons.title: Compression, Rarefaction, and What Actually Travels
glossary: Longitudinal wave
A wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of propagation. Sound in air, water and most solids-in-bulk is longitudinal.
Sound pressure
The instantaneous deviation from ambient static pressure caused by a sound wave, measured in pascals (Pa).
Particle velocity
The oscillating velocity of the medium itself, in m/s. Distinct from the propagation speed of the wave.
Acoustic impedance
The ratio of sound pressure to particle velocity, Z = p/u. For air at 20 degrees C it is about 413 rayls (Pa s/m).
Threshold of hearing
The reference pressure 20 micropascals, chosen because it is roughly the quietest 1 kHz tone a healthy young ear detects.

blocks.html: Sound is a propagating disturbance in pressure. Air at rest sits at roughly 101,325 Pa (one standard atmosphere). When a loudspeaker cone pushes forward it locally squeezes the air in front of it, raising pressure by a tiny amount; when it retreats it leaves the air slightly rarefied. Those alternating regions of high and low pressure move outward at the speed of sound. The air itself goes almost nowhere: individual molecules jiggle back and forth over distances measured in micrometres and return to where they started.

The numbers are worth internalising because they explain why audio engineering is a business of extremes. A sound at the threshold of hearing has an RMS pressure of 20 micropascals — two ten-billionths of atmospheric pressure. A rock concert at 120 dB SPL is about 20 pascals. That is a ratio of one million to one in pressure, and one trillion to one in power. No linear scale survives that range comfortably, which is the entire reason the decibel exists (Module 2).

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 1
items: Master Handbook of Acoustics (6th ed.) — F. Alton Everest & Ken Pohlmann

Required. Chapters 1-3: the nature of sound, sound levels, and the ear. Read Ch. 1 for the pressure-wave model and Ch. 2 for the decibel groundwork we formalise next week. Skip the appendices for now.
Modern Recording Techniques (9th ed.) — David Miles Huber & Robert E. Runstein
Required. Chapter 2, "Sound and Hearing", in full. It is the least mathematical treatment of this material you will meet and it is a good first pass before Everest.
Sound Reproduction: The Acoustics and Psychoacoustics of Loudspeakers and Rooms (3rd ed.) — Floyd E. Toole
Required. Chapter 1 and Section 4.1 only. Read for Toole’s framing of the loudspeaker-room-listener system as a single problem; the deep listening-test evidence comes later in the course.
Acoustics: Sound Fields and Transducers — Leo L. Beranek & Tim Mellow
Optional but recommended for the mathematically inclined. Chapter 2, sections 2.1-2.4, gives the wave equation derivation this lesson deliberately skips.
ISO 226:2023 Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours
Optional now, required in Module 3. Skim the scope and Table 1 so you know the standard exists and what it standardises.

blocks.text: Pressure and particle velocity are not the same thing

blocks.html: Beginners conflate three quantities that behave differently. Sound pressure (p, in pascals) is a scalar: it is what a pressure microphone measures, and it has no direction. Particle velocity (u, in m/s) is a vector: it is what a ribbon or pressure-gradient microphone responds to, and it does have direction. Intensity (I, in W/m2) is their product, p·u, and it is the actual flow of acoustic energy. In a free-field plane wave, pressure and particle velocity are in phase and related by the acoustic impedance of air.

blocks.label: Specific acoustic impedance of a plane wave
blocks.caption: Density of air times speed of sound. This single number explains why a bare loudspeaker driver is such a bad radiator: it is trying to couple a heavy cone to a medium with almost no impedance.

blocks.html: Think of a long line of people packed shoulder to shoulder. Shove the person at one end and a bunching-up travels down the line at some speed determined by how stiff and how heavy the people are. Nobody walks from one end to the other. The bunching travels; the people only sway. The speed of the bunching (the speed of sound) has nothing to do with how hard you shoved (the amplitude) — a fact that surprises people who expect louder sounds to arrive first.

blocks.label: A very common error
blocks.html: Sound does not travel faster when it is louder, and low frequencies do not travel more slowly than high frequencies in air. Air is a very nearly non-dispersive medium for audio-band sound. If bass seems to arrive late from a distant PA system it is because of loudspeaker phase response, crossover filters and room reflections — not because the physics of air delayed it. (Extremely high levels, above roughly 150 dB SPL, do become nonlinear, which is why shock waves are a separate topic.)

blocks.text: Why the medium matters more than you think

blocks.html: The speed of sound is set by the stiffness and density of the medium: c = √(K/ρ) for a fluid. Stiffer media transmit faster; denser media transmit slower. Air is neither stiff nor dense, and lands around 343 m/s. Water is far stiffer relative to its density and manages roughly 1,480 m/s. Steel, stiffer again, reaches about 5,100 m/s — which is why structure-borne transmission through a building frame beats airborne transmission to the neighbour downstairs, and why isolation work is mostly about breaking mechanical paths rather than adding foam.

head: Medium
Speed (m/s, approx.)
Practical consequence
rows: Cold outdoor gigs: your delay-tower timings drift by roughly 3-4% from a warm rehearsal.
The default value used for every calculation in this course unless stated otherwise.
A packed venue that heats up during a set will subtly detune every distance-based alignment.
Voice pitch does not change; the vocal-tract formants shift up, which is what you actually hear.
Hydrophone work: wavelengths are 4x longer, so a 1 kHz wavelength is 1.48 m.
Structure-borne flanking dominates poorly decoupled studio builds.
Coincidence dip: a 12.5 mm sheet loses transmission loss around 2.5-3 kHz.

blocks.q: A singer inhales helium and sings the same note. What actually changes?
options: The fundamental frequency rises because the vocal folds vibrate faster
The vocal-tract resonances (formants) move up because sound travels faster in helium
The amplitude rises because helium is less dense
Nothing changes; the effect is psychological
blocks.explain: Vocal fold vibration rate is set by muscle tension and airflow, not by the gas in the tract, so the fundamental is essentially unchanged. What changes is the resonant frequencies of the tube above the folds: resonance frequency scales with c, and c in helium is nearly three times that in air, so the formants shift up and the timbre changes. This is a clean demonstration that pitch and timbre are separable.

blocks.html: One more distinction that will matter for the rest of the course: power is what a source emits (watts), intensity is power per unit area at a point (W/m2), and pressure is what a microphone measures (pascals). A loudspeaker radiating one acoustic watt into a hemisphere is startlingly loud; typical loudspeakers convert well under 1% of their electrical input into acoustic power. Efficiency, not amplifier size, is why a horn-loaded system can be 15 dB louder than a direct-radiator box on the same amplifier.

lessons.title: Frequency, Period and Wavelength
glossary: Frequency
Cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). Named for Heinrich Hertz; the unit replaced "cycles per second" formally in 1960.
Period
The duration of one cycle, T = 1/f, in seconds.
Wavelength
The physical distance between successive identical points of a wave, lambda = c/f, in metres.
Octave
A doubling of frequency. Ten octaves span 20 Hz to 20,480 Hz, which is why the audible band is often described as "ten octaves".
Dispersion
Frequency-dependent propagation speed. Air is essentially non-dispersive for audio; bending waves in panels are strongly dispersive.

blocks.html: Frequency, period and wavelength are three views of the same thing. Frequency is a rate you hear as pitch. Period is the same fact expressed as time, and it is the view you need when you set a delay, a gate hold, or a tape flutter rate. Wavelength is the same fact expressed as distance, and it is the view you need for every acoustics problem: microphone placement, room modes, speaker spacing, absorber thickness, comb filtering.

blocks.label: The three relations you will use constantly
blocks.caption: With c = 343 m/s, the pair worth memorising is 343 Hz = 1 m and 1 kHz = 34.3 cm. Everything else you can scale by ear.
One cycle of a sinusoid with its amplitude descriptions marked. Peak, peak-to-peak and RMS differ by fixed factors for a sinusoid only; for speech or music the crest factor varies constantly.

blocks.text: The speed of sound is a temperature problem, not a constant

blocks.html: In dry air the speed of sound depends on temperature and essentially nothing else in the range we care about. Pressure does not affect it (density and stiffness change together), and humidity affects it by well under 1%. The exact relation and the linear approximation good to about 0.1% over normal room temperatures:

blocks.label: Speed of sound in air
blocks.caption: Theta is temperature in degrees Celsius. At 20 °C this gives 343.4 m/s; at 0 °C, 331.3 m/s. The linear form is accurate to better than 0.5 m/s from -20 to +40 °C.

blocks.label: Field rule
blocks.html: Roughly 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius. A 15-degree swing between a morning line-check and a hot evening show shifts c by about 9 m/s, or 2.6%. On a 100 m delay tower that is 8 ms of drift — audible as a smeared transient. Serious touring systems re-measure temperature and re-time delays before doors.

head: Frequency
Period
Wavelength at 343 m/s
Why it matters
rows: Longer than most rooms. Below the lowest room mode you are in the pressure zone, not a wave field.
A kick drum fundamental. Half-wavelength 4.3 m — the length of a typical bedroom studio.
Where most small-room modal problems cluster.
The anchor value. Memorise this one.
The reference frequency for almost every acoustic standard.
Peak ear-canal sensitivity; also the width of a typical tweeter faceplate, hence diffraction.
Head-shadow and pinna effects dominate; mic capsule size becomes significant.
Comparable to a 1/2-inch measurement microphone diaphragm, which is why sub-miniature capsules exist.

blocks.html: Look at the wavelength column and a great deal of practical acoustics becomes obvious. A 5 cm foam panel is a quarter-wavelength at about 1.7 kHz, so it absorbs well above that and does almost nothing at 100 Hz. A microphone 15 cm from a boundary produces a cancellation whose first null is near 570 Hz. A pair of speakers 2 m apart cannot possibly produce a stable stereo image below about 170 Hz. None of this requires memorisation once you can convert frequency to distance in your head.

blocks.text: Why 20 Hz to 20 kHz?

blocks.html: The lower bound is not a hard wall. Below about 20 Hz the auditory system stops producing a clear pitch percept and the sensation becomes one of pressure and vibration felt through the body; the middle-ear reflex and the mechanics of the cochlear helicotrema roll off the response. The upper bound is set by the mass and stiffness of the basilar membrane at its base and by the middle-ear ossicles acting as a mechanical low-pass. It degrades with age at a rate that would alarm most people: presbycusis typically costs the average 60-year-old everything above about 10-12 kHz. Your ears are a moving target, which is one reason measurement matters.

cards.label: What wavelength is 80 Hz?
cards.html: 343 / 80 = 4.29 m. A quarter-wavelength is 1.07 m, which is roughly how far from the rear wall a subwoofer would have to sit to avoid the worst boundary cancellation at that frequency.

cards.label: What frequency has a 25 cm wavelength?
cards.html: 343 / 0.25 = 1,372 Hz. Also the frequency whose half-wavelength equals the 12.5 cm spacing of a typical spaced-pair microphone technique.

cards.label: What period is 250 Hz?
cards.html: 1 / 250 = 4 ms. If a delay of 4 ms is mixed with the dry signal, the comb notches land at odd multiples of 125 Hz.

cards.label: How long is 20 Hz?
cards.html: 17.2 m and a 50 ms period. No domestic room supports a full wavelength, so what you hear at 20 Hz indoors is pressure, not a travelling wave.

blocks.q: A control room is 4.3 m long. Which statement follows directly from the wavelength table?
options: A 40 Hz tone has a half-wavelength equal to the room length, so the room will strongly support a mode near 40 Hz
A 40 Hz tone cannot exist in the room because its wavelength is too long
A 40 Hz tone will be absorbed by the walls because 8.6 m exceeds the room dimension
A 40 Hz tone will travel faster than a 4 kHz tone across the room
blocks.explain: The lowest axial mode of a dimension L sits where the half-wavelength equals L, i.e. f = c/2L = 343/8.6 = 39.9 Hz. Sound of any wavelength can exist in the room; what changes is whether the boundaries reinforce it. Nothing here implies absorption, and air is non-dispersive.

blocks.html: An opinion, marked as such: the single highest-leverage skill in this whole course is the ability to convert a frequency into a distance without a calculator. Engineers who can do it diagnose comb filtering, modal ringing and boundary cancellation on the spot; engineers who cannot reach for a graphic EQ and guess. Drill the table until 100 Hz means 3.4 m to you as automatically as 60 mph means a mile a minute.

lessons.title: Amplitude, Intensity and the Fall-Off with Distance
glossary: RMS
Root mean square: the square root of the mean of the squared instantaneous values. It is the amplitude measure that tracks power.
Crest factor
The ratio of peak to RMS, usually expressed in dB. A sine wave is 3.01 dB; unprocessed drums can exceed 20 dB.
Free field
An idealised environment with no reflecting boundaries, approximated in an anechoic chamber or outdoors well above ground.
Critical distance
The distance from a source at which the direct and reverberant sound fields are equal in level.
Inverse-square law
In a free field, intensity falls as 1/r squared and sound pressure as 1/r, giving 6 dB per doubling of distance.

blocks.html: Amplitude has four common descriptions and they are not interchangeable. Peak is the largest instantaneous excursion and it is what clips a converter. Peak-to-peak is twice that for a symmetric signal and is the number you read off an oscilloscope. RMS is the amplitude that carries the same power as an equivalent DC value, and it is what correlates with perceived loudness over short windows. Average rectified is what cheap analogue VU meters actually measure, calibrated to read RMS for sinusoids and therefore wrong for everything else.

blocks.label: Root mean square of a continuous signal
blocks.caption: For a sinusoid this evaluates to peak divided by the square root of two, i.e. 0.7071 x peak. That factor is true for sinusoids and for nothing else.

blocks.html: Crest factor is the practical reason a level meter alone never tells you enough. Two mixes can share an identical RMS level and differ by 14 dB in peak level; one will clip a converter and the other will not. It is also why loudness normalisation on streaming services (Module 2, and ITU-R BS.1770) had such a violent effect on mastering practice: once playback is normalised by loudness, crushing crest factor buys you nothing and costs you transients.

blocks.text: How level falls with distance

blocks.html: A point source radiating into free space spreads its power over a sphere whose area grows as the square of the radius. Intensity therefore falls as 1/r<sup>2</sup>, and since intensity is proportional to pressure squared, pressure falls as 1/r. In decibels of sound pressure level that is a loss of 20 log<sub>10</sub>(2) = 6.02 dB per doubling of distance.

blocks.label: Inverse-square law in level terms
blocks.caption: Going from 1 m to 4 m loses 20 log(4) = 12.04 dB. Going from 1 m to 10 m loses 20 dB. Note that the second formula uses 4-pi-r-squared for a full sphere; halve the area (2-pi-r-squared) for a source on a hard floor and you gain 3 dB.

blocks.label: Where the 6 dB rule fails
blocks.html: It fails inside rooms beyond the critical distance, where the reverberant field dominates and level stops falling. It fails for line arrays in their near field, which behave cylindrically at 3 dB per doubling. It fails close to any source where the source is not small compared with the distance — this is exactly the near-field region that produces the proximity effect on directional microphones. And over long outdoor distances it under-predicts loss, because air absorption removes an additional frequency-dependent amount (roughly 0.5 dB per 100 m at 1 kHz, but 5 dB or more per 100 m at 10 kHz in dry air).

blocks.title: Estimating SPL at a listening position
steps: Start from the sensitivity spec
A loudspeaker rated 88 dB SPL for 1 W at 1 m tells you the anchor point. Treat manufacturer numbers with suspicion; they are often measured on-axis with a favourable smoothing.
Add amplifier gain in power terms
Every doubling of electrical power adds 3 dB. 100 W is 20 dB above 1 W, so 88 + 20 = 108 dB at 1 m.
Subtract distance loss
At 3 m, subtract 20 log(3) = 9.5 dB, giving 98.5 dB.
Add for a second speaker
Two correlated sources add 6 dB in the sum region; two uncorrelated sources add 3 dB. Stereo programme material sits somewhere between.
Add room gain
In a small control room, expect 2-4 dB of reverberant support at the mix position, and considerably more below 100 Hz.
Sanity-check against headroom
If the answer exceeds the driver excursion or amplifier rating, you have found your real ceiling. Peaks 15-20 dB above the average are normal, so a 98 dB average implies 115 dB peaks.

blocks.q: A measurement mic reads 94 dB SPL at 1 m from a point source outdoors. What does it read at 6 m, ignoring air absorption?
options: 88 dB
82 dB
70 dB
blocks.explain: 20 log10(6/1) = 20 x 0.778 = 15.56 dB of loss. 94 - 15.56 = 78.4 dB. The tempting wrong answer, 88 dB, comes from applying only one 6 dB doubling; 6 m is between two and three doublings from 1 m.

blocks.html: Finally, a warning about adding sources. Levels in decibels never add arithmetically. Two uncorrelated sources of equal level (two different instruments, or two speakers playing decorrelated content) sum in power and give +3 dB. Two correlated sources (the same signal from two speakers, in phase, at a point equidistant from both) sum in pressure and give +6 dB. Two correlated sources in opposite polarity give, in principle, silence. Which case you are in is the single most important question in Module 4.

lessons.title: Waves Meeting Objects: Reflection, Absorption, Diffraction, Refraction
glossary: Specular reflection
Mirror-like reflection from a surface large compared with the wavelength; angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Diffraction
The bending of waves around obstacles and through apertures, significant when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the object.
Refraction
Bending of the propagation path caused by a gradient in the speed of sound, typically from temperature or wind shear.
Absorption coefficient
Alpha: the fraction of incident sound energy not reflected by a surface, from 0 (perfect reflector) to 1 (perfect absorber).
Boundary interference
Cancellation and reinforcement caused by a reflection from a nearby surface combining with the direct sound.

blocks.html: What a wave does when it meets an object is decided almost entirely by one ratio: wavelength relative to the size of the object. If the object is much larger than the wavelength, the wave reflects specularly and casts an acoustic shadow. If the object is much smaller, the wave diffracts around it as though it were not there. Between those extremes lies scattering, where the object redistributes energy in complicated directions. This one ratio explains why a 2 m acoustic panel controls 500 Hz beautifully and 50 Hz not at all, and why you can hear someone talking around a corner but cannot see them.

blocks.label: The regime boundary
blocks.caption: Here d is the characteristic dimension of the obstacle. A 60 cm panel starts behaving like a mirror above roughly 570 Hz and like a non-obstacle below about 150 Hz.

blocks.title: Four things a wave can do at a boundary

items.label: Reflect
items.html: Energy returns into the room. The reflection retains the waveform but arrives later and, in a room, from a different direction. A hard plaster wall reflects better than 95% of incident energy above 250 Hz (alpha around 0.02-0.05).

items.label: Absorb
items.html: Energy is converted to heat, mostly by viscous losses as air moves through a porous material. Porous absorbers work on particle velocity, which is why they must be placed where velocity is high — a quarter-wavelength from a boundary — and why a thin panel flat against a wall is nearly useless at low frequencies.

items.label: Transmit
items.html: Energy passes through into the next space. Governed by the mass law: transmission loss rises about 6 dB per doubling of surface mass and 6 dB per doubling of frequency, with a dip at the coincidence frequency where bending waves in the panel match the airborne wavelength.

items.label: Diffract
items.html: Energy bends around edges. Every cabinet edge, console lip, mic stand and desk surface is a secondary source. Diffraction from a loudspeaker baffle edge is a leading cause of the ripples you see in a measured frequency response between 1 and 4 kHz.

blocks.text: Boundary interference: the first acoustic problem you will actually hear

blocks.html: Put a microphone or a listener near a hard surface and the reflected sound arrives with a delay equal to the extra path length divided by c. When the extra path equals half a wavelength, the reflection arrives in antiphase and cancels. For a surface at perpendicular distance d with the source far away, the first null lands where the extra path 2d equals half a wavelength.

blocks.label: First cancellation from a nearby boundary
blocks.caption: A microphone 20 cm above a hard table sees its first null at 343/(4 x 0.2) = 429 Hz, then further nulls at odd multiples: 1,287 Hz, 2,145 Hz. This is exactly why boundary (PZM) microphones sit flush on the surface — at d = 0 the null moves to infinity.

blocks.label: The practical fix
blocks.html: Either get the microphone very close to the boundary (so the null moves above the audio band) or very far from it (so the reflection is weak enough not to matter, and late enough to be perceived as a separate event). The worst place is the intuitive middle — 10 to 60 cm — which is unfortunately where most people instinctively put a stand.

blocks.text: Refraction outdoors, and why sound carries at night

blocks.html: Sound bends toward regions where it travels more slowly. On a sunny afternoon the ground is hot and the air above it is cooler, so sound near the ground travels faster and the wavefront bends upward, away from listeners — this is why a distant festival sounds thin at 3 pm. After sunset the ground cools faster than the air, producing a temperature inversion, so sound bends downward and is refracted back to earth. The same mechanism operates with wind gradients: downwind the effective speed increases with height, bending sound down, which is why complaints from a venue neighbour are essentially a wind-direction forecast.

head: Condition
Gradient
Effect on a distant listener
rows: Rays bend upward; a shadow zone forms; the show sounds quiet and dull at distance.
Rays bend downward and focus; levels 10-20 dB higher than daytime at the same distance.
Effective c increases with height; rays bend down; noise complaints.
Rays bend up; a pronounced shadow zone within a few hundred metres.

blocks.html: Absorption by the air itself is the last mechanism, and it is strongly frequency-dependent and humidity-dependent. ISO 9613-1 gives the standard model. The engineering summary: at 20 °C and 50% relative humidity you lose roughly 0.1 dB per 100 m at 125 Hz, about 1 dB per 100 m at 2 kHz, and about 8-10 dB per 100 m at 8 kHz. That is why every large outdoor system applies high-frequency shading to the long-throw boxes, and why distant thunder is a rumble while nearby thunder is a crack.

blocks.q: Why does a 60 cm x 60 cm absorption panel do very little at 60 Hz?
options: Because absorption coefficients are always lower at low frequencies for physical reasons unrelated to size
Because the 5.7 m wavelength is far larger than the panel, so the wave diffracts around it rather than interacting
Because low frequencies carry less energy
Because the panel reflects low frequencies specularly
blocks.explain: The wavelength at 60 Hz is 5.72 m, nearly ten times the panel dimension, so the wave simply bends around it. Panel thickness matters too (a porous absorber needs depth comparable to a quarter wavelength) but the size-versus-wavelength argument is the primary one, and it is why low-frequency control requires large devices: bass traps, membrane absorbers, or whole-wall construction.

blocks.title: Assignment 1 — The wavelength audit of your own space
blocks.brief: Measure your listening or recording room and produce a one-page quantitative audit. Report: (a) the three principal dimensions in metres; (b) the frequency whose wavelength equals each dimension and the frequency whose half-wavelength equals each dimension; (c) the perpendicular distance from your usual microphone or listening position to the nearest three hard boundaries, with the first boundary-cancellation frequency for each; (d) the expected free-field level at your listening position given your loudspeaker sensitivity and a stated amplifier power, showing the arithmetic; (e) a short paragraph naming which of your calculations you expect the room to violate, and why. Show every formula in symbolic form before substituting numbers.
items: A strong result states the assumed speed of sound and justifies it from the actual room temperature rather than defaulting to 343 m/s without comment.
A strong result gets the boundary-null frequencies right, including the odd-multiple higher nulls, and does not confuse the c/4d and c/2L relations.
A strong result computes distance loss with 20 log(r2/r1), not by counting doublings approximately, and states the answer to one decimal place.

A strong result identifies the critical-distance problem explicitly: it predicts that measured level will exceed the free-field prediction at the listening position, and gives a numerical estimate of by how much.
A weak result reports numbers without units, rounds prematurely, or asserts that the room "sounds boomy" without connecting the claim to a specific calculated frequency.

questions.q: Which quantity does a standard pressure microphone actually respond to?
options: Particle velocity
Instantaneous deviation from ambient static pressure
Acoustic intensity
The net displacement of air molecules from their rest position
why: Particle velocity is what a pressure-gradient transducer such as a ribbon responds to; a pressure capsule is sealed on one side and is insensitive to direction.
Correct. A pressure capsule has one side exposed and converts the scalar pressure deviation into voltage.
Intensity is the product of pressure and particle velocity and requires two transducers (or a p-u probe) to measure directly.
Net displacement over a cycle is zero; the air returns to where it started. Displacement amplitude is also vanishingly small, on the order of nanometres at conversational levels.
questions.explain: Sound is a pressure disturbance. Distinguishing pressure (scalar), particle velocity (vector) and intensity (their product) is the foundation for understanding why different microphone designs have different polar patterns.

questions.q: What is the wavelength of a 125 Hz tone in air at 20 degrees Celsius? Use c = 343 m/s.
questions.explain: 343 / 125 = 2.744 m. A quarter of that is 68.6 cm, which is roughly the depth a porous absorber would need to be maximally effective at this frequency — an immediately useful consequence.

questions.q: A show is line-checked at 8 degrees C and performed at 26 degrees C. Using c = 331.3 + 0.606 theta, by how many metres per second does the speed of sound increase between check and show?
questions.explain: 0.606 x (26 - 8) = 10.91 m/s, a change from 336.1 to 347.1 m/s, or 3.2%. On a 90 m delay tower the propagation time falls from 267.8 ms to 259.3 ms — 8.5 ms of drift, easily audible as smearing on transients. This is why touring system engineers re-time before doors.

questions.q: A point source outdoors produces 102 dB SPL at 2 m. Ignoring air absorption, what is the level at 25 m?
questions.explain: 20 log10(25/2) = 20 log10(12.5) = 21.94 dB of loss. 102 - 21.94 = 80.06 dB SPL. Counting doublings (2 to 4 to 8 to 16) gets you to 18 dB and then stalls, which is exactly why the logarithm is the reliable method.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true of sound propagation in air at ordinary levels.
options: Propagation speed is independent of amplitude
Low frequencies propagate more slowly than high frequencies
Propagation speed rises with temperature
Propagation speed rises with static air pressure at constant temperature
High frequencies are attenuated more than low frequencies over long distances
why: True. Air is linear at audio levels; nonlinear propagation only appears above roughly 150 dB SPL.
False. Air is essentially non-dispersive across the audio band; apparent bass delay comes from transducers and rooms, not from air.
True. c is approximately 331.3 + 0.606 theta, about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius.
False. Raising pressure raises both bulk modulus and density proportionally, so c is unchanged. Only temperature (and very slightly humidity and composition) matters.
True. Air absorption is strongly frequency-dependent, roughly 0.1 dB per 100 m at 125 Hz versus 8-10 dB per 100 m at 8 kHz at 50% relative humidity.
questions.explain: The recurring theme is that air is a simple, linear, non-dispersive medium whose only significant variable is temperature — plus a frequency-dependent absorption term that only matters over long distances.

questions.q: Place these wavelengths in order from longest to shortest.
items: 125 Hz
440 Hz
2 kHz
12 kHz
questions.explain: Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency, so the ordering by wavelength is simply the reverse of the ordering by frequency: 10.9 m, 2.74 m, 78 cm, 17.2 cm, 2.9 cm.

questions.q: Match each quantity to its unit.
pairs: Sound pressure
pascal (Pa)
Sound intensity
watt per square metre (W/m2)
Particle velocity
metre per second (m/s)
Specific acoustic impedance
rayl (Pa s/m)
Sound power
watt (W)
questions.explain: Keeping these units straight prevents the most common conceptual error in acoustics: treating pressure, intensity and power as interchangeable. They differ dimensionally, and that difference is exactly why some decibel formulas use 10 log and others use 20 log.

questions.q: A vocal microphone is placed 25 cm above a hard wooden desk, with the singer well in front. Where is the first cancellation notch?
options: Near 343 Hz
Near 686 Hz
Near 1,372 Hz
Near 172 Hz
why: Correct. f = c/4d = 343/(4 x 0.25) = 343 Hz. The reflected path is 50 cm longer, which equals half a wavelength at 343 Hz.
This would be the answer for d = 12.5 cm; it also corresponds to the extra path being a full wavelength, which produces reinforcement rather than cancellation.
This is the third null (odd multiple 3 would give 1,029 Hz) or a miscalculation using c/d.
This uses c/2d, which is the room-mode relation for a dimension of 25 cm, not the boundary-null relation.
questions.explain: The c/4d relation follows from requiring the extra path length 2d to equal half a wavelength. Nulls repeat at odd multiples (343, 1029, 1715 Hz) with peaks in between. The two safe strategies are flush-mounting (PZM) or getting far enough away that the reflection is weak and late.

questions.stem: You are consulting on an outdoor amphitheatre. The main hangs are 12 m above the stage. The nearest complaining residence is 900 m away across open ground. Rehearsals at 2 pm on a hot, still, sunny day generate no complaints; the same programme at 10 pm on a clear, calm night generates several. The measured level at front-of-house (30 m from the array) is identical on both occasions, and the programme material is identical.

qs.q: What is the most likely physical explanation?
options: Ambient noise is lower at night, so the same level is more noticeable
A nocturnal temperature inversion refracts sound rays downward toward the residence
Air absorption is greater during the day because warm air is drier
The system was driven harder at night without the operator noticing
why: Lower ambient masking is a genuine contributing factor and worth mentioning, but it cannot explain a difference of the size typically observed, and the question asks for the primary physical mechanism.

Correct. After sunset the ground cools by radiation faster than the air, so temperature rises with height. Sound travels faster higher up, wavefronts tilt, and rays that would have escaped upward are bent back to the ground — commonly worth 10-20 dB at distance.
Absorption does depend on humidity, but the dependence is not monotonic in the direction implied, and the effect at 900 m would not reverse between conditions by anything like the observed amount.
The stem explicitly holds front-of-house level and programme constant, which rules this out.
qs.explain: Refraction from vertical temperature and wind gradients is the dominant long-distance propagation variable outdoors. It is also the reason noise-impact predictions must specify meteorological conditions; ISO 9613-2 models downwind or moderate-inversion conditions precisely because they are the worst case.

qs.q: Ignoring refraction and air absorption, and treating the array as a point source, how many decibels lower should the level be at 900 m than at 30 m?
qs.explain: 20 log10(900/30) = 20 log10(30) = 29.54 dB. In practice a large array behaves as a line source in its near field and loses closer to 3 dB per doubling there, so the real figure is smaller — which is precisely why arrays project.

qs.q: Propose two mitigations, one acoustic and one operational, and state honestly what each cannot fix.
qs.model: Acoustic: steer or shade the array so that energy above the audience plane is minimised — mechanical downtilt of the lower boxes, reduced level on the long-throw cabinets, and cardioid subwoofer configurations to cut rear and far-field low-frequency radiation. This cannot fix low frequencies well, because the wavelengths are too long for practical directivity control at 40-60 Hz without very large arrays, and it is precisely the low frequencies that survive 900 m of air absorption. Operational: schedule the loudest material earlier in the evening, impose a curfew before the inversion strengthens, and instrument the site with a remote logging SPL meter at the property line tied to a level limit. This cannot fix the fact that the resident hears the show at all on a still night, and it trades artistic control for compliance. Both approaches should be paired with measurement under the actual complaint conditions rather than at 2 pm, since the daytime measurement is systematically optimistic.
points: Names a directivity or level-shading measure and connects it to the physics
Names an operational or scheduling measure
Acknowledges that low-frequency directivity control is hard because wavelengths are long
Notes that daytime measurements systematically under-predict night-time impact

questions.q: A colleague argues that because sound pressure falls as 1/r, moving a microphone from 30 cm to 60 cm from a guitar amplifier should cost exactly 6 dB. Explain, with reference to specific mechanisms, why the measured change will not be 6 dB.
questions.model: The 6 dB figure assumes a point source in a free field, and neither assumption holds. First, a 12-inch driver in a cabinet is not a point source at 30 cm: 30 cm is comparable to the radiating dimension, so the listener is in the near field where pressure does not follow 1/r and where the effective acoustic centre is ill-defined. Second, the room is not a free field: at 60 cm the reverberant and early-reflection contributions are a larger fraction of the total, which reduces the measured loss; the effect grows as one approaches the critical distance. Third, the change is frequency-dependent rather than broadband: high frequencies from the cone are strongly directional and fall faster off-axis as the mic distance and angle change, while low frequencies are more nearly omnidirectional and are additionally reinforced by floor and wall boundaries, so the tonal balance shifts as well as the level. Fourth, if the microphone is directional, the proximity effect gives it substantial low-frequency boost at 30 cm that largely disappears by 60 cm, so the measured broadband level change depends heavily on the spectral content of the source. A realistic expectation is 3-5 dB of broadband change with a noticeable loss of low end, not a clean 6 dB.
points: Identifies the point-source / near-field assumption failure
Identifies the free-field assumption failure and mentions the room or critical distance
Notes frequency dependence, directivity, or proximity effect
Gives a plausible quantitative expectation rather than only qualitative hedging

questions.q: Two identical loudspeakers reproduce the same mono signal, in phase, and you stand equidistant from both. Compared with one speaker alone, the level at your position is:
options: +3 dB, because power adds
+6 dB, because pressures add coherently
+3 dB at low frequencies and +6 dB at high frequencies
Unchanged, because the sources are identical
why: Power addition (+3 dB) applies to uncorrelated sources, such as two different instruments or two speakers fed decorrelated noise.
Correct. Identical, in-phase, equidistant sources sum in pressure: doubling pressure is 20 log(2) = 6.02 dB. This is a coherent sum.

The relationship is reversed in practice: coherent summation is easiest to maintain at low frequencies where the wavelength is long compared with any position error, and degrades at high frequencies where a few centimetres of path difference destroys the coherence.
Identical sources reinforce; they only cancel if one is polarity-inverted.
questions.explain: Coherent versus incoherent summation is the distinction that Module 4 develops in full. The practical corollary: the +6 dB figure holds only at points genuinely equidistant from both sources. Move off the centre line and you enter the comb-filter region.

questions.q: Why must a porous absorber be spaced away from a wall to work at low frequencies?
options: Because the air gap adds mass to the system
Because porous absorbers dissipate energy through particle velocity, which is zero at a rigid boundary and maximal a quarter wavelength away
Because the gap allows the panel to resonate at the target frequency
Because reflections from the wall would otherwise cancel the incoming wave inside the material
why: An air gap adds compliance, not mass; mass-spring behaviour is the mechanism of membrane and Helmholtz absorbers, not porous ones.

Correct. At a rigid boundary the wave reflects with pressure doubling and particle velocity going to zero. A porous absorber converts energy through viscous drag as air moves through the fibres, so it must sit where air is actually moving — ideally a quarter wavelength out, which for 100 Hz is 86 cm.
A porous absorber is deliberately non-resonant; resonance is the mechanism of tuned membrane and Helmholtz devices.
The interference pattern is real, but the reason it matters is the velocity distribution, not cancellation of the incoming wave.
questions.explain: This is why "more foam on the wall" fails at low frequencies while a thick, spaced, or fully-filled corner trap succeeds. It also explains the standard rule of thumb that a porous absorber becomes effective from roughly the frequency at which its total depth (material plus gap) equals a quarter wavelength.

modules.title: The Decibel
modules.tagline: One unit, many references. Why 10 log and 20 log are the same rule, and how to read dBSPL, dBu, dBV, dBFS and LUFS without ever confusing them.
objectives: Able to state the definition of the bel and derive both the 10 log and 20 log forms from it.
Able to convert fluently between voltage, power and level, and between dBu, dBV and volts.
Able to sum uncorrelated and correlated levels correctly and explain why decibels never add arithmetically.
Able to choose the appropriate reference and weighting for a stated purpose, including dBFS, dBTP and LUFS under ITU-R BS.1770.
Able to critique a level specification that omits its reference, its weighting or its time constant.

lessons.title: Why Logarithms: The Bel and Its Two Faces
glossary: Bel
The base-10 logarithm of a power ratio. Named after Alexander Graham Bell; introduced at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the 1920s to quantify transmission loss.
Decibel
One tenth of a bel. The tenth was chosen because a decibel is close to the smallest level change a listener reliably notices under ideal conditions.
Power quantity
A quantity proportional to energy flow: acoustic power, electrical power, intensity. Uses 10 log.
Field quantity
A quantity whose square is proportional to power: voltage, current, sound pressure. Uses 20 log.
Level
A logarithmic measure of a ratio relative to a stated reference. A level without a stated reference is meaningless.

blocks.html: The decibel is not a unit of loudness, and it is not a unit at all in the ordinary sense. It is a dimensionless logarithmic ratio. The bel was defined at Bell Labs to express transmission loss on telephone lines, where a 100 km run might attenuate a signal by a factor of ten thousand and engineers were tired of writing that down. Because the quantity being compared was power, the definition was fixed on power from the start, and every apparent complication in the decibel follows from that single fact.

blocks.label: The definition, and the two forms that follow
blocks.caption: The second is not a separate rule. Because power is proportional to amplitude squared, 10 log(A squared) = 20 log(A). There is one decibel, not two.

blocks.html: This is the point at which most self-taught engineers acquire a permanent confusion, so it is worth being very explicit. If you double the voltage across a fixed load, the power quadruples. Expressed as a level, the power went up by 10 log(4) = 6.02 dB, and the voltage went up by 20 log(2) = 6.02 dB. Both calculations give the same answer, because they describe the same physical event. The 20 in the second formula exists precisely so that the two agree.

blocks.caption: Both curves are correct simultaneously. Which one you use depends only on whether the ratio you are given is a ratio of powers or a ratio of amplitudes.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 2
items: Master Handbook of Acoustics (6th ed.) — F. Alton Everest & Ken Pohlmann
Required. Chapter 2, "Sound Levels and the Decibel", in full, including the worked examples. This is the clearest treatment of reference levels in print.
Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science (3rd ed.) — Bob Katz

Required. Chapters 1-2 and Chapter 14 on metering and the K-System. Read Katz for the argument about why loudness normalisation should have ended the loudness war, and note that he wrote it before streaming normalisation existed.
ITU-R BS.1770-5, "Algorithms to measure audio programme loudness and true-peak audio level"

Required. Read the K-weighting filter definition and the gating description in Annex 1. It is short, it is free from the ITU, and it is the single most consequential audio standard of the last twenty years.
EBU R 128, "Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals"
Required. Four pages. Note the -23 LUFS target, the +/-0.5 LU tolerance, and the -1 dBTP ceiling, and contrast with the streaming targets discussed in the lesson.
IEC 61672-1, "Electroacoustics — Sound level meters"
Optional. Skim the definitions of frequency weightings A, C and Z and time weightings F, S and I so that you can read a specification sheet critically.

blocks.text: The numbers worth knowing cold

head: Change
Power ratio
Amplitude ratio
Perceptual note
rows: About the smallest broadband change detectable in an A/B test on programme material.
Doubling power. Adding a second identical uncorrelated source.
Doubling voltage or pressure. Also one bit of digital resolution.
Widely quoted as "twice as loud"; the true figure varies with level and spectrum.
Ten times the pressure. The span from a whisper to a conversation.
Half power. The conventional definition of a filter corner frequency.
Roughly a typical microphone preamplifier gain setting for a quiet source.

blocks.label: Mental arithmetic that actually works
blocks.html: Memorise three anchors and add them: 3 dB = x2 power, 6 dB = x2 amplitude, 10 dB = x10 power / 20 dB = x10 amplitude. Then 26 dB of voltage gain is 20 + 6, i.e. x10 then x2, i.e. x20. And 15 dB of power is 10 + 3 + ... roughly x10 x2 x1.26 = x31.6. This gets you within a few percent without a calculator, which is enough for every field decision you will ever make.

Think of decibels as an exchange rate between multiplication and addition. Every gain stage in a signal chain multiplies. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, so a chain of gains becomes a column of numbers you can total in your head. That is the entire reason the profession uses them, and it is also why a gain-staging error compounds: you are adding in a domain where the underlying quantity is multiplying.

blocks.text: Adding levels: the rule people get wrong

blocks.html: You cannot add decibels arithmetically because they are logarithms. To combine uncorrelated sources you must convert back to power, add, and convert forward again.

blocks.label: Combining n uncorrelated levels
blocks.caption: Two sources at 85 dB give 88.01 dB, not 170. Ten sources at 85 dB give 95 dB. A hundred give 105 dB. Crowd noise is exactly this calculation.

head: Difference between two levels
Add this to the higher level

blocks.html: That last row is the practically important one. If your air-conditioning contributes 40 dB and your programme is at 65 dB, the HVAC is adding 0.01 dB to the total — irrelevant to the sum, and yet devastating to a quiet recording, because what matters there is not the sum but the signal-to-noise ratio. Decibel arithmetic tells you the total; it does not tell you what you can hear. That distinction returns in Module 3 as masking.

blocks.q: An amplifier is changed from 50 W to 200 W into the same loudspeaker. How much louder, in dB, at the same distance?
options: +3 dB
+6 dB
+12 dB
+4 dB
blocks.explain: 200/50 = 4, a power ratio, so 10 log(4) = 6.02 dB. The tempting +12 dB comes from wrongly applying the 20 log formula to a power ratio. Six decibels for four times the amplifier is the classic argument for buying more sensitive loudspeakers rather than bigger amplifiers.

blocks.html: An opinion: the claim that "+10 dB is twice as loud" is repeated far too confidently. It comes from Stevens' sone scale work of the 1930s using 1 kHz tones at moderate levels. For broadband programme material at typical monitoring levels the doubling figure is often nearer 6-8 dB, and for low-frequency-heavy material it can be smaller still. Use +10 dB as a rough teaching device, but never as the basis for a specification.

lessons.title: References: dB SPL, dBu, dBV, dBm and dBFS
glossary: dB SPL
Sound pressure level referenced to 20 micropascals RMS.
dBu
Voltage level referenced to 0.7746 V RMS, the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 ohms.
dBV
Voltage level referenced to 1 V RMS. 0 dBV = +2.21 dBu.
dBm
Power level referenced to 1 milliwatt. Requires a stated impedance to be meaningful.
dBFS
Digital level referenced to full scale, the largest representable sample value. All real digital audio levels are negative.
dBTP
True-peak level: the peak of the reconstructed continuous waveform, estimated by oversampling, as defined in ITU-R BS.1770.

blocks.html: A decibel figure with no stated reference tells you a change, not a level. "Turn it up 3 dB" is complete. "The level is 3 dB" is not. The suffix after dB names the reference, and the reference is the whole content of the statement. What follows are the six references you will meet daily, together with what each one is actually good for.

items.label: dB SPL (20 µPa)
items.html: Acoustic. Reference chosen in the 1930s as the approximate threshold of hearing for a 1 kHz tone. Always state the weighting and time constant: 94 dB SPL is incomplete; 94 dB SPL, A-weighted, slow is a measurement. The 94 dB figure is special because it corresponds to exactly 1 Pa, which is why calibrators produce it.

items.label: dBu (0.7746 V)
items.html: Electrical, voltage. The reference is the voltage that would dissipate 1 mW into 600 ohms — a legacy of telephone line matching that has been irrelevant since the 1970s but survives in the number. Professional nominal operating level is +4 dBu = 1.228 V RMS.

items.label: dBV (1 V)
items.html: Electrical, voltage, with a sane reference. Consumer nominal level is -10 dBV = 0.316 V RMS. The gap between pro and consumer nominal levels is therefore 11.79 dB, not 14 dB, which is a very common error.

items.label: dBm (1 mW)
items.html: Electrical, power. Only meaningful with a stated load impedance. In modern audio, where outputs are low-impedance and inputs are high-impedance (voltage bridging), almost nobody transfers a defined power, so dBm is nearly always the wrong unit. It persists on old test equipment and in RF.

items.label: dBFS (full scale)
items.html: Digital. 0 dBFS is the largest number the word length can represent. There is no headroom above it — clipping is not soft, it is arithmetic. AES17 defines 0 dBFS as the RMS of a full-scale sine, which means a full-scale square wave measures +3.01 dBFS RMS. Read the fine print on your meter.

items.label: LUFS / LKFS
items.html: Perceptual. Loudness units relative to full scale, per ITU-R BS.1770: K-weighted, channel-weighted, mean-square, with a two-stage gate. 1 LU = 1 dB by construction. This is the only one of the six that attempts to model hearing.

blocks.label: Voltage to level and back
blocks.caption: 0.7746 V is the square root of 0.001 W times 600 ohms. The 2.21 dB offset between the scales is 20 log(0.7746).
