blocks.caption: The dB SPL scale with landmarks. The bottom of the scale is a physiological reference and the top is a mechanical damage threshold; the entire useful working range of audio sits between them.

blocks.text: Alignment: the bridge between analogue and digital

blocks.html: Because dBFS has a hard ceiling and dBu does not, every studio has to decide what analogue voltage corresponds to which digital number. This is alignment, and it is not standardised worldwide. The EBU (R 68) aligns 0 dBu to -18 dBFS, giving 18 dB of digital headroom above nominal. SMPTE RP 155 in North America aligns +4 dBu to -20 dBFS. Film post frequently uses -20 dBFS as well; some broadcast facilities use -24. If you have ever plugged a machine from one facility into another and found everything 2 to 6 dB off, this is why.

blocks.label: dBFS is not comparable across meters
blocks.html: AES17 defines full scale by the RMS value of a full-scale sinusoid. Under that definition a full-scale square wave reads +3.01 dBFS RMS, which looks like an error and is not. Meanwhile many DAW meters read sample peak, some read true peak, and some read an RMS with an undocumented window length. Two meters reading the same file can legitimately differ by 4 dB or more. Always know which convention your meter uses before you make a decision based on it.

blocks.q: A console output is set to +4 dBu. What is the RMS voltage?
blocks.explain: 0.7746 x 10^(4/20) = 0.7746 x 1.5849 = 1.228 V RMS. 0.775 V is 0 dBu, and 1.55 V would be +6 dBu. This voltage matters because it sets how much gain a preamp or converter needs to reach full scale.

blocks.html: One further trap: microphone sensitivity is usually specified in mV/Pa or in dBV re 1 V/Pa, and the two look confusingly similar. A Neumann U 87 Ai is quoted at 28 mV/Pa, which is 20 log(0.028) = -31 dBV/Pa. A Shure SM57 is 1.6 mV/Pa, or -56 dBV/Pa. That 25 dB difference is why the SM57 needs so much more preamp gain and why preamp noise performance matters far more with dynamic microphones than with capacitors.

blocks.title: Tracing a signal from air to file
steps: Acoustic level
A loud snare at 30 cm reaches roughly 130 dB SPL peak. 130 dB SPL is 20 log(p/20 µPa) = 130, so p = 63 Pa.
Microphone output
At 1.6 mV/Pa an SM57 produces 63 x 1.6 mV = 101 mV peak, or about -20 dBV peak.
Preamp gain
To reach -12 dBFS peak in a system aligned at +4 dBu = -20 dBFS, you need the peak at +12 dBu = 3.08 V. From 0.101 V that is 20 log(3.08/0.101) = 29.7 dB of gain.
Converter input
The converter maps its own full-scale input voltage to 0 dBFS. Check the spec: many are +18 to +24 dBu at full scale.
Digital word
At -12 dBFS peak in 24-bit, you are using about 22 bits of the available word. There is no benefit to pushing closer to 0 dBFS.
Metering
Confirm with a true-peak meter, not a sample-peak meter, if the file will ever be lossy-encoded.

lessons.title: Meters: Peak, RMS, VU, PPM, True Peak and LUFS
glossary: VU meter
A 1939-era average-responding meter with a 300 ms integration time, calibrated so that 0 VU corresponds to +4 dBu in professional use.
PPM
Peak programme meter. Fast attack (a few ms) and slow decay, standardised in several national variants (BBC, EBU, DIN, Nordic).
True peak
The maximum of the analogue waveform reconstructed from samples, which can exceed the maximum sample value. Estimated by 4x or higher oversampling.
LUFS
Loudness units relative to full scale, per ITU-R BS.1770. Identical in scale to LKFS.
Gating
The BS.1770 mechanism that excludes silence and quiet passages from the integrated loudness measurement, using an absolute gate at -70 LUFS and a relative gate 10 LU below the ungated mean.
Loudness range (LRA)
A statistical measure of the distribution of short-term loudness in a programme, in LU, defined in EBU Tech 3342.

blocks.html: A meter answers exactly one question, and different meters answer different questions. The mistake is not choosing the wrong meter; it is failing to notice that you asked a question the meter cannot answer. Peak meters answer "will this clip?". RMS meters answer "how much power is here?". Loudness meters answer "how loud will this seem?". No single number does all three.

blocks.caption: The same passage read four ways. The vertical gap between the peak line and the RMS line is the crest factor, and the gap between RMS and LUFS is mostly the K-weighting acting on the spectral balance.

head: Meter
What it integrates
Answers
Fails at
rows: Inter-sample peaks; says nothing about loudness.
Will the D/A or codec clip?
Still says nothing about loudness; costs CPU.
Misses transients by 10-20 dB; frequency response is flat and therefore not perceptual.
Different national variants have different scales and reference points.
Window length is often undocumented; not frequency weighted.
How loud does this section feel?
Hides dynamics entirely; pair it with LRA.

blocks.text: K-weighting and why BS.1770 works

blocks.html: ITU-R BS.1770 does something modest and effective. It applies a two-stage filter: a high-shelf approximating the acoustic effect of the head (roughly +4 dB above 2 kHz) and a high-pass at about 38 Hz to discount inaudible rumble. It then takes the mean square of each channel, applies channel weights (centre and left/right at 1.0, surrounds at 1.41, LFE excluded), sums, and takes 10 log. Finally it gates: anything below -70 LUFS absolute is discarded, then anything more than 10 LU below the resulting mean is discarded, and the measurement is recomputed.

blocks.label: BS.1770 loudness of a multichannel programme
blocks.caption: z-sub-i is the mean square of the K-weighted channel i; G-sub-i is the channel weight. The -0.691 offset calibrates a full-scale 997 Hz sine on the front-left-and-right pair to read 0 LUFS.

blocks.html: The genius of the gate is that it makes the measurement robust to silence. Without it, a film with three minutes of quiet before the titles would measure quieter than the same film without the silence, which would be absurd. With it, integrated loudness measures the loudness of the programme, not of the file duration. The relative gate at -10 LU was chosen empirically in the EBU PLOUD group's listening tests and is the reason R 128 measurements agree with listeners far better than the earlier peak-normalised practice.

head: Platform / standard
Target
Peak ceiling
Notes
rows: Basis of the US CALM Act.
Louder masters are turned down, not up.
Only attenuates; does not amplify quiet content.
Uses a dialogue-gated variant, not plain BS.1770.

blocks.label: Why -1 dBTP, not 0
blocks.html: Sample values below full scale can still reconstruct to a waveform peak above full scale — inter-sample peaks. Lossy codecs (AAC, MP3, Opus) make this worse because the decoded waveform is not sample-identical to the original and routinely overshoots by 1-2 dB. A master that sample-peaks at -0.1 dBFS can clip audibly after AAC encoding. The 1 dB ceiling is cheap insurance; for heavily limited material 1.5 to 2 dB is safer.

blocks.q: Two masters of the same song measure -8 LUFS and -14 LUFS integrated. Played back on a loudness-normalising service, which sounds louder?
options: The -8 LUFS master, because it is louder
Neither; they will play back at the same loudness, and the -8 master will have less dynamic range
The -14 LUFS master, because it will be turned up
It depends on the true-peak levels
blocks.explain: Normalisation applies a gain offset so that both hit the platform target. The louder master is attenuated by 6 dB more, arriving at the same loudness with its transients already destroyed by the limiting that made it loud. This is the argument that ended the loudness war on streaming; note that it does not apply to media without normalisation, such as a club PA or a DJ file.

blocks.html: The genuine disagreement: mastering engineers still argue about whether loudness normalisation has actually settled anything. One camp (Katz, Ian Shepherd) holds that the maths is decisive: since loudness is normalised at playback, clipping for loudness is now pure loss. The other camp points out that a large fraction of listening happens on systems with normalisation disabled or absent (car radio, club, DJ software, TikTok re-encodes), that heavily limited masters can survive small-speaker playback better, and that artists judge references by ear against other loud records. The evidence that would settle it is a large-scale controlled study of real playback chains with normalisation state logged, and it has not been done. My own view, marked as opinion: master for the medium you actually care about, deliver at a sane -1 dBTP ceiling, and stop treating an integrated LUFS number as an artistic target.

lessons.title: Weighting, Time Constants and Reading a Specification Critically
glossary: A-weighting
A frequency weighting loosely based on the inverted 40-phon equal-loudness contour, standardised in IEC 61672. Heavily discounts low frequencies.
C-weighting
A near-flat weighting with gentle roll-off below 30 Hz and above 8 kHz, intended for high levels and for peak measurements.
Z-weighting
Zero weighting: flat from 10 Hz to 20 kHz. What you want when you are characterising a system rather than a hazard.
Exchange rate
The number of decibels that halves the permitted exposure time. NIOSH and the EU use 3 dB; US OSHA uses 5 dB.
Leq
Equivalent continuous sound level: the steady level with the same energy as the varying signal over the measurement period.

blocks.html: The number on a sound level meter is the product of three choices: the reference (20 µPa), the frequency weighting, and the time weighting. Change either of the latter two and the number changes, sometimes by 20 dB or more, without anything physical having changed at all. A specification that omits them is not a measurement; it is a rumour.

head: Weighting
Response at 31.5 Hz
at 1 kHz
at 8 kHz
Proper use
rows: Occupational noise exposure, environmental noise limits.
Peak measurements, high-level assessment, subwoofer content.
System measurement, room analysis, anything scientific.

blocks.html: A-weighting is used far outside its original justification. It was derived from the 40-phon contour — the shape of hearing at a quiet level — and then applied to concert and industrial levels at 100 dB and above, where the ear's frequency response is much flatter. The consequence is systematic: a dance venue measured A-weighted can read 100 dBA while a C-weighted reading is 110 dBC, and the 10 dB difference is entirely the low-frequency energy that A-weighting throws away and that your cochlea does not. Many modern noise regulations therefore specify both, or specify a maximum LAeq together with a maximum C-minus-A difference.

blocks.label: Equivalent continuous level (Leq)
blocks.caption: Leq is an energy average, so a few loud moments dominate it. Ten minutes at 105 dB contributes more to an 8-hour Leq than seven hours at 80 dB.

blocks.text: Time weighting

items: Fast (F) — 125 ms time constant. The default on most meters. Tracks syllables and beats but still under-reads true transients.
Slow (S) — 1 s. Used for environmental noise and for stable readings; smooths out programme dynamics almost completely.
Impulse (I) — 35 ms attack, 1.5 s decay. Largely deprecated; it was intended for impulsive industrial noise and tends to overstate.
Peak — no averaging at all, typically C-weighted. This is the number that matters for acute mechanical damage from gunfire or a dropped microphone stand.

blocks.label: A specification that means nothing
blocks.html: A loudspeaker rated "126 dB max SPL" is unfalsifiable without: the distance (1 m? 4 m?), the drive signal (sine? pink noise? music with what crest factor?), the bandwidth, whether it is peak or continuous, whether it is measured or calculated from sensitivity plus power handling, and the permitted distortion. Manufacturers exploit every one of these. AES2-2012 defines an honest power-handling test; comparatively few consumer specifications follow it.

blocks.text: Exposure, and the arithmetic of hearing damage

blocks.html: Noise-induced hearing loss is a dose problem: level times time. The NIOSH criterion, which is the one supported by the underlying physiology, permits 85 dBA for 8 hours and halves the permitted time for every 3 dB increase, because 3 dB is a doubling of energy. US OSHA's legally enforceable standard uses a 5 dB exchange rate, which is more permissive and is not defensible on energy grounds; it survives for historical and economic reasons. The EU Physical Agents (Noise) Directive 2003/10/EC uses 3 dB, with action values at 80 and 85 dBA and a hard limit of 87 dBA at the ear.

head: Level (dBA)
NIOSH permitted daily exposure (3 dB rule)
OSHA (5 dB rule)

blocks.html: Read the 100 dBA row again. Fifteen minutes. A typical club night runs four hours at that level or above, and a monitor engineer stands in wedge spill all evening. Hearing loss in this profession is not bad luck; it is an entirely predictable consequence of an exposure calculation that most people never perform. Do the calculation once for your own working week and then decide about protection.

blocks.q: A mix engineer works at 92 dBA for 3 hours. Using the NIOSH 3 dB exchange rate (85 dBA for 8 h), what fraction of the daily allowance is used?
options: About 37%
About 100%
About 190%
About 75%
blocks.explain: The permitted time at 92 dBA is 8 h divided by 2^((92-85)/3) = 8 / 2^2.333 = 8 / 5.04 = 1.59 hours, i.e. about 95 minutes. Three hours is 3/1.59 = 1.89, or roughly 190% of the daily dose. The engineer has exceeded the criterion before lunch.

blocks.title: Assignment 2 — A level audit of your own signal chain and your own ears
blocks.brief: Produce a two-part technical note. Part A: trace a real signal through your chain, from acoustic source to stored file, giving a level in the correct unit at every stage — dB SPL at the microphone, mV or dBV at its output, dBu after the preamp, dBFS at the converter, and the file's integrated LUFS and true peak. State your interface's full-scale input in dBu (from its manual) and use it. Show all arithmetic. Part B: measure your monitoring level with a calibrated meter or a calibrated phone app at your listening position while playing typical programme, record LAeq and LCeq over five minutes, compute your daily dose against the NIOSH criterion for a realistic working day, and state what you will change.
items: A strong result uses the correct formula at each conversion and never applies 20 log to a power ratio or 10 log to a voltage ratio.
A strong result quotes the interface's actual full-scale input voltage from documentation rather than assuming +4 dBu = -18 dBFS.
A strong result reports both A- and C-weighted levels and comments on the difference as an indicator of low-frequency content.
A strong result computes exposure with the 3 dB exchange rate, states the permitted time explicitly, and gives the dose as a percentage.
A strong result names at least one measurement it does not trust and says why (meter calibration, app accuracy, microphone position).
A weak result reports "about -18 dB" style figures without references, or asserts a monitoring level without measuring it.

questions.q: Why does the decibel use 20 log for voltage and 10 log for power?
options: Because voltage is twice as important perceptually as power
Because power is proportional to the square of voltage, and log of a square is twice the log
Because the two scales have different references
Because voltage is a vector quantity and power is a scalar
why: Perceptual importance has nothing to do with it; the decibel is a mathematical definition predating any perceptual calibration.
Correct. P is proportional to V squared, so 10 log(V squared / V0 squared) = 20 log(V/V0). The two forms are algebraically identical statements about the same physical change.
References are a separate matter entirely; the factor of two appears even when comparing two quantities with the same reference.
Voltage is not a vector in this sense, and the scalar/vector distinction does not enter the definition.
questions.explain: There is one decibel, defined on power. The 20 log form is a derived convenience for field quantities whose square is proportional to power: voltage, current, sound pressure, particle velocity.

questions.q: A microphone preamp raises a signal from 2 mV to 250 mV RMS. What is the gain in dB?
questions.explain: 20 log10(250/2) = 20 log10(125) = 20 x 2.0969 = 41.94 dB. Using 10 log would give 20.97 dB, which is the classic error. A useful check: x125 is about x100 (40 dB) times x1.25 (about 2 dB).

questions.q: Three uncorrelated noise sources measure 74, 78 and 80 dB SPL individually. What is the total level with all three running?
questions.hint: Convert to power, sum, convert back.
questions.explain: 10^7.4 + 10^7.8 + 10^8.0 = 2.512e7 + 6.310e7 + 1.000e8 = 1.882e8. 10 log10(1.882e8) = 82.75 dB. Note how little the 74 dB source contributes: removing it entirely would drop the total by only 0.25 dB. Fixing the loudest source first is not a slogan, it is arithmetic.

questions.q: What RMS voltage corresponds to -10 dBV?
questions.explain: 1 V x 10^(-10/20) = 10^-0.5 = 0.3162 V RMS. Expressed in dBu that is -7.78 dBu, so the gap between consumer -10 dBV and professional +4 dBu nominal is 11.78 dB, not the 14 dB that is often repeated.

questions.q: A calibrator produces exactly 1 pascal RMS at the microphone diaphragm. What is that in dB SPL?
questions.explain: 20 log10(1 / 20e-6) = 20 log10(50,000) = 93.98 dB SPL. This is why acoustic calibrators are labelled 94 dB, and why 114 dB (10 Pa) is the other common calibration point.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about dBFS.
options: 0 dBFS is the largest value representable in the word length
A signal can legitimately exceed 0 dBFS in the analogue domain after reconstruction
Under AES17 a full-scale square wave measures +3.01 dBFS RMS
dBFS has a fixed relationship to dBu defined by international standard
Sample-peak and true-peak meters can differ by more than 1 dB on the same file
why: True by definition; 0 dBFS is the ceiling imposed by the number of bits.
True. Inter-sample peaks in the reconstructed waveform can exceed the largest sample value, which is exactly why dBTP exists.
True. AES17 anchors 0 dBFS to the RMS of a full-scale sine, so a square wave of the same peak has 3.01 dB more RMS.
False. Alignment between analogue and digital levels is a facility or regional convention (EBU R 68, SMPTE RP 155), not a single global standard.
True. Heavily limited material routinely shows 1-2 dB of inter-sample overshoot invisible to a sample-peak meter.
questions.explain: The unifying idea is that dBFS describes the numbers in the file, not the waveform they will become. Everything downstream — reconstruction filters, lossy codecs, sample-rate conversion — can produce a waveform that exceeds what the samples suggest.

questions.q: Match each decibel suffix to its reference quantity.
pairs: dB SPL
20 micropascals
dBu
0.7746 volts RMS
dBV
1 volt RMS
dBm
1 milliwatt
dBFS
digital full scale
LUFS
K-weighted full scale per ITU-R BS.1770
questions.explain: Every one of these is a level, meaning a logarithm of a ratio against a stated reference. Learning the six references is most of what it takes to read a spec sheet without being misled.

questions.q: Order these from the shortest to the longest integration window.
items: Sample peak (instantaneous)
PPM (10 ms)
Fast time weighting (125 ms)
LUFS momentary (400 ms)
Slow time weighting (1 s)
LUFS short-term (3 s)
LUFS integrated (whole programme, gated)
questions.explain: Integration time determines what a meter can see. Anything slower than about 10 ms will systematically under-read transients, which is why a VU meter can sit at 0 while a snare drum is clipping the converter 15 dB above it.

questions.stem: A client delivers a master that sample-peaks at -0.2 dBFS and measures -7.4 LUFS integrated, with a loudness range of 3 LU. They complain that on Spotify it "sounds smaller and duller" than a competing record that measures -11 LUFS with an LRA of 7 LU. Both files are 44.1 kHz, 24-bit, and both were made from the same mixes.

qs.q: What is the primary reason the client's master sounds smaller on the service?
options: Spotify applies a low-pass filter to loud material
Normalisation attenuates the louder master by more, so both play at the same loudness but the client's has already had its dynamics removed
The 24-bit file is being truncated to 16-bit
The loudness range measurement is unreliable below 5 LU
why: No such filter exists; the encoder is not level-dependent in that way.
Correct. Normalisation to roughly -14 LUFS attenuates the -7.4 LUFS master by about 6.6 dB and the -11 LUFS master by about 3 dB. Both arrive at the same loudness, but only one still has transients.
Bit depth reduction to 16 bits with dither is inaudible here and is not level-dependent.
LRA is perfectly well defined at 3 LU; a small LRA is a symptom, not a measurement fault.
qs.explain: This is the central practical consequence of loudness normalisation: loudness is given away for free at playback, so anything you destroyed to obtain it is a pure loss. The audible difference the client hears is crest factor, not level.

qs.q: If the service normalises to -14 LUFS, how many decibels of gain will be applied to the client's -7.4 LUFS master?
qs.explain: -14 - (-7.4) = -6.6 dB, i.e. 6.6 dB of attenuation. LU and dB are the same size by construction, so loudness offsets are simple subtraction.

qs.q: The client's file sample-peaks at -0.2 dBFS. What additional risk does this create?
options: None, since it is below 0 dBFS
Inter-sample peaks after lossy encoding may exceed full scale and clip in the decoder or D/A
The file will fail to import into most DAWs
It will cause aliasing on playback
why: Being below 0 dBFS in sample terms does not guarantee the reconstructed waveform stays below full scale.
Correct. Ogg Vorbis or AAC encoding of heavily limited material routinely overshoots by 1-2 dB true peak; the standard mitigation is a -1 dBTP delivery ceiling.
Import is unaffected by level.
Aliasing is a sampling phenomenon and is unrelated to peak level in a correctly implemented chain.
qs.explain: True-peak headroom and loudness are independent decisions. Even a quiet master should respect a true-peak ceiling if it will be transcoded, and a loud one certainly must.

questions.q: A venue is measured at 99 dBA and 110 dBC at the mix position. What does the 11 dB difference tell you?
options: The meter is faulty, since C-weighting should read lower
There is substantial low-frequency energy that A-weighting is discounting
The measurement was taken with the wrong time constant
The system is distorting
why: C-weighting reads higher than A whenever significant energy exists below about 500 Hz; the two are equal only for high-frequency-dominated content.
Correct. A-weighting rolls off 39 dB at 31.5 Hz and 16 dB at 125 Hz; a large C-minus-A difference is the standard indicator of bass-heavy content, which is why many noise conditions now specify both.
Time weighting affects both readings similarly and cannot create an 11 dB spectral difference.
Distortion would add high-frequency energy and, if anything, narrow the gap.
questions.explain: The C-minus-A difference is a cheap, robust spectral diagnostic. Values above about 10 dB indicate that A-weighted limits are badly under-representing what the audience and the neighbours are actually experiencing.

questions.q: A colleague says: "I always record with peaks hitting -0.5 dBFS so I use all 24 bits and get the best signal-to-noise ratio." Evaluate this claim rigorously.
questions.model: The claim confuses the analogue and digital noise floors. In a 24-bit system the theoretical dynamic range is about 144 dB, but no converter achieves it: the best commercial converters manage roughly 120-125 dB A-weighted, limited by analogue circuitry, and the microphone plus preamp plus room noise floor is typically far higher still — a quiet studio at 20 dB SPL with a microphone whose self-noise is 12 dBA sets the real floor. Recording peaks at -18 dBFS instead of -0.5 dBFS therefore costs nothing audible: the noise you hear is acoustic and analogue, not quantisation. Meanwhile the practice is actively risky. It removes all headroom for an unexpected transient, so a single louder take clips irrecoverably. It pushes the converter's analogue input stage toward its distortion limit, where THD rises well before hard clipping. It creates true-peak overshoots that will clip downstream reconstruction and codecs. And it leaves no room for the level increases that summing many tracks and adding plug-in gain inevitably produce, forcing corrective attenuation later. The defensible practice is to align nominal levels around -18 to -20 dBFS RMS with peaks around -10 dBFS, matching the analogue alignment standards, and to reserve 0 dBFS discipline for the mastering stage where a true-peak ceiling is set deliberately.
points: Distinguishes theoretical 24-bit dynamic range from real converter and analogue noise floors
Notes that the dominant noise source is acoustic/analogue, so extra digital level buys nothing audible
Identifies headroom loss and clipping risk on unexpected transients
Mentions gain accumulation through summing and plug-ins, or true-peak/codec risk
Recommends a specific, defensible alignment such as -18 dBFS nominal

questions.q: Using the NIOSH 3 dB exchange rate with 85 dBA permitted for 8 hours, what is the permitted daily exposure time at 100 dBA, in minutes?
questions.explain: 8 hours / 2^((100-85)/3) = 8 / 2^5 = 8/32 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes. Under the more permissive OSHA 5 dB rule the same level allows 2 hours, which is a policy choice rather than a physiological one.

questions.q: Which meter reading is the correct basis for deciding whether a master will clip a consumer D/A converter?
options: Integrated LUFS
Sample peak in dBFS
True peak in dBTP
RMS over a 300 ms window
why: Integrated loudness says nothing about instantaneous level; a quiet-measuring file can still clip.
Sample peak misses inter-sample overshoots entirely and is systematically optimistic on limited material.
Correct. dBTP estimates the peak of the reconstructed continuous waveform by oversampling, which is what the converter will actually produce.
A 300 ms RMS window averages away the very transients that cause clipping.
questions.explain: Each meter answers one question. "Will it clip?" is a true-peak question; "how loud is it?" is a LUFS question; "how much power?" is an RMS question. Confusing them is the most common metering error in delivery.

modules.title: The Human Hearing System
modules.tagline: Equal-loudness contours, critical bands, masking and damage — the transfer function you are actually mixing through.
objectives: Able to trace the path of acoustic energy from pinna to auditory nerve and name what each stage contributes.
Able to read ISO 226 equal-loudness contours and predict how a mix will change with monitoring level.
Able to explain critical bands and use masking, both simultaneous and temporal, to diagnose a crowded mix.
Able to compute noise dose and argue for a specific hearing-protection strategy from the physiology.
Able to state honestly where psychoacoustic generalisations break down for individual listeners.

lessons.title: From Pinna to Hair Cell
glossary: Pinna
The external ear. Its folds impose direction-dependent spectral notches that the brain uses for elevation judgements.
Ossicles
Malleus, incus and stapes. A lever system providing roughly 30 dB of impedance matching between air and cochlear fluid.
Basilar membrane
The tapered membrane inside the cochlea whose stiffness gradient produces the tonotopic frequency map.
Inner hair cells
About 3,500 cells that transduce membrane motion into neural firing. They are the actual sensors.
Outer hair cells
About 12,000 cells that actively amplify low-level motion by up to 50 dB. Their loss is the main cause of sensorineural hearing loss.
Acoustic reflex
A protective contraction of the stapedius muscle, giving 10-20 dB of low-frequency attenuation with a 50-150 ms latency.

blocks.html: Your ear is not a microphone. A microphone converts pressure to voltage with a response that is, ideally, flat and linear. The ear performs a real-time frequency analysis on a mechanically tuned membrane, actively amplifies quiet signals by up to 50 dB using motile cells, compresses a 120 dB dynamic range into a neural code with a far smaller range, and hands the result to a brain that has strong priors about what it expects to hear. Every "psychoacoustic" phenomenon in this module falls out of one of those four facts.

blocks.title: The signal path
steps: Pinna and concha

Direction-dependent filtering. The concha resonance sits near 5 kHz and the pinna imposes a notch that sweeps from about 6 to 10 kHz with elevation. This is the physical basis of the head-related transfer function and of the entire binaural-rendering industry.
Ear canal

A tube about 25 mm long, closed at one end, resonating near a quarter wavelength: 343/(4 x 0.025) = 3.4 kHz. This resonance gives 10-15 dB of gain around 2.5-4 kHz and is why that region is both the most sensitive and the most easily damaged.
Tympanic membrane and ossicles

Impedance matching. Air is a light, compliant medium; cochlear fluid is heavy and stiff. Without the ossicular lever and the 17:1 area ratio between eardrum and stapes footplate, about 98% of incident energy would reflect.
Cochlea
A 35 mm coiled tube, tapering in stiffness by a factor of about 10,000 from base to apex. A travelling wave peaks at a place determined by frequency: high at the base, low at the apex.
Outer hair cells

Active amplification. They contract in time with the wave via the protein prestin, sharpening the mechanical tuning and boosting low-level responses. This is why hearing is nonlinear and why loudness does not scale simply with level.
Inner hair cells and auditory nerve
Transduction. Stereocilia deflection opens ion channels; nerve fibres fire in phase-locked fashion up to about 4-5 kHz, above which only firing rate carries information.
Brainstem and cortex
Binaural comparison in the superior olivary complex (interaural time and level differences), then pattern recognition. Much of what you call "hearing" happens here, which is why it is trainable.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 3
items: An Introduction to the Psychology of Hearing (6th ed.) — Brian C. J. Moore
Required. Chapters 1-3 (the ear, frequency selectivity, masking) and Chapter 4 (loudness). This is the standard graduate text and it is worth owning.
Fletcher, H. & Munson, W. A., "Loudness, Its Definition, Measurement and Calculation", JASA 5(2), 1933, pp. 82-108
Required. Read the method section and look at the original curves. Then note where ISO 226:2003 disagrees with them and ask why the 1933 data were wrong at low frequencies.
ISO 226:2023, Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours

Required as reference. You are not expected to read it end to end; know the contour shapes, the definition of the phon, and that the 2003 revision moved the low-frequency curves by up to 10-15 dB from the 1933 data.
Sound Reproduction (3rd ed.) — Floyd E. Toole
Required. Chapters 3, 4 and 12 on perception, adaptation and listener training. Toole is the best available argument that trained listening is a real, measurable skill and not mysticism.
NIOSH Publication 98-126, "Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Noise Exposure"
Required. Read the summary and the exchange-rate justification in Chapter 3. It is free from the CDC and it is the document that settles the 3 dB versus 5 dB argument on evidence.
Zwicker, E. & Fastl, H., Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models (3rd ed.)
Optional, for the quantitative treatment of critical bands, loudness summation and roughness. Consult Chapter 6 for the Bark scale.

blocks.text: The dynamic range of hearing, and why it is not what it looks like

blocks.html: From the 0 dB SPL threshold to the 120 dB threshold of discomfort is 120 dB, a trillion to one in power. But you do not have 120 dB of instantaneous resolution. The system uses gain control: the acoustic reflex, outer-hair-cell compression, and neural adaptation all reduce sensitivity in loud environments over timescales from tens of milliseconds to minutes. What you have is a 120 dB operating range with perhaps 40-50 dB of usable instantaneous window at any one adaptation state. This is the direct auditory analogue of a camera with a wide ISO range and a limited per-shot dynamic range.

blocks.label: Outer hair cells do not regenerate
blocks.html: Mammalian cochlear hair cells are formed before birth and are never replaced. Birds and fish regenerate theirs; we do not. Every one you destroy with a loud night is gone permanently, and because outer hair cells provide the active gain, their loss shows up first as difficulty understanding speech in noise — not as a simple volume reduction. An audiogram that still looks acceptable can coexist with substantial synaptic damage ("hidden hearing loss", Kujawa & Liberman, 2009).

blocks.q: Why is the ear most sensitive between roughly 2 and 5 kHz?
options: Because most musical fundamentals lie there
Because the ear canal is a quarter-wave resonator with a resonance near 3.4 kHz, reinforced by the concha resonance
Because the basilar membrane is widest there
Because the acoustic reflex boosts that region
blocks.explain: It is a plumbing effect, not a neural one. A 25 mm canal closed at the eardrum resonates near c/4L = 3.4 kHz, and the concha adds a broader resonance around 5 kHz. Together they contribute 10-20 dB of acoustic gain in exactly the band that carries most speech intelligibility cues — and, unhappily, the band where noise damage appears first.

blocks.html: That last coincidence deserves emphasis. The 4 kHz region is acoustically amplified by your own anatomy, which is why the classic noise-induced hearing loss audiogram shows a notch at 4 kHz before anything else goes. Your ear focuses damage on the frequencies it most amplifies. Nothing about this is designed well; it is simply what evolution produced for an animal that never encountered a 110 dB sustained sound source.

lessons.title: Equal Loudness: Phons, Sones and Monitoring Level
glossary: Phon
The loudness level of a sound, defined as the SPL of an equally loud 1 kHz pure tone. By definition, at 1 kHz phons equal dB SPL.
Sone
A ratio scale of loudness. 1 sone is defined as 40 phon; doubling sones is intended to correspond to doubling perceived loudness.
Fletcher-Munson curves
The original 1933 equal-loudness contours measured at Bell Labs, superseded by ISO 226 but still widely named.
Loudness compensation
A level-dependent frequency correction (the "loudness" button) intended to offset the changing contour shape at low playback levels.
K-System
Bob Katz's proposal linking monitoring gain to metering: K-20, K-14 and K-12 reference levels tied to 83 dB SPL per channel.

blocks.html: Fletcher and Munson published the first systematic equal-loudness contours in 1933 using headphone presentation and a loudness-balance procedure with a small number of listeners. Their curves were qualitatively right and quantitatively wrong, especially below 100 Hz. ISO 226 has been revised twice on far better data (Suzuki and Takeshima's work at Tohoku University underpins the 2003 revision); at 25 Hz the 2003 threshold sits roughly 10-15 dB away from the 1933 estimate. Practitioners still say "Fletcher-Munson" as a generic term. Say ISO 226 if you want to be precise, and know that the shape, not the label, is what matters.

blocks.caption: The contours computed from the ISO 226:2003 parameter tables. Follow any single curve: it is the set of levels that sound equally loud. The flattening at high levels is the whole story of monitoring discipline.

blocks.text: Reading the contours like an engineer

blocks.html: Take the 20-phon and 80-phon contours and compare their shapes. At 20 phon, reaching threshold-plus-20 at 40 Hz needs about 74 dB SPL while 1 kHz needs 20 dB SPL — a 54 dB tilt. At 80 phon the same comparison needs about 105 dB at 40 Hz against 80 dB at 1 kHz, a 25 dB tilt. The contours flatten as level rises. Consequently, turning a mix up makes bass and extreme treble grow faster than the midrange, and turning it down makes them vanish faster. Nothing about the signal changed.

head: Frequency
SPL for 20 phon
SPL for 60 phon
SPL for 90 phon
Tilt relative to 1 kHz at 20 / 90 phon

blocks.label: The practical rule that follows
blocks.html: Make tonal balance decisions at a consistent, moderately loud level — commonly 79-85 dBC slow per channel for music, 85 dBC for film dubbing stages per SMPTE ST 202. Make arrangement and balance decisions quietly, because low-level listening exaggerates midrange and exposes anything hiding behind the bass. Check at both. What you must not do is make bass decisions at whatever level you happen to have the monitor controller set to, because that is equivalent to using a different EQ curve every session.

blocks.label: Loudness in sones from loudness level in phons (above 40 phon)
blocks.caption: The scale that encodes "10 phon is twice as loud". Below about 40 phon loudness grows faster than this power law, which is why quiet sounds seem to disappear abruptly.

blocks.html: The sone scale comes from S. S. Stevens' magnitude-estimation work in the 1930s-1950s and it deserves scepticism. It was derived from pure tones presented to small groups of listeners under laboratory conditions, and magnitude estimation is famously sensitive to the range of stimuli presented and to instructions given. Modern loudness models (Moore-Glasberg, DIN 45631, ISO 532-1/-2) do considerably better on real signals by integrating specific loudness across critical bands. Use sones as a concept; do not use the 10-phon doubling as a design rule.

blocks.text: Why the "loudness" button was not a gimmick

blocks.html: Domestic amplifiers used to include a loudness contour switch that boosted bass and a little treble at low volume settings. The physics is sound: if the mix was balanced at 85 dB SPL and you play it at 55 dB SPL, the 30 dB reduction costs you far more perceived bass than midrange, so a compensating boost restores the intended balance. The implementations were bad — most were not tied to an absolute calibrated level, so the correction was applied by guesswork — but the principle is correct and is being revived in properly calibrated systems and in some car audio.

blocks.q: You mix at 95 dB SPL and the client listens at 65 dB SPL. What will they most likely complain about?
options: Too much sibilance
Not enough bass and a thin, midrange-forward sound
Too much bass
Excessive stereo width
blocks.explain: Dropping 30 dB moves you to a steeper contour, so low frequencies lose proportionally more loudness than the midrange. A mix balanced loud will sound bass-light quiet. The converse trap is equally real: mixing at 65 dB and checking at 95 dB typically reveals far too much low end. Consistent calibrated monitoring plus deliberate level checks is the only defence.

blocks.html: Opinion, defended: calibrate your monitoring. Buy a meter, play pink noise at -20 dBFS RMS, set each channel to a repeatable reference (79 dBC for a small room, 83-85 dBC for a large one), and mark the knob. Every argument about "translation" that I have watched consume a studio afternoon dissolved once the participants discovered they had been listening 12 dB apart. Calibration costs one hour, once.

lessons.title: Critical Bands and Masking
glossary: Critical band
The bandwidth within which the auditory system integrates energy as though through a single filter. Roughly 100 Hz wide below 500 Hz, then about 1/6 to 1/3 octave.
ERB
Equivalent rectangular bandwidth. Moore and Glasberg: ERB = 24.7 (4.37 f/1000 + 1), with f in hertz.
Bark scale
Zwicker's 24-band division of the audible range into critical bands.
Simultaneous masking
A loud sound raising the audible threshold for a quieter sound present at the same time.
Temporal masking
Masking that extends before (about 5-20 ms) and after (100-200 ms) the masker.
Comodulation masking release
A reduction in masking when the masker is amplitude-modulated coherently across bands, allowing the ear to segregate sources.

blocks.html: The cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping bandpass filters. Two tones falling inside one filter are integrated together and interact strongly; two tones in different filters are analysed separately. Georg von Bekesy won the 1961 Nobel Prize for demonstrating the travelling-wave mechanism, and Harvey Fletcher had already inferred the filters from masking experiments in the 1940s without seeing them. That inference — measure masking, deduce the filter — is the model for most of psychoacoustics.

blocks.label: Equivalent rectangular bandwidth (Moore & Glasberg, 1990)
blocks.caption: At 100 Hz this gives 36 Hz. At 1 kHz, 133 Hz. At 5 kHz, 565 Hz. Below about 500 Hz the bandwidth is nearly constant in hertz; above it, nearly constant in fractional octaves.

head: Centre frequency
ERB (Hz)
ERB as a fraction of an octave
Consequence
rows: The whole sub-bass region is only a handful of filters wide. Everything down there masks everything else.
Kick and bass share a filter unless separated by more than roughly a third of an octave.
The "mud" region; small EQ moves have large audible effects.
Fine resolution; two sources 500 Hz apart here are analysed separately.
Air band; wide filters mean broad EQ moves are appropriate.

blocks.caption: The masking pattern of a 1 kHz masker. The upward spread is the reason masking is a mixing problem rather than a curiosity: low-frequency energy contaminates the region above it, not below.

blocks.text: The upward spread of masking, and what to do about it

blocks.html: Masking is strongly asymmetric. A masker raises the threshold above its own frequency far more than below, and the asymmetry increases with level: at 40 dB the upper slope is around 25 dB/octave, at 80 dB it flattens toward 10 dB/octave, spreading masking over two octaves or more. This single fact explains a large fraction of mixing practice.

items: A loud bass guitar at 80-120 Hz will obscure vocal warmth at 200-400 Hz. High-pass filtering the bass does not help; reducing the bass in the octave below the vocal does.
Cutting a hole in the masker at the masked frequency is more effective than boosting the masked source, because boosting also raises the masker's own masking through the shared filter.
Two sources within one ERB cannot be separated by EQ at all. They can be separated by level, by time (arrangement), by stereo position, or by pitch.
Dynamic EQ and sidechained multiband compression are, precisely, tools for time-varying masking release. That is the theory behind "ducking the guitars under the vocal".
Distortion adds upper harmonics, which raises the source's masking footprint upward. This is why a distorted bass can suddenly make a mix sound cluttered without measuring louder.

blocks.html: Temporal masking extends the effect in time. Backward (pre-) masking lasts roughly 5-20 ms and is weak and highly trainable; forward (post-) masking lasts 100-200 ms and is strong. Post-masking is why a snare hit conceals the room decay immediately behind it, why gates can be set surprisingly aggressively without audible artefacts, and why the pre-echo of a transform codec is far more objectionable than the same amount of post-echo. It is also the mechanism the precedence effect (Module 4) exploits.

Think of the cochlea as a row of about 40 buckets under a waterfall, each catching a different part of the flow. If one bucket is already full to the brim, a small extra trickle into that bucket is invisible. That is masking. And because the buckets slope downhill to the right, an overflowing bucket spills into its higher-frequency neighbours but not into its lower-frequency ones — the upward spread.

blocks.text: The industrial application: perceptual coding

blocks.html: MP3, AAC, Vorbis and Opus all work by computing a masking threshold from the signal and then allocating just enough bits per band that the quantisation noise stays under it. Karlheinz Brandenburg's work at Fraunhofer and Erlangen through the late 1980s turned Zwicker's masking models into MPEG-1 Layer III in 1993. The compression is not "removing frequencies you cannot hear"; it is shaping quantisation noise to hide beneath the signal's own masking curve. When a codec fails audibly, it is because the masking model mispredicted — most often on transients (pre-echo), on very tonal material (pitch-pipe, harpsichord), or on applause, which is broadband, dense and has no useful masking structure.

blocks.q: A vocal sits at 250 Hz fundamental and is being obscured by an electric bass. Which intervention is most likely to work, and why?
options: Boost the vocal at 250 Hz, because that raises it above the masker
Cut the bass around 200-350 Hz, because reducing the masker lowers the masking threshold in that band
High-pass the bass at 100 Hz, because that removes energy below the vocal
Compress the vocal harder, because that raises its average level
blocks.explain: Masking is set by the masker. Boosting the masked source works against the shared filter and usually makes the mix louder without making it clearer; high-passing the bass at 100 Hz removes energy well below the problem region and does not affect the 200-350 Hz masker at all; compression raises average level but also raises the masker-to-signal ratio problem elsewhere. Removing the masking energy is the direct causal intervention.

blocks.html: Finally, the honest limit: masking data are averages over listeners under controlled conditions with simple stimuli. Real listeners differ; trained listeners can extract signals that models predict should be masked (this is one form of comodulation masking release, and part of why "golden ears" claims are sometimes real and sometimes not). Treat masking curves as a good first-order prediction and your own ears — calibrated, rested, and level-matched — as the arbiter.

lessons.title: Damage, Dose and the Limits of Psychoacoustics
glossary: TTS
Temporary threshold shift: a reversible loss of sensitivity after exposure, typically recovering in hours to days.
PTS
Permanent threshold shift: irreversible loss from hair-cell death or synaptic loss.
Tinnitus
Perception of sound without an external source, commonly a correlate of cochlear damage and of central gain increase.
Presbycusis
Age-related hearing loss, characteristically high-frequency first and roughly symmetric.
NRR / SNR
Noise reduction rating (US) and single number rating (EU): laboratory-derived attenuation figures for hearing protectors that overstate real-world performance.
Hidden hearing loss
Cochlear synaptopathy without threshold elevation; identified by Kujawa & Liberman (2009) and detectable as poor speech-in-noise performance despite a normal audiogram.

blocks.html: Hearing damage is the occupational disease of this profession and it is almost entirely preventable by arithmetic. The mechanism is straightforward: excessive basilar-membrane motion mechanically damages stereocilia and, at higher doses, kills outer and then inner hair cells; the synapses between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibres are even more fragile and die at exposures that leave the audiogram intact. Loss accumulates. There is no recovery mechanism.

blocks.label: Permitted exposure time under a 3 dB exchange rate
blocks.caption: The 3 dB rule is the equal-energy hypothesis: doubling intensity halves permitted time. NIOSH and the EU adopt it; US OSHA's 5 dB rule permits roughly four times the dose at 100 dBA and is not supported by the epidemiology.

blocks.html: Partial doses add. If you spend time t<sub>i</sub> at level L<sub>i</sub> with permitted time T<sub>i</sub>, the total daily dose is the sum of t<sub>i</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>, and it must stay at or below 1. A monitor engineer who spends 90 minutes at 97 dBA (permitted 30 min, dose 3.0) and four hours at 88 dBA (permitted 4 h, dose 1.0) has a dose of 4.0 — four times the criterion — and will tell you the show "wasn't that loud".

head: Protection
Real-world attenuation
Spectral behaviour
Verdict for engineers
rows: Foam plugs, correctly rolled and inserted
Excellent for survival, useless for judgement.
The gap between NRR and reality is mostly insertion technique.
Approximately flat to within a few dB
The correct default for anyone in a loud room who still needs to hear.
Worth the money if you work in loud rooms weekly.
Best for very high levels; poor comfort over a long shift.
Variable isolation, but you control the level
Depends entirely on the mix level you set
A protection tool only if you actually monitor the level you send yourself.

blocks.label: The IEM trap
blocks.html: In-ear monitors isolate, which lets you work at a lower level. They also put a transducer millimetres from the eardrum with no acoustic distance loss and no reflex-triggering room energy, and the wearer sets their own level by ear in an environment where their ear is already fatigued. Measured doses on touring musicians using IEMs are frequently higher than with wedges. Use a limiter in the IEM path, and measure with a probe microphone or an in-ear dosimeter rather than trusting your own judgement.

blocks.text: Where psychoacoustics stops being reliable

blocks.html: This module has given you population averages. Four honest caveats before you use them as engineering constants.

items: Individual variation is large. ISO 226 describes otologically normal 18-25 year-olds. Threshold spread at 4 kHz across healthy young listeners is easily 15 dB, and by age 50 the population spread exceeds 40 dB.

Adaptation confounds everything. Loudness, tonal balance and even localisation judgements shift over minutes of exposure. Any comparison not made rapidly and level-matched is suspect. This is why proper listening tests use short, switched, level-matched, blind comparisons.

Level matching is not optional. Louder is preferred, consistently, at differences as small as 0.2-0.5 dB. Almost every sighted audio comparison that reports a difference is confounded by level, by expectation, or by both. Toole and Olive's loudspeaker work at the NRC and Harman is the reference here.

The brain is doing most of it. Stream segregation, timbre identification and speech-in-noise performance are learned and trainable. That cuts both ways: your judgements improve with deliberate practice, and they can be trained into idiosyncrasy if you only ever listen to one system in one room.

blocks.q: An engineer spends 2 hours at 91 dBA and 1 hour at 97 dBA. What is the daily noise dose under the NIOSH criterion?
options: About 1.0 (at the limit)
About 2.0
About 3.0
About 0.75
blocks.explain: Permitted time at 91 dBA is 8/2^2 = 2 h, so 2 hours is a dose of 1.0. Permitted time at 97 dBA is 8/2^4 = 0.5 h, so 1 hour is a dose of 2.0. Total 3.0, or 300% of the criterion. Note how the shorter, louder exposure dominates: this is why "just the encore" and "just the soundcheck at full level" are not small decisions.

blocks.title: Assignment 3 — Predict and verify a masking problem
blocks.brief: Take a multitrack mix you have access to, or record a simple four-source arrangement (bass, kick, a mid-range instrument, a voice). Part A, prediction: from the spectra alone, using an analyser with 1/6-octave or ERB-scaled resolution, predict which pairs of sources occupy overlapping critical bands and which source will mask which. State the ERB at each conflict frequency using the Moore-Glasberg formula and show the arithmetic. Part B, intervention: implement one masker-side intervention (cut in the masker), one masked-side intervention (boost in the masked source) and one non-spectral intervention (level, timing, or panning). Part C, verification: level-match all versions to within 0.2 LU using integrated LUFS, then evaluate blind, and report which intervention worked and whether it matched your prediction. Report honestly if it did not.
items: A strong result computes ERBs numerically at the specific conflict frequencies rather than describing overlap qualitatively.
A strong result uses ERB- or fractional-octave-resolution analysis, not a linear FFT display, and explains why that choice matters.
A strong result level-matches before evaluation and states the matching tolerance achieved.
A strong result explicitly compares masker-side and masked-side interventions and connects the outcome to the upward spread of masking.
A strong result reports at least one prediction that failed and offers a mechanism for why.
A weak result substitutes a list of standard EQ frequencies ("cut 300 Hz for mud") for analysis of the actual material.

questions.q: What does the phon scale measure?
options: Absolute sound pressure level
Loudness level, defined by the SPL of an equally loud 1 kHz tone
Perceived loudness on a ratio scale where doubling means twice as loud
The width of a critical band
why: That is dB SPL. The phon coincides with dB SPL only at 1 kHz, and diverges everywhere else.
Correct. A 60-phon sound is one judged as loud as a 60 dB SPL 1 kHz tone, whatever its own spectrum.
That is the sone. The phon is an ordinal loudness-level scale, not a ratio scale.
That is the critical band or ERB, a bandwidth in hertz.
questions.explain: Phons anchor loudness to a reference tone; sones attempt to express loudness as a ratio. Confusing the two is common and leads to nonsense such as "a 70-phon sound is 17% louder than a 60-phon sound".

questions.q: Using the Moore-Glasberg formula ERB = 24.7(4.37 f/1000 + 1), what is the equivalent rectangular bandwidth at 2,000 Hz?
questions.explain: 24.7 x (4.37 x 2 + 1) = 24.7 x 9.74 = 240.6 Hz. Two tones at 1,950 and 2,050 Hz therefore fall inside one auditory filter and cannot be separated by EQ; two tones at 1,800 and 2,400 Hz can.

questions.q: A monitor engineer is exposed to 103 dBA. Under the NIOSH 3 dB exchange rate with 85 dBA for 8 hours, what is the permitted daily exposure in minutes?
questions.explain: 8 h / 2^((103-85)/3) = 8 / 2^6 = 8/64 = 0.125 h = 7.5 minutes. Under OSHA's 5 dB rule the same level permits about 78 minutes, which is a policy difference of an order of magnitude on the same physiology.

questions.q: Select every statement supported by the ISO 226 equal-loudness contours.
options: The contours flatten as level increases
The ear is most sensitive around 3-4 kHz
Low frequencies require more SPL to reach a given loudness than midrange frequencies
At 90 phon the ear responds essentially flat from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
A mix balanced at 90 dB SPL will sound bass-light at 60 dB SPL
why: True. The 20-phon curve tilts about 51 dB between 31.5 Hz and 1 kHz; the 90-phon curve tilts about 25 dB.
True, largely because of ear-canal and concha resonances, giving thresholds that dip below 0 dB SPL near 3.15 kHz.
True at every level, though the amount decreases as level rises.
False. Flatter is not flat: even at 90 phon there is roughly 25 dB more SPL needed at 31.5 Hz than at 1 kHz.
True, and it is the single most practically important consequence of the contours.
questions.explain: The contours are the reason monitoring level must be calibrated and consistent. They also explain why loudness compensation circuits exist and why they only work when tied to a known absolute level.

questions.q: Order the stages of the auditory pathway from outside inward.
items: Pinna and concha
Ear canal
Tympanic membrane
Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes)
Oval window and cochlear fluid
Basilar membrane travelling wave
Inner hair cells
Auditory nerve
Superior olivary complex
questions.explain: Each stage contributes something specific: direction cues from the pinna, a 3.4 kHz resonance from the canal, impedance matching from the ossicles, frequency analysis from the membrane, transduction from the hair cells, and binaural comparison in the olivary complex.

questions.q: Match each phenomenon to its mechanism.
pairs: 4 kHz notch in a noise-damaged audiogram
Ear-canal resonance concentrates energy near 3-4 kHz
Upward spread of masking
Asymmetric excitation pattern on the basilar membrane
Active amplification of quiet sounds
Outer hair cell motility via prestin
Elevation localisation
Direction-dependent spectral notches from the pinna
Speech-in-noise difficulty with a normal audiogram
Cochlear synaptopathy (hidden hearing loss)
Pre-echo artefacts in codecs
Backward temporal masking is weak and short
questions.explain: Every psychoacoustic effect in this module has a mechanical or physiological cause. Knowing the cause lets you predict when the effect will and will not apply, which is exactly what a rule of thumb cannot do.

questions.q: Why is boosting a masked source usually less effective than cutting the masker?
options: Because boosts add noise while cuts do not
Because both signals pass through the same auditory filter, so raising the masked source raises the total level without improving the signal-to-masker ratio as efficiently
Because equalisers have better cut than boost characteristics
Because masking only responds to reductions
why: Digital EQ noise is irrelevant at these levels and this is not the mechanism.

Correct. Masking depends on the ratio between masker and target within the shared filter. Removing masker energy improves that ratio directly and also lowers the overall level; boosting the target raises level and only improves the ratio in proportion, often pushing the mix louder without making it clearer.
Minimum-phase EQ behaves symmetrically enough that this is not the reason, though cuts do sound subjectively gentler.
Masking responds to any change in the ratio; the claim is simply false.
questions.explain: This is the most useful single consequence of critical-band theory for mixing. It also explains sidechained dynamic EQ: cut the masker only while the target is present, so nothing is lost when it is not.

questions.stem: A mastering client sends two versions of a track for comparison. Version A was processed with a new analogue compressor; version B is unprocessed. The client reports that "A is obviously better — wider, more open, more depth". You measure both: A is 1.4 LU louder than B, has 0.9 dB less crest factor, and their frequency responses differ by less than 0.3 dB in any third-octave band below 10 kHz. Above 10 kHz, A is 0.6 dB higher.

qs.q: What is the most probable explanation of the client's preference?
options: The compressor introduced harmonic distortion that the analyser cannot show
Loudness bias: a 1.4 LU level difference is more than sufficient to produce a consistent preference in a sighted comparison
The 0.6 dB difference above 10 kHz created the sense of openness
The reduced crest factor genuinely increased perceived depth
why: Harmonic distortion would show in the spectrum and in a null test; and the measured third-octave agreement makes a large distortion contribution unlikely.

Correct. Preference for the louder of two otherwise similar signals is one of the most robust findings in audio perception, appearing at differences well under 1 dB. Any comparison not level-matched to about 0.1-0.2 dB is uninterpretable.
A 0.6 dB difference above 10 kHz is near or below the difference limen for a broad shelf on programme material, and cannot plausibly dominate a 1.4 LU level difference.
Reducing crest factor tends to reduce perceived depth, not increase it; and the causal claim cannot be tested without level matching.
qs.explain: The correct professional response is not to argue but to re-present the comparison level-matched and blind. In the great majority of cases the reported difference shrinks or reverses. This is not cynicism about analogue gear; it is the minimum standard of evidence before spending money.

qs.q: To level-match version A to version B for a fair comparison, how many decibels of gain should you apply to A?
qs.explain: A is 1.4 LU louder, so apply -1.4 dB. LU and dB are the same size. A tolerance of about 0.1-0.2 dB is the practical target; below roughly 0.2 dB the loudness bias is generally no longer decisive.

qs.q: Design a listening test that would actually settle whether the compressor improves the track. Name the specific threats to validity your design controls.
qs.model: Use an ABX or a level-matched blind A/B with forced choice and a defined number of trials. Controls: (1) Level: match integrated loudness to within 0.1-0.2 LU using BS.1770, and verify with a meter rather than by ear. (2) Sight: the listener must not know which version is playing, and ideally the operator should not either, so use software that randomises and logs. (3) Switching: use instantaneous, sample-aligned switching, because auditory memory for timbre decays within a few seconds; long crossfades destroy the comparison. (4) Trial count and statistics: decide in advance how many trials and what significance threshold; 16 trials with 12 or more correct is significant at about p = 0.04 under a binomial null. (5) Order and fatigue: randomise presentation order, keep sessions under about 20 minutes, and allow breaks, because adaptation shifts loudness and timbre judgements. (6) Programme material: use several excerpts, including at least one that stresses the mechanism under test (dense transients for a compressor), since a null on one excerpt does not generalise. (7) Reporting: report the result even if it is null, and state the statistical power; a non-significant result with eight trials means almost nothing. Honest limitation: a positive ABX result shows only that a difference is audible, not that it is preferable, so preference must be tested separately with a level-matched paired-comparison design.
points: Specifies level matching with a stated tolerance and a measurement method
Specifies blinding and randomisation
Specifies fast switching and short auditory memory as the reason
Specifies a trial count and a statistical criterion decided in advance
Distinguishes audibility (ABX) from preference

questions.q: Forward (post-) masking lasts substantially longer than backward (pre-) masking. Which practical consequence follows most directly?
options: Gates can close quickly after a transient without audible artefacts, while codec pre-echo before a transient is highly objectionable
Reverb pre-delay must always exceed 20 ms
Compressor attack times below 1 ms are inaudible
Low frequencies mask high frequencies more than the reverse
why: Correct. Post-masking of 100-200 ms conceals what follows a loud event, so gate release and decay artefacts hide easily; pre-masking of only 5-20 ms leaves quantisation noise spread before a transient plainly audible, which is exactly the pre-echo problem in transform codecs.
Pre-delay choices are about perceived distance and clarity, not temporal masking limits, and useful pre-delays range from 0 to 100 ms.
Fast attack times are audible as a change in transient shape; this is a different mechanism.
True as a statement about the upward spread of simultaneous masking, but it is not a consequence of the temporal asymmetry the question asks about.
questions.explain: Temporal masking asymmetry is why MDCT codecs use block switching: they shorten the transform window around transients so that the quantisation noise cannot spread further back in time than pre-masking can hide it.

questions.q: A producer insists that mixing quietly is "safer for your ears and just as accurate". Give the strongest version of their argument, then give the strongest counter-argument, and state your own position with a reason.
questions.model: For: exposure is a dose problem, and reducing monitoring level by 10 dB reduces the dose by a factor of about ten under a 3 dB exchange rate, so quiet mixing genuinely protects hearing over a career. Quiet listening also flattens nothing but does expose balance problems: at low levels the midrange dominates, so anything hidden behind bass energy becomes obvious, and arrangement and vocal-level decisions are often better made quietly. Against: the equal-loudness contours mean that at low levels the low-frequency and extreme-high-frequency content of the mix is systematically under-represented, so tonal-balance and low-end decisions made quietly will not translate to loud playback. There is also a signal-to-noise argument: at very low monitoring levels the room noise floor and the loudspeakers own distortion floor become a larger fraction of what you hear, and small details are simply inaudible. My position: use a calibrated moderate reference for tonal balance decisions — around 79 dBC per channel in a small room — and deliberately drop 15-20 dB for balance and arrangement checks, returning to the reference before any low-frequency judgement. The dose argument is answered by shortening total listening time and taking breaks, not by moving the reference, because an uncalibrated reference reintroduces the exact translation problem the contours predict.
points: States the exposure/dose case correctly with reference to the exchange rate
States the low-level advantage for balance and arrangement decisions
States the equal-loudness counter-argument for tonal balance and low end
Takes a defended position rather than hedging
Mentions calibration or a specific reference level

questions.q: Which finding best explains why a listener with a normal audiogram can still struggle badly to follow speech in a noisy restaurant?
options: Presbycusis affecting only frequencies above 16 kHz
Cochlear synaptopathy, in which auditory-nerve synapses are lost without threshold elevation
Middle-ear stiffening
Increased acoustic reflex sensitivity
why: Loss above 16 kHz has essentially no effect on speech, which carries almost all of its information below 8 kHz.

Correct. Kujawa and Liberman (2009) showed that noise exposure destroys inner-hair-cell synapses at doses that produce only temporary threshold shift. Pure-tone thresholds recover; suprathreshold coding, which is what speech-in-noise requires, does not.
Middle-ear stiffening (as in otosclerosis) produces a conductive loss that does show on an audiogram.
A more sensitive reflex would attenuate loud low frequencies and would not degrade speech in moderate noise.
questions.explain: This is why the audiogram is a necessary but insufficient test for people who work in audio. Speech-in-noise tests and extended high-frequency audiometry catch damage the standard test misses, and the practical implication is that "my hearing test was fine" is not evidence that your exposure has been safe.

modules.title: Phase, Interference and Comb Filtering
modules.tagline: Superposition is the most powerful idea in audio and the most frequently mishandled. Polarity, phase, delay and the comb filter that results.
objectives: Able to distinguish polarity inversion from phase shift and predict when each is audible.
Able to compute comb-filter notch frequencies, spacing and depth from a delay time and a reflection level.
Able to convert between path difference, delay and phase angle at any frequency.
Able to diagnose a comb-filtering problem in the field and choose between distance, absorption, and alignment as the fix.
Able to explain the precedence effect and use it to reason about localisation, the 3:1 rule and delay-tower design.

lessons.title: Polarity Is Not Phase
glossary: Polarity
The sign of a signal. Inverting polarity multiplies every sample by -1 and is frequency-independent.
Phase
The position within a cycle, expressed in degrees or radians. A phase relationship is meaningful only between two signals at a stated frequency.
Delay
A constant time offset. Its phase consequence grows linearly with frequency: 1 ms is 36 degrees at 100 Hz and 360 degrees at 1 kHz.
Minimum phase
A system whose phase response is uniquely determined by its magnitude response. Most analogue EQs and many acoustic resonances are minimum phase.
All-pass
A filter with flat magnitude and frequency-dependent phase. It changes waveform shape without changing the spectrum.
Group delay
The negative derivative of phase with respect to angular frequency: the delay experienced by the envelope of a narrow band of frequencies.

blocks.html: The word "phase" is used in studios to mean at least four different things, and the resulting confusion costs real work. The button labelled Ø on your console is a polarity inversion: it multiplies the signal by -1, affecting all frequencies identically and instantaneously. A phase shift is frequency-dependent by definition; you cannot shift the phase of a broadband signal by 180 degrees without specifying at which frequency. A delay produces a phase shift proportional to frequency. These three are not interchangeable and the first step to competence is refusing to call them all "phase".

blocks.label: Delay expressed as phase
blocks.caption: A 1 ms delay is 36 degrees at 100 Hz, 180 degrees at 500 Hz, 360 degrees at 1 kHz and 3,600 degrees at 10 kHz. A single delay is therefore a different phase problem at every frequency, which is precisely why it produces a comb rather than a simple cancellation.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 4
items: Sound Reproduction (3rd ed.) — Floyd E. Toole

Required. Chapters 6 and 7 on reflections, comb filtering and the precedence effect, and Section 4.5 on the audibility of phase. Toole is unusually careful about separating what is measurable from what is audible.
Master Handbook of Acoustics (6th ed.) — Everest & Pohlmann
Required. Chapter 6 (Reflection) and Chapter 8 (Diffraction), plus the comb-filter treatment. Use the worked notch-frequency examples to check your own arithmetic.
Modern Recording Techniques (9th ed.) — Huber & Runstein

Required. The microphone chapter section on the 3:1 rule and multi-microphone leakage. Read it critically: the rule is a rule of thumb derived from the inverse-square law, and the book states it without the derivation you now know.
Blauert, J., Spatial Hearing: The Psychophysics of Human Sound Localization (revised ed., 1997)
Optional but the definitive reference. Chapter 3 for the precedence effect and the summing-localisation literature.
Wallach, H., Newman, E. B. & Rosenzweig, M. R., "The Precedence Effect in Sound Localization", American Journal of Psychology 62(3), 1949
Required. The original paper is short and readable and it names the effect. Note how modest the original claims were compared with how the effect is described today.

tabs.label: Polarity error
tabs.html: A cable wired pin 2 to pin 3, or a bottom snare microphone facing the opposite way to the top one. The fix is a polarity flip and it is exact: the two signals become correctly aligned in sign at all frequencies. Symptom: the combination is thinner and quieter than either source alone, most obviously in the low end. Test: sum to mono and flip; the correct choice is louder and fuller.

tabs.label: Time-of-arrival error
tabs.html: Two microphones at different distances from the same source. A polarity flip will not fix this, because the offset is a delay, not a sign. The comb notches simply move. The fixes are alignment (delay one signal), attenuation (turn the more distant one down), or distance (move them so the delay exceeds the fusion window).

tabs.label: Filter phase shift
tabs.html: Every minimum-phase EQ, crossover and loudspeaker introduces phase shift as an unavoidable consequence of its magnitude response. This is usually benign on its own and usually catastrophic when two paths with different filters are summed — which is exactly the crossover-region problem in every multi-way loudspeaker.

blocks.text: Is phase audible on its own?

blocks.html: Here is a genuine and unresolved dispute. Ohm's acoustic law, as refined by Helmholtz, holds that the ear is largely insensitive to the relative phase of harmonics: a signal and its phase-scrambled version with identical magnitude spectra sound the same. Careful experiments (Craig & Jeffress, 1962; Patterson, 1987) largely support this for steady tones. But it is not universally true. Large phase differences within a critical band alter waveform crest factor and are audible; all-pass networks with severe group delay are audible on transients; and on headphones, where there is no room to smear things, listeners detect phase manipulations that are inaudible on loudspeakers.

My position: absolute phase (the polarity of a whole programme) is at most marginally audible on most material, and demonstrably audible on asymmetric waveforms such as solo brass, kick drum and some voices. Relative phase between summed sources is enormously audible, because it produces amplitude changes. When someone tells you "phase is inaudible", they are almost always making a claim about the first case while you are asking about the second. Keep them separate and most of the argument evaporates.

blocks.caption: Two equal-amplitude sinusoids summed at four relative phase angles. Note that 120 degrees produces no change in level at all, which is why "out of phase" is a useless description without a number.

blocks.label: The 120-degree fact
blocks.html: Two equal signals at 120 degrees of relative phase sum to exactly the same level as one alone. Below 120 degrees you gain level; above it you lose. This is why small time offsets in the low frequencies (where 1 ms is only 36 degrees at 100 Hz) usually help rather than hurt, while the same offset in the high frequencies is destructive.

blocks.q: Two microphones on a snare drum, one above and one below, both facing the head. The engineer flips polarity on the bottom mic and it sounds much fuller. Why?
options: Because the bottom mic is 180 degrees out of phase at every frequency
Because the two diaphragms move in opposite directions for the same head motion, so their outputs are opposite in sign
Because the bottom mic is further away
Because the bottom mic has a different frequency response
blocks.explain: When the head moves down, it compresses the air below and rarefies the air above. The two capsules therefore produce opposite-signed voltages for the same physical event, which is a genuine polarity relationship rather than a phase relationship. There is also a small time-of-arrival difference from the drum depth (roughly 0.4 ms for a 14 cm drum), which polarity inversion does not fix and which is why aligning the two tracks in the DAW usually improves things further.

lessons.title: Superposition and the Comb Filter
glossary: Superposition
The principle that in a linear medium the total disturbance is the sum of the individual disturbances. Air is linear at all normal audio levels.
Comb filter
The magnitude response resulting from summing a signal with a delayed copy of itself: regularly spaced notches and peaks.
Notch spacing
The frequency interval between adjacent comb notches, equal to the reciprocal of the delay.
Reflection coefficient
The amplitude ratio of the reflected to the incident wave at a boundary.
Flanging
A comb filter with a time-varying delay of roughly 0-10 ms, producing a sweeping notch pattern.
Phasing
A related effect produced by cascaded all-pass filters, giving a small number of non-harmonically spaced notches.

blocks.html: When a signal is summed with a delayed copy of itself, the result is a comb filter. At frequencies where the delay corresponds to a whole number of cycles, the copies reinforce; where it corresponds to a half-cycle plus a whole number, they cancel. Because the delay is fixed and the cycle length is not, this happens repeatedly across the spectrum — hence a "comb" of notches, evenly spaced in linear frequency.

blocks.label: Comb filter magnitude, notch and peak frequencies
blocks.caption: a is the amplitude of the delayed copy relative to the direct signal, tau the delay in seconds, n = 1, 2, 3 ... The first notch always sits at half the notch spacing.
A 1 ms delay at two reflection levels. Notice that reducing the reflection by 6 dB reduces the notch depth by 20 dB. Absorption is a far more powerful tool than repositioning.

head: Delay
Extra path at 343 m/s
First notch
Notch spacing
Typical cause
rows: Two capsules of a stereo pair slightly misaligned.
A microphone near a music stand or a lyric sheet.
Vocal mic near a hard console surface.
Desk reflection to a mix position; the classic control-room dip.
A wall reflection in a medium room. Perceived as tonal colouration and image shift.
Beyond the fusion window for speech; heard as a distinct echo.

blocks.html: Imagine two people clapping in time, one standing a little further away. For any given tempo there is a distance at which the far clap lands exactly between the near claps and the pattern sounds twice as fast. Change the tempo and that same distance now puts them together again. The comb filter is that experiment run simultaneously at every frequency: some "tempos" land in step and some land exactly between.

blocks.text: What a comb filter sounds like

blocks.html: The perceptual result depends almost entirely on the delay. Under about 1 ms the notch spacing is so wide that only one or two notches fall in the audible range and the result is heard as a tonal change, usually a thinning or a hollowness. Between roughly 1 and 20 ms the notches crowd together and the result is the familiar hollow, tubular, "on the phone" quality — this is where flangers live. Between roughly 20 and 40 ms the ear starts to resolve the copy as a separate event and it is heard as spaciousness or as a doubling. Beyond about 40-50 ms for speech (longer for sustained music) it is a distinct echo.

blocks.label: A comb filter is not fixed by EQ
blocks.html: A notch produced by cancellation is not a resonance you can boost back. If two signals cancel at 500 Hz, there is no 500 Hz energy left to raise; boosting there raises noise and everything else that survived at 500 Hz, and the notch reappears the instant the geometry changes. Comb filtering is fixed at its cause: change the delay, change the level of the reflection, or remove the reflection.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a comb filter in the field
steps: Identify the notch spacing
Sweep a sine or look at a transfer function. Evenly spaced notches on a linear frequency axis mean a comb; unevenly spaced ones mean a resonance or a room mode.
Convert spacing to delay
tau = 1 / delta-f. Notches 400 Hz apart mean a 2.5 ms delay.
Convert delay to distance
Extra path = c x tau. 2.5 ms is 86 cm of extra path length.
Find the geometry
Look for a surface whose reflected path is 86 cm longer than the direct path. Half of that, 43 cm, is roughly the perpendicular distance if the surface is behind the microphone.
Choose the intervention
Absorb the reflection (best), move the source or receiver so the delay leaves the problem band, or, if the two paths are separate electrical signals, delay one to align them.
Verify
Re-measure. A genuine fix removes the notches; a cosmetic EQ fix leaves them and adds noise.

blocks.q: A measurement shows notches at 250, 750, 1250 and 1750 Hz. What delay is responsible?
options: 4 ms
2 ms
1 ms
0.5 ms
blocks.explain: The spacing is 500 Hz, so tau = 1/500 = 2 ms. Check: the first notch should be at half the spacing, 250 Hz — it is. A 2 ms delay corresponds to 68.6 cm of extra path, which for a boundary behind the microphone means a surface about 34 cm away.

blocks.html: Comb filtering is not always an enemy.
