Flanging, phasing and chorus are deliberate comb effects; the Haas-style short delay used to widen a source is a comb filter you have decided to like; and the spaced-pair microphone techniques that produce lush stereo do so partly through decorrelation that is comb filtering in disguise. The distinction between artefact and effect is entirely whether you chose it and whether it survives mono summation.

lessons.title: Two Sources in a Room: Interference Patterns and Mono Compatibility
glossary: Coherent summation
Adding correlated signals; pressures add, giving up to +6 dB.
Incoherent summation
Adding uncorrelated signals; powers add, giving +3 dB.
Power alley
The region along the centre line of a stereo subwoofer pair where low frequencies sum coherently, with cancellation lobes either side.
Mono compatibility
The degree to which a stereo mix survives summation to a single channel without cancellation.
Correlation meter
A display of the normalised cross-correlation between left and right, from +1 (identical) through 0 (uncorrelated) to -1 (inverted).
Decorrelation
Deliberately reducing the correlation between channels, e.g. by short delays, all-pass networks or differing reverberation.

blocks.html: Two loudspeakers reproducing the same signal do not produce "twice the sound". They produce an interference pattern in space: a set of surfaces where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (reinforcement) alternating with surfaces where it is a half-wavelength (cancellation). Move your head 20 cm and the pattern shifts. This is not a defect of the loudspeakers; it is superposition, and it is unavoidable whenever the same signal arrives from two places.

blocks.label: Cancellation condition for two coherent sources
blocks.caption: Delta-d is the path difference between the two sources and the listening point. A 30 cm path difference cancels first at 572 Hz, then 1,716 Hz, then 2,860 Hz.

blocks.text: The subwoofer problem, worked through

blocks.html: Consider two subwoofers 6 m apart on a stage front, both fed the same mono low frequencies. On the centre line the path difference is zero, so everything sums coherently: +6 dB. Move 3 m off centre at a distance of 20 m and the path difference becomes roughly 0.44 m, which cancels at 390 Hz — irrelevant for subs. But at 30 m distance and 12 m off axis the path difference grows to about 2.3 m, cancelling at 75 Hz, which is squarely in the sub band. The audience on the centre line gets a bass-heavy show; the audience at the sides gets a hole. This is the "power alley", and it is the reason large systems use end-fire, cardioid or gradient subwoofer arrays rather than simple left-right stacks.

blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 250" role="img" aria-label="Two microphones on two sources illustrating the three to one rule, in which the second microphone is three times further from the first source than the first microphone is"><text x="24" y="24" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="var(--ink)">The 3:1 rule is an inverse-square-law argument, nothing more</text><circle cx="110" cy="180" r="12" fill="var(--fig)" fill-opacity="0.25" stroke="var(--fig)"/><text x="110" y="212" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">source A</text><circle cx="430" cy="180" r="12" fill="var(--fig)" fill-opacity="0.25" stroke="var(--fig)"/><text x="430" y="212" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">source B</text><rect x="102" y="92" width="16" height="24" rx="3" fill="var(--fig)"/><text x="110" y="84" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">mic 1</text><rect x="422" y="92" width="16" height="24" rx="3" fill="var(--fig)"/><text x="430" y="84" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">mic 2</text><line x1="110" y1="168" x2="110" y2="120" stroke="var(--fig)" stroke-width="2"/><text x="118" y="148" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--fig)">d</text><line x1="122" y1="176" x2="418" y2="112" stroke="#ef5f6b" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/><text x="250" y="132" font-size="10.5" fill="#ef5f6b">leakage path ≥ 3d</text><line x1="130" y1="230" x2="410" y2="230" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 130 230 l 6 -3.5 l 0 7 z" fill="var(--line)"/><path d="M 410 230 l -6 -3.5 l 0 7 z" fill="var(--line)"/><text x="270" y="246" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">source separation</text><text x="24" y="62" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--muted)">At 3x the distance the leakage is 9.5 dB down, so the notch is only 3.5 dB deep.</text></svg>
blocks.caption: The 3:1 rule. It is often taught as an incantation; it is really a statement that 9.5 dB of leakage attenuation limits comb notch depth to about 2.6 dB, which is usually tolerable.

blocks.html: The 3:1 rule deserves the derivation nobody gives it. If microphone 1 is at distance d from its source, and microphone 2 is at least 3d from that same source, then the leakage into microphone 2 is 20 log(3) = 9.54 dB below the direct signal in microphone 1. When those two are summed, the comb notch depth is 20 log(1 - 10<sup>-9.54/20</sup>) = 20 log(1 - 0.3333) = -3.52 dB, and the peak is +2.5 dB, so the total ripple is about 6 dB. That is audible but rarely fatal. If you want the ripple under 2 dB you need roughly a 5:1 ratio. The rule is a tolerance choice, not a law.

blocks.label: Read the table as a design tool
blocks.html: This table answers "how much leakage can I tolerate?" for any multi-microphone situation: drum overheads and close mics, orchestral spot mics against a main pair, a podium pair, a guitar cabinet with two mics. Decide the ripple you will accept, read off the required attenuation, then achieve it with distance, with directivity (aim the null of a cardioid at the offending source), or with gating.

blocks.text: Mono compatibility, and why it still matters

blocks.html: Anything you do to widen a stereo image by phase or delay manipulation is a comb filter waiting to happen when the channels are summed. Club systems, many television broadcasts, phone speakers, most smart speakers, and every venue with a mono delay fill will sum your mix. The correlation meter is the cheap check: sustained readings near -1 mean the two channels are close to inverted and will largely disappear in mono. But the meter is broadband; a mix can read +0.6 and still lose its bass guitar entirely.

items: Check mono at least once per mix, at the same monitoring level, and listen specifically for elements that change level rather than elements that change position.

Keep low frequencies mono or near-mono below roughly 100-150 Hz. This is not superstition: it protects against cancellation, it improves vinyl cutting, and it keeps subwoofer arrays behaving predictably.
Prefer decorrelation techniques that survive summation (differing reverb, differing performances, differing EQ) over polarity or all-pass tricks that do not.
Be sceptical of "stereo widener" plug-ins. Many implement a Haas delay or a mid-side polarity trick; both collapse badly. Test before you commit.
Test spaced-pair recordings in mono early, because spaced pairs are inherently comb-filtered when summed, and the notch frequencies depend on the source position.

blocks.q: A listener sits 8 m from a left speaker and 8.6 m from a right speaker, both playing the same mono signal. At what frequency is the first cancellation?
options: 286 Hz
572 Hz
143 Hz
blocks.explain: The path difference is 0.6 m. First cancellation is where that equals half a wavelength, so lambda = 1.2 m and f = 343/1.2 = 286 Hz. Subsequent nulls fall at odd multiples: 858 Hz, 1,430 Hz. The lesson for control-room layout is that the listening position must be genuinely symmetrical, because 60 cm of asymmetry puts a notch in the middle of the vocal range.

lessons.title: Precedence, Localisation and Using Time Deliberately
glossary: Interaural time difference (ITD)
The arrival-time difference between the two ears, dominant for localisation below about 1.5 kHz. Maximum around 690 microseconds.
Interaural level difference (ILD)
The level difference between the ears caused by head shadowing, dominant above about 1.5 kHz.
Precedence effect
The perceptual fusion of a direct sound and a delayed copy, with the location determined by the first arrival. Also called the law of the first wavefront.
Haas effect
Specifically, the finding that a delayed copy up to about 30 ms can be raised roughly 10 dB above the direct sound before it is heard as a separate event.
Echo threshold
The delay beyond which a reflection is heard as a separate event: roughly 30-50 ms for speech, longer for sustained music, shorter for clicks.
Summing localisation
For delays below about 1 ms, the two arrivals fuse into a single image whose position depends on both time and level differences.

blocks.html: Your two ears are about 20-23 cm apart around the head, which puts the maximum interaural time difference at roughly 690 microseconds. Below about 1.5 kHz the auditory nerve phase-locks well enough to compare arrival times directly and localisation is dominated by ITD. Above that, the wavelength becomes shorter than the head and phase becomes ambiguous, so the system switches to comparing levels (ILD), exploiting the acoustic shadow the head casts. Elevation, which produces neither ITD nor ILD, is judged from pinna-imposed spectral notches — which is why elevation cues are so individual and why generic binaural rendering rarely places sounds convincingly above you.

blocks.label: Interaural time difference for a spherical head (Woodworth)
blocks.caption: r is head radius (about 8.75 cm), theta the azimuth in radians. At 90 degrees this gives (0.0875/343)(1.571 + 1) = 656 microseconds, close to the measured maximum.

blocks.text: The precedence effect

blocks.html: Wallach, Newman and Rosenzweig named the precedence effect in 1949, though Haas's 1951 dissertation on speech intelligibility is the reference most engineers cite. The finding: when a sound and a delayed copy arrive from different directions within roughly 1-30 ms, the listener hears a single fused event located at the first arrival, even when the later arrival is substantially louder. Haas found that for speech, a copy delayed 10-20 ms could be up to about 10 dB louder before it began to dominate.

head: Delay between arrivals
Perception
Engineering use
rows: Summing localisation: image pulls toward the earlier source
Time-based panning; ORTF and NOS microphone pairs; the reason a small head movement shifts the image.
Fused, single image at the first arrival; tonal colouration from comb filtering
The danger zone. Early reflections from a console or a nearby wall live here and damage imaging.
Fused; adds loudness, spaciousness and apparent source width
Delay towers, under-balcony fills, doubling effects, the Haas trick for making a fill inaudible as a separate source.
Slapback; the boundary where fills start to smear speech intelligibility.
Explicit delay effects; a serious problem in large reverberant spaces.

blocks.label: How to time a delay tower
blocks.html: Set the delay to the acoustic propagation time from the main array to the tower, then add 5-15 ms. The extra delay guarantees that the main system still arrives first, so the precedence effect keeps the image locked on the stage even though the nearby fill is louder at that seat. Then re-check when the temperature changes, because c moves 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius and a 100 m throw drifts several milliseconds across an evening.

The precedence effect has limits that get glossed over. It breaks down for continuous, unmodulated signals — it depends on transients and onsets. It is weaker for delays under about 1 ms, where summing localisation takes over instead. It builds up and breaks down over several seconds of repeated exposure (the Clifton effect: change the geometry and the echo becomes briefly audible again before the system re-adapts). And it does not suppress the timbral consequence: a reflection you localise correctly is still comb-filtering the sound you hear.

Precedence is the auditory equivalent of a courtroom rule that the first witness sets the story. Later witnesses can be louder and more detailed, and they will be integrated into the account, but they do not change where the event is judged to have happened — unless they contradict the first witness so grossly, or arrive so much later, that the fusion collapses and they are treated as a separate incident.

blocks.q: An under-balcony fill is timed to arrive exactly with the main system at a particular seat. What is the likely complaint?
options: The fill will be inaudible
The image will pull toward the nearby fill speaker, and comb filtering between the two arrivals will colour the sound
The fill will produce a distinct echo
The fill will cancel the main system entirely
blocks.explain: With zero relative delay the two arrivals are equally "first", so localisation is determined by level — and the fill is much closer, hence much louder. The listener localises the show at the ceiling. Simultaneously, the arrivals are correlated and time-offset by only a few hundred microseconds across a range of seats, producing severe comb filtering. Adding 10-15 ms restores stage localisation and moves the comb notches to a spacing so fine that the ear integrates rather than resolving them.

blocks.title: Assignment 4 — Comb filter forensics
blocks.brief: Produce a short technical report with measurements. Part A: deliberately create three comb filters — (1) a microphone at a measured distance above a hard surface, (2) two microphones on one source at a measured distance apart, summed, and (3) a signal summed with a delayed copy in your DAW at a delay you choose. For each, predict the first notch frequency, the notch spacing and the notch depth from your measured geometry and reflection level before measuring. Part B: measure each with a transfer function or a swept sine and report the actual notch frequencies. Part C: for case (1), apply three fixes — move the microphone closer to the surface, move it much further away, and place absorption on the surface — and quantify the improvement in notch depth for each. Part D: state which of your predictions were wrong and give a physical reason.
items: A strong result predicts before measuring and shows the arithmetic, including the conversion from distance to delay via c.
A strong result correctly predicts that halving the reflection amplitude reduces notch depth far more than it reduces peak height, and quantifies it.
A strong result reports measured notch frequencies with an uncertainty, and reconciles discrepancies with geometry (e.g. the reflection point is not directly below the capsule).
A strong result distinguishes the three fixes by mechanism: changing tau, changing a, and removing the reflection entirely.
A strong result comments on what the comb filter sounds like at each delay and relates it to the fusion and echo thresholds.
A weak result reports a spectrum without predicting it, or attributes an unevenly spaced set of dips to comb filtering when the spacing indicates a modal or resonant cause.

questions.q: What is the difference between polarity inversion and a 180-degree phase shift?
options: They are the same operation described in two ways
Polarity inversion multiplies the signal by -1 at all frequencies; a 180-degree phase shift is defined only at a specified frequency
Polarity inversion applies only to analogue signals
A phase shift is instantaneous and polarity inversion is not
why: They coincide only for a single sinusoid. For a broadband signal they are entirely different operations.
Correct. Inversion is frequency-independent and preserves waveform shape (mirrored). A phase shift is frequency-dependent and, applied broadband via a delay or all-pass, changes waveform shape.
Inversion is trivially available in both domains.
Both can be instantaneous; the distinction is frequency dependence, not latency.
questions.explain: This distinction is the root of most "phase" confusion in studios. A polarity button will fix a wiring error or an opposed-diaphragm situation, and will never fix a time-of-arrival difference.

questions.q: A reflection arrives 1.6 ms after the direct sound. At what frequency is the first comb notch?
questions.explain: 1/(2 x 0.0016) = 312.5 Hz. Notches then repeat at 937.5, 1562.5 Hz and so on, spaced 1/tau = 625 Hz apart. A 1.6 ms delay corresponds to 55 cm of extra path.

questions.q: A microphone measurement shows evenly spaced notches 800 Hz apart. What is the delay in milliseconds?
questions.explain: tau = 1/delta-f = 1/800 = 1.25 ms. That corresponds to 42.9 cm of extra path, so a reflecting surface roughly 21 cm from the microphone if the surface is directly behind it. Even spacing on a linear axis is the diagnostic signature of a comb; unequal spacing indicates resonance or modal behaviour.

questions.q: How many degrees of phase shift does a 0.25 ms delay produce at 2 kHz?
questions.explain: phi = 360 f tau = 360 x 2000 x 0.00025 = 180 degrees. The same delay is only 18 degrees at 200 Hz, which is exactly why a delay cannot be described as "a phase shift" without naming a frequency.

questions.q: A reflection arrives at 0.4 of the direct amplitude. How deep is the resulting comb notch, in dB relative to the direct signal alone?
questions.hint: The notch value is 20 log10(1 - a).
questions.explain: 20 log10(1 - 0.4) = 20 log10(0.6) = -4.44 dB. The corresponding peak is 20 log10(1.4) = +2.92 dB, giving 7.4 dB of total ripple. Note the asymmetry: notches are always deeper than peaks are tall, and the disparity grows sharply as a approaches 1.

questions.q: Select every situation in which a polarity flip is the correct fix.
options: Top and bottom snare microphones facing the head from opposite sides
A microphone cable miswired pin 2 to pin 3
Two microphones at different distances from the same guitar cabinet
A bass DI summed with a bass amplifier microphone 1.2 m away
A woofer wired out of polarity relative to the tweeter in a two-way loudspeaker
why: Correct. The two diaphragms move oppositely for the same head displacement; this is a genuine sign relationship.
Correct. A pin swap inverts the differential signal at all frequencies.
Wrong fix. This is a time-of-arrival difference; flipping polarity only moves the comb notches, it does not remove them. Delay alignment or attenuation is required.
Wrong fix for the same reason: 1.2 m is about 3.5 ms of delay. Polarity flip changes which frequencies cancel, not whether they do.

Correct in the sense that the error is a polarity error, and it is fixed by rewiring. Note that in the crossover region the summed response also depends on the filter phase, so a flip can be the deliberate design choice with certain filter orders.
questions.explain: The rule: flip polarity when the relationship between the two signals is a sign, and align time when it is a delay. Mistaking one for the other wastes an enormous amount of studio time.

questions.q: Order these delays by increasing perceptual consequence for speech, from tonal colouration through to a distinct echo.
items: 0.3 ms — image shift, minimal colouration
2 ms — hollow comb colouration
12 ms — fused but wider and louder (precedence)
35 ms — near the echo threshold, smearing
120 ms — clearly separate echo
questions.explain: The perceptual regimes are set by fusion and echo thresholds, which are material-dependent: transient speech separates earlier than sustained music, and clicks earlier still. The Haas region of 5-30 ms is the one engineers exploit deliberately.

questions.q: Match each symptom to its most likely cause.
pairs: Evenly spaced notches at 500, 1500, 2500 Hz
A 1 ms delayed reflection
A single broad dip at 63 Hz at one listening position only
A room mode null
A mix that loses its lead vocal when summed to mono
Polarity or all-pass width processing on the vocal
Image locked to a nearby fill speaker
Fill not delayed relative to the main system
Sound is thin and quiet only when two mics are combined
Polarity error between the two microphones
questions.explain: Diagnosis in acoustics is mostly pattern recognition on the frequency and spatial signature. Evenly spaced means comb; isolated and position-dependent means modal; level change on summation means correlation problems.

questions.stem: A live engineer is mixing a conference in a 40 m long hall. The main array is at the stage; a delay ring hangs 26 m back. The room is 21 degrees C. Speech is intelligible at the front but muddy from the delay ring back, and audience members under the ring report that the speaker "sounds like they are above us". The delay ring is currently set to 0 ms and is running 4 dB louder at its seats than the main array.

qs.q: What is the propagation time from the main array to the delay ring, in milliseconds? Use c = 331.3 + 0.606 theta.
qs.explain: c = 331.3 + 0.606 x 21 = 344.0 m/s. 26 / 344.0 = 0.0756 s = 75.6 ms. Setting the ring to 0 ms therefore makes it arrive 75.6 ms EARLY relative to the main system, far beyond the echo threshold, which is why speech is smeared.

qs.q: What delay should be dialled into the ring, and why?
options: 0 ms, so both systems arrive together
75.6 ms, exactly matching the propagation time
About 85 ms — the propagation time plus 5-15 ms so the main system still arrives first
About 40 ms, half the propagation time, to split the difference
why: Zero delay is the current, broken condition; the ring arrives 75.6 ms before the main system.
Exact matching makes both arrive simultaneously, so localisation is decided by level and the louder ring wins; the image goes to the ceiling and comb filtering is severe.
Correct. The extra 5-15 ms ensures the main system is the first wavefront, so the precedence effect locks the image on stage even though the ring is 4 dB louder locally. This is standard practice.
Half the delay is arbitrary and leaves a 35 ms early arrival, right at the echo threshold — close to the worst possible choice for intelligibility.
qs.explain: Delay towers exploit the precedence effect deliberately: be second, be louder, be fused. Being first and louder puts the show in the wrong place; being second by too much becomes an echo.

qs.q: The client asks why the delay must be re-checked when the hall fills with people and warms up. Answer quantitatively.
qs.model: The delay is a distance divided by the speed of sound, and the speed of sound rises about 0.606 m/s per degree Celsius. If the hall warms from 21 to 28 degrees during the session, c rises from 344.0 to 348.3 m/s, so the propagation time over 26 m falls from 75.6 ms to 74.6 ms — about 1 ms. That alone is small. But two other things change with it: the array is often much further from the furthest fills in a large system, so on a 100 m throw the same 7 degree change is worth about 3.6 ms; and an audience absorbs and scatters high frequencies, which reduces the direct-to-reverberant ratio and changes both the level balance between systems and the perceived intelligibility. The safe practice is to set delays at the measured temperature, re-measure or recompute after the room has stabilised with an audience, and to keep the extra precedence offset (5-15 ms) large enough that a millisecond or two of drift cannot make the fill arrive first. The offset is a tolerance budget as well as a perceptual device.
points: States that c changes about 0.6 m/s per degree C
Computes an actual change in delay time for a stated distance and temperature change
Notes that longer throws suffer proportionally larger drift
Notes that the precedence offset provides tolerance against this drift

questions.q: Two identical sinusoids at the same level are summed with a relative phase of 120 degrees. The result is:
options: 3 dB louder than one alone
6 dB louder than one alone
The same level as one alone
Complete cancellation
why: +3 dB corresponds to incoherent (power) addition, not to a defined phase relationship between identical tones.
+6 dB occurs only at 0 degrees of relative phase.
Correct. The vector sum of two unit vectors 120 degrees apart has magnitude 1, so the level is unchanged. Below 120 degrees you gain, above it you lose.
Cancellation occurs at exactly 180 degrees with equal amplitudes.
questions.explain: The 120-degree crossover point is worth memorising: it tells you that modest phase misalignments are harmless and that the damage begins only when the offset exceeds a third of a cycle. At 100 Hz that is 3.3 ms of time offset; at 5 kHz it is 67 microseconds.

questions.q: A colleague fixes a hollow-sounding vocal recording by applying a narrow 6 dB boost at each of the measured comb notch frequencies. Explain why this is a poor solution and what you would do instead.
questions.model: A comb notch is a cancellation, not an attenuation of a resonance: at the notch frequency the direct and reflected components have subtracted, so there is very little signal energy left to restore. Boosting there raises whatever survives — largely noise, room tone and non-cancelling components — so the signal-to-noise ratio at those frequencies worsens while the perceived hollowness barely improves. Worse, the notch frequencies depend on geometry: the singer moves a few centimetres, the delay changes, and the boosts now sit on peaks instead of notches, producing an even more erratic response. The boosts also introduce their own phase shift, which does nothing helpful, and they will not survive any change in microphone position between takes. The correct approach is to remove the cause. In order of preference: absorb or remove the reflecting surface, since reducing the reflection amplitude from say 0.9 to 0.3 turns a 20 dB notch into a 3 dB one; move the microphone very close to the surface so the first notch moves above the audible band, or far enough away that the reflection is weak; change the microphone pattern or angle so the null points at the reflecting surface; or if it is a two-microphone sum rather than an acoustic reflection, align the tracks in time and re-check polarity. If the recording already exists and cannot be redone, gentle broadband EQ plus a small amount of pitch- or time-modulated processing to break up the fixed notch pattern is more effective than surgical boosts, and one should be honest with the client that the artefact cannot be fully removed.
points: Explains that a notch has no energy to restore, so boosting mainly raises noise
Notes that notch frequencies move with geometry, so the correction is unstable
Prescribes reducing the reflection amplitude as the highest-leverage fix, ideally with a quantitative statement
Offers at least two alternative interventions (distance, directivity, time alignment)
Acknowledges the limits of repair on an existing recording

questions.q: Why is low-frequency content usually kept mono or near-mono in a mix?
options: Because human hearing cannot localise low frequencies at all
Because decorrelated low frequencies cancel unpredictably when summed and behave erratically in subwoofer arrays and on vinyl
Because subwoofers cannot reproduce stereo
Because low frequencies use more bits
why: Localisation below about 80 Hz is poor but not absent; the argument for mono bass is practical, not a claim of total inaudibility.

Correct. Correlated bass sums predictably; decorrelated bass produces position-dependent cancellation in rooms and arrays, causes excessive vertical stylus excursion on a lacquer, and makes subwoofer management unpredictable.
A subwoofer reproduces whatever it is fed; the constraint is spatial and practical, not a limitation of the driver.
Bit usage is unrelated to channel correlation.
questions.explain: This is a good example of a practice that is often justified with a bad reason (you cannot hear stereo bass) when a much better reason exists (decorrelated bass sums unpredictably and causes mechanical problems downstream).

modules.title: Harmonics, Timbre and the Fourier View
modules.tagline: Why every periodic signal is a sum of sinusoids, what that buys you, and what timbre actually is once you stop hand-waving.
objectives: Able to state the Fourier theorem for periodic signals and compute harmonic frequencies and amplitudes for standard waveforms.
Able to explain the time-frequency uncertainty relation and choose analysis parameters for a stated diagnostic purpose.
Able to decompose timbre into spectral envelope, temporal envelope, transient content and inharmonicity, and to justify the decomposition with evidence.
Able to distinguish harmonic from intermodulation distortion and predict the spectral consequences of a given nonlinearity.
Able to read a spectrogram and a spectrum analyser critically, including the artefacts each introduces.

lessons.title: The Harmonic Series and the Fourier Theorem
glossary: Partial
Any sinusoidal component of a complex tone, harmonic or not.
Harmonic
A partial whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental.
Fundamental
The lowest partial of a harmonic series, normally the perceived pitch.
Inharmonicity
Departure of partial frequencies from exact integer ratios, caused in strings by bending stiffness.
Missing fundamental
The perception of a pitch corresponding to a fundamental that is not physically present, inferred from the spacing of upper harmonics.
Fourier series
The representation of a periodic function as a sum of sinusoids at integer multiples of its repetition rate.

blocks.html: Joseph Fourier published the claim in 1822, in the course of solving heat conduction, that any periodic function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines at integer multiples of its repetition rate. Mathematicians spent a century establishing the conditions under which this is true. For audio it is true enough to build an industry on: every steady periodic sound is a harmonic series, and every non-periodic sound is a continuous spectrum obtained by the same machinery in the limit.

blocks.label: Fourier series of a periodic signal
blocks.caption: The n-th harmonic sits at n times the fundamental. Its amplitude and phase are the two numbers you need per harmonic; the ear cares enormously about the first and comparatively little about the second.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 5
items: The Science of Musical Sound (revised ed.) — John R. Pierce
Required. Chapters 4-6 on periodicity, spectra and timbre. Pierce ran the acoustics research group at Bell Labs, named the transistor, and writes better than almost anyone in the field.
Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics (2nd ed.) — Arthur H. Benade
Required. Chapters 6-9 on modes, harmonics and the behaviour of real instruments. Benade on inharmonicity and on why brass instruments have a "regime of oscillation" is unmatched.
The Scientist and Engineer's Guide to Digital Signal Processing — Steven W. Smith
Required. Chapters 8-11 on the DFT, windowing and spectral leakage. Free online at dspguide.com. Read it for the practical treatment of windows; the mathematics is deliberately gentle.
Risset, J.-C. & Wessel, D. L., "Exploration of Timbre by Analysis and Synthesis", in The Psychology of Music (2nd ed., ed. Deutsch), 1999
Required. The analysis-by-synthesis argument: you have understood a timbre when you can resynthesise it convincingly. Read for the trumpet and bell examples.
Grey, J. M., "Multidimensional perceptual scaling of musical timbres", JASA 61(5), 1977, pp. 1270-1277
Optional. The study that established spectral centroid and attack time as the dominant perceptual dimensions of timbre. Short and still cited constantly.

blocks.caption: Additive construction of a square wave. Gibbs overshoot at the discontinuities persists at about 9% no matter how many terms you add — a fact with direct consequences for oversampling and for the ringing of steep filters.

head: Waveform
Harmonics present
Amplitude law
Spectral slope
Character
rows: Soft, flute-like, few audible upper partials.
Hollow, clarinet-like at low levels; harsh when loud.
Bright, buzzy, the basis of most subtractive synthesis.
Maximally bright; the excitation model for the vocal tract.
Nasal; duty cycle controls which harmonics are nulled.

blocks.text: Why odd-only spectra are "hollow"

blocks.html: A square wave and a sawtooth both roll off at 6 dB per octave, yet they sound quite different. The square lacks all even harmonics, and the even harmonics are exactly the ones that reinforce octave relationships: the 2nd is an octave above the fundamental, the 4th two octaves, the 6th an octave above the 3rd. Removing them removes the octave reinforcement and leaves a spectrum dominated by fifths and their derivatives, which the ear reports as "hollow" or "woody". A stopped organ pipe and a clarinet both produce predominantly odd spectra for the same physical reason: a tube closed at one end resonates at odd multiples of its quarter-wave frequency.

blocks.label: Modes of a tube open at both ends versus stopped at one
blocks.caption: A stopped pipe sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length and produces only odd harmonics. This is the same c/2L relation you will meet again next week as the room mode formula, because a room is a very large pipe.

blocks.caption: Harmonics of A2. The 7th harmonic at 770 Hz is 31 cents below equal-tempered G5, and the 11th is 49 cents from F#6 — nearly a quarter tone. Barbershop and brass-band intonation exploit these deviations; equal temperament fights them.

blocks.label: The missing fundamental
blocks.html: Play the harmonics 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz with no 100 Hz component and listeners hear a pitch of 100 Hz. The auditory system infers the fundamental from the spacing of the partials. This is why a small radio can convey a bass line it cannot physically reproduce, why psychoacoustic bass enhancers (adding harmonics rather than boosting the fundamental) work on laptop speakers, and why judging low-end balance on small speakers is deceptive: you are hearing an inference, not a measurement.

blocks.q: A piano string's partials are measured at 220, 441, 663, 887 and 1,114 Hz. What does this indicate?
options: A measurement error
Inharmonicity from string bending stiffness, which stretches upper partials progressively sharp
The presence of a second string slightly out of tune
Intermodulation distortion in the analyser
blocks.explain: Exact harmonics of 220 Hz would be 440, 660, 880, 1,100. The measured partials are progressively sharper — the signature of inharmonicity. Real strings have bending stiffness, so the restoring force is not purely tension; the standard model is f_n = n f0 sqrt(1 + B n squared), with B larger for short, thick, stiff strings. This is why piano tuners stretch octaves and why sampled pianos sound wrong if you transpose them far.

blocks.html: That last point generalises. The harmonic series is an idealisation. Real instruments deviate: strings are inharmonic, drums are strongly inharmonic (a circular membrane's modes are Bessel-function ratios, not integers), bells are deliberately tuned inharmonic, and brass instruments only become harmonic because the player's lips lock into a regime of oscillation that forces the modes into cooperation. Treat "harmonic series" as a first approximation and expect the deviations to carry the character.

lessons.title: Reading the Spectrum: Windows, Resolution and Artefacts
glossary: DFT / FFT
The discrete Fourier transform, and the fast algorithm (Cooley-Tukey, 1965) that made it practical.
Bin
One output frequency of a DFT. Bin spacing equals sample rate divided by transform length.
Spectral leakage
Energy spreading into neighbouring bins when a component does not fall exactly on a bin centre.
Window function
A taper applied before the transform (Hann, Hamming, Blackman-Harris, Kaiser) trading main-lobe width against side-lobe level.
Spectrogram
A sequence of short-time spectra displayed as time versus frequency with magnitude as intensity.
Constant-Q transform
An analysis with logarithmically spaced bins of constant fractional bandwidth, closer to how the ear analyses.

blocks.html: A spectrum analyser does not show you "the spectrum". It shows you the spectrum of a windowed chunk of your signal, computed at a finite set of frequencies, smeared by the window's own transform. Every one of those qualifications produces artefacts that are routinely mistaken for properties of the sound. Learning to read an analyser is largely learning which parts of the picture are the signal and which are the instrument.

blocks.label: Frequency resolution of a DFT
blocks.caption: At 48 kHz a 4,096-point transform gives 11.7 Hz resolution over an 85.3 ms window. You cannot improve one without degrading the other; zero-padding interpolates the display but adds no real resolution.
