blocks.caption: The time-frequency trade-off. The rectangles have equal area because the product of time and frequency resolution is bounded from below. Your cochlea makes the same compromise, with wider bandwidth (better time resolution) at high frequencies.

blocks.html: Consider what 11.7 Hz resolution means musically. At 4 kHz it is a fortieth of a semitone — absurd precision. At 40 Hz it is more than a fifth. A linear-frequency FFT is therefore hopelessly over-resolved at the top and hopelessly under-resolved at the bottom, which is why serious acoustic measurement uses fractional-octave smoothing (1/3 or 1/6 octave) or a constant-Q transform, and why an unsmoothed FFT of a room response looks like a hedgehog and tells you almost nothing actionable.

head: Window
Main lobe width (bins)
Highest side lobe
Use it for
rows: Transient analysis where the event fits entirely inside the window.
The sensible default for general spectral analysis.
Slightly better near-in rejection, worse far-out roll-off than Hann.
Measuring a small component next to a large one, e.g. distortion products.
Accurate amplitude measurement of a single tone; terrible frequency resolution.
When you want to dial the trade-off explicitly.

blocks.label: Two artefacts that fool everyone
blocks.html: Leakage: a 1,000 Hz tone analysed with 11.7 Hz bins does not fall on a bin centre, so its energy smears across neighbours and can look like a broad hump or like sidebands. Choose a window, or choose an analysis length that makes the tone periodic in the window. Scalloping: a tone halfway between two bin centres reads up to 3.9 dB low with a rectangular window. If you are measuring a level from an FFT and you have not thought about the window, your number is wrong by an unknown amount.

blocks.title: Choosing analysis parameters for a purpose
steps: Finding a room mode near 45 Hz
You need a few hertz of resolution, so N/fs must be at least 0.25 s. Use 16,384 points at 48 kHz (2.9 Hz, 341 ms) with a Hann window, and 1/12-octave smoothing for reading.
Finding a comb filter from a 1 ms reflection
Notches are 1 kHz apart, so resolution is easy; you need enough bandwidth and a display that shows even spacing. A linear frequency axis makes the comb obvious; a log axis hides it.
Locating a click or a transient
You need time resolution, so use a short window (256-512 points) and accept coarse frequency resolution. A spectrogram with a short window shows a vertical stripe.
Measuring THD at 1 kHz

Use a long window, a low-side-lobe window such as Blackman-Harris, and choose the tone frequency so that it lands exactly on a bin centre. Otherwise leakage will bury the harmonics you are trying to measure.
Judging tonal balance of a mix
Use fractional-octave averaging (1/3 octave) with a long integration time, or better, use your ears on calibrated monitors. A high-resolution FFT of music is close to useless for this.

blocks.html: A window function is a camera exposure. A short exposure freezes motion but starves the sensor of light, so you cannot distinguish fine tonal gradations; a long exposure captures subtle gradations but smears anything that moves. Asking for both is asking to violate a conservation law, and the various window shapes are just different lens coatings: they change how flare from a bright object spreads across the frame.

blocks.q: You need to resolve two partials 8 Hz apart at a 44.1 kHz sample rate. What is the minimum practical transform length?
options: 1,024 points
4,096 points
8,192 points
16,384 points
blocks.explain: Bin spacing must be at most 8 Hz, so N is at least 44,100/8 = 5,513, and the next power of two is 8,192 (5.4 Hz bins, 186 ms window). In practice you want better than one bin of separation — a Hann window has a 4-bin main lobe — so 16,384 is the safer choice. This is exactly why resolving low-frequency detail requires long time windows, and why a fast-updating real-time analyser cannot show you the bottom octave properly.

blocks.html: Opinion: the real-time FFT display in your DAW is a diagnostic tool for finding specific problems, not a mixing tool. Watching a spectrum while mixing trains you to make the picture look like other pictures you have seen, which is not the same as making the sound work. Use it to answer a question you have already formed in words — "is there a resonance around 180 Hz?" — and then close it.

lessons.title: Timbre: What Actually Distinguishes a Trumpet from a Violin
glossary: Spectral envelope
The overall shape of the spectrum, independent of which harmonics happen to be present.
Formant
A fixed resonance of the sound-producing body that shapes the spectral envelope regardless of pitch.
Spectral centroid
The amplitude-weighted mean frequency of a spectrum; correlates strongly with perceived brightness.
Attack transient
The initial, usually inharmonic and rapidly changing portion of a note, disproportionately important for identification.
ADSR
Attack, decay, sustain, release: a coarse but useful parameterisation of the amplitude envelope.
Spectral flux
The rate of change of the spectrum over time. High flux signals such as speech are perceptually distinct from static ones.

blocks.html: The ANSI definition of timbre is famously unhelpful: the attribute by which a listener can judge two sounds of the same loudness and pitch to be dissimilar. It defines timbre by what it is not. The useful definition is operational: timbre is the joint pattern of the spectral envelope and the temporal envelope, together with the behaviour of the attack transient and any inharmonic content. Grey (1977) showed with multidimensional scaling that listeners' timbre judgements collapse onto roughly three dimensions, of which spectral centroid and attack time are the two clearest.

items.label: Spectral envelope
items.html: The shape of the harmonic amplitudes, best described by its peaks (formants) rather than by individual harmonics. A violin has body resonances near 280 Hz and 460 Hz; a trumpet has a broad formant near 1.2-1.5 kHz that stays put as the player changes note. Because formants are fixed and harmonics move with pitch, transposing a sample shifts the formants too, which is why a pitched-down voice sounds like a giant and a pitched-up one like a chipmunk.

items.label: Temporal envelope
items.html: Attack, decay, sustain, release. Risset and Wessel's classic demonstration: record a trumpet note, remove the first 50 ms, and listeners identify it far less reliably. Play a piano recording backwards and it stops being a piano entirely, though its spectrum at every instant is unchanged.

items.label: Attack transient
items.html: The first 5-50 ms contains bow noise, breath noise, hammer thud, pick click and reed chiff. It is inharmonic, noisy, and it carries a disproportionate share of identification information. This is the part that data-reduction codecs handle worst and that transient designers manipulate.

items.label: Inharmonicity and noise
items.html: Piano stretch, cymbal chaos, drum modal ratios, breath and bow noise. Perfectly harmonic synthetic tones sound sterile; adding controlled inharmonicity and noise is most of what separates a convincing sample library from a bad one.

blocks.label: Spectral centroid
blocks.caption: The centre of mass of the spectrum. It correlates well with perceived brightness and is the single most useful one-number description of a timbre. It is also what most "brightness" controls are really adjusting.

blocks.text: Formants and why the vocal tract is the clearest example

blocks.html: The vocal folds produce a roughly sawtooth-like excitation whose fundamental is the pitch. The tract above them — pharynx, mouth, sometimes nose — is a resonant tube whose shape you control with tongue, jaw and lips. Its resonances (formants) impose peaks on the spectral envelope, and the first two formants alone determine the vowel almost completely. This source-filter separation is the basis of speech science, of the vocoder, of linear predictive coding, and of formant-corrected pitch shifting.

head: Vowel (as in)
F1 (Hz, approx.)
F2 (Hz, approx.)
Note
rows: Low F1, very high F2: the widest spread of any vowel.
High F1, low F2: the two formants converge.
Both low; lip rounding lowers all formants.
Neutral tract, roughly evenly spaced resonances.

blocks.html: Values after Peterson and Barney's 1952 measurements, which remain the reference despite being drawn from a specific American English population — a good example of how a "standard" table encodes a sample. Formant frequencies scale roughly inversely with tract length, so a child's formants sit 20-25% higher than an adult male's for the same vowel. This is why a naive pitch shift changes perceived body size: it moves the formants along with the pitch, which never happens in nature.

blocks.label: The practical consequence for EQ
blocks.html: Because formants are fixed and harmonics move, a fixed-frequency EQ boost on a melodic instrument is a formant operation, not a harmonic one. Boosting 3 kHz on a vocal emphasises whichever harmonics happen to land there, which changes with the sung note. This is why a static EQ that sounds right on the verse can sound aggressive on the chorus a fifth higher, and why dynamic EQ tied to level often behaves more musically than a fixed filter.

blocks.q: Why does playing a piano recording backwards make it sound unlike a piano?
options: Because the spectrum is reversed
Because the temporal envelope is reversed, and the sharp attack followed by exponential decay is a primary identification cue
Because the harmonics become inharmonic
Because the phase relationships invert
blocks.explain: At any instant the spectrum is essentially unchanged. What changes is the envelope: a slow swell into an abrupt cut-off is a shape no struck string produces, so the auditory system has no matching template. It is the clearest single demonstration that timbre is not a property of the spectrum alone, and it undermines any account of instrument identity based only on harmonic content.

blocks.html: The unresolved part: we still do not have a timbre space that predicts perceptual similarity reliably across instrument families and playing styles. Grey's three dimensions work within a set of orchestral tones at matched pitch and loudness; they generalise poorly to percussion, to electronic sounds, and to real performances where dynamics change the spectrum continuously (a trumpet played loudly is not a louder version of a trumpet played softly — its spectral centroid moves up by an octave or more). Any plug-in advertising "timbre matching" is doing something considerably narrower than its name suggests.

lessons.title: Nonlinearity: Harmonic and Intermodulation Distortion
glossary: Linear system
One obeying superposition and homogeneity. A linear system can change the amplitude and phase of existing frequencies but can never create new ones.
THD
Total harmonic distortion: the RMS sum of harmonic products relative to the fundamental, usually as a percentage or in dB.
THD+N
Total harmonic distortion plus noise, measured by notching out the fundamental and measuring everything left.
Intermodulation distortion (IMD)
Sum and difference products created when two or more tones pass through a nonlinearity.
Even-order distortion
Products at 2f, 4f ... produced by asymmetric transfer curves. Musically consonant (octaves).
Odd-order distortion
Products at 3f, 5f ... produced by symmetric compression. Musically dissonant (fifths and beyond) and characteristic of hard clipping.

blocks.html: A linear system cannot create a frequency that was not already present. This is not a rule of thumb; it is the definition. Filters, delays, mixers and level controls are linear (to a good approximation) and therefore cannot add harmonics. Any device that adds harmonics is nonlinear, which means its output is not a scaled copy of its input. All the interesting colour in audio — valves, tape, transformers, saturation, clipping — comes from deliberate nonlinearity, and all the ugliest artefacts come from accidental nonlinearity.

blocks.label: Total harmonic distortion
blocks.caption: 1% THD is -40 dB; 0.1% is -60 dB; 0.01% is -80 dB. A number this compact hides everything that matters: which harmonics, at what level, and how they behave with frequency and amplitude.

blocks.html: A polynomial transfer curve makes the mechanism concrete. If the output is y = x + a2x2 + a3x3, then feeding in a sine at frequency f gives, from the squared term, a component at 2f plus a DC offset, and from the cubed term a component at 3f plus a change in the level at f. Squaring is an asymmetric operation and produces even harmonics; cubing is symmetric and produces odd. This is why a single-ended valve stage (asymmetric) is described as producing "warm" second-harmonic colour while a push-pull stage or a hard clipper (symmetric) produces third-harmonic hardness.

head: Order
Products from a 1 kHz tone
Musical interval above fundamental
Typical source
rows: Asymmetric clipping, single-ended valve stages, transformer core.
Symmetric compression, push-pull stages, tape at high level.
Hard clipping; the first order that sounds clearly unpleasant.
Hard digital clipping; crossover distortion in class-B stages.

blocks.text: Intermodulation is the one that actually hurts

blocks.html: Harmonic distortion products are, by construction, musically related to the source. Intermodulation products are not. Two tones at f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> through a second-order nonlinearity produce f<sub>2</sub> - f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> + f<sub>1</sub>; through a third-order nonlinearity they produce 2f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub> and 2f<sub>2</sub> - f<sub>1</sub>. On real programme material with dozens of simultaneous partials, the number of products grows combinatorially and they land at frequencies unrelated to anything musical. This is why 1% IMD is far more objectionable than 1% THD, and why the SMPTE (60 Hz + 7 kHz, 4:1) and CCIF/DIN (19 kHz + 20 kHz) intermodulation tests exist alongside THD.

blocks.label: Second- and third-order intermodulation products
blocks.caption: With f1 = 19 kHz and f2 = 20 kHz, the third-order difference product 2f1 - f2 lands at 18 kHz and 2f2 - f1 at 21 kHz. The CCIF test looks for the 1 kHz difference tone, which is inaudible in the source and glaring in the output.

blocks.label: Why a THD figure alone is nearly meaningless
blocks.html: A device with 0.5% THD that is entirely 2nd harmonic can sound rich and pleasant. A device with 0.02% THD that is entirely 9th and 11th harmonic can sound brittle and unpleasant. Two amplifiers with identical THD specifications can differ audibly because one produces a distortion spectrum that falls steeply with order and the other does not. Ask for a distortion spectrum against level and frequency, not a single percentage. This point was made forcefully by Peter Baxandall in the 1970s and is still routinely ignored in marketing.

blocks.q: A guitar amplifier is driven into symmetric clipping. Which harmonics dominate?
options: Even harmonics: 2nd, 4th, 6th
Odd harmonics: 3rd, 5th, 7th
All harmonics equally
Only the fundamental, at reduced level
blocks.explain: A symmetric transfer curve — one where f(-x) = -f(x) — contains only odd powers, so it can only generate odd harmonics. Asymmetric clipping (one half of the waveform flattening before the other) is what produces even-order products. This is a real design lever: valve amplifiers biased asymmetrically produce a mix of both, which is a large part of why they are described as sounding different from a symmetric solid-state clipper at the same THD.

blocks.html: An opinion worth arguing about: "analogue warmth" is not a mystery. It is a measurable combination of low-order harmonic distortion that rises with level, frequency-dependent compression, a limited bandwidth that removes the harshest upper products, and small amounts of noise and wow that decorrelate the signal. Every one of those is reproducible digitally, and good emulations do reproduce them. What emulations often miss is the interaction: real circuits change their distortion characteristics with source impedance, with supply sag, and with temperature, so the same setting behaves differently from moment to moment. That dynamic behaviour, not some unmeasurable essence, is what still separates the best hardware from most plug-ins.

blocks.title: Assignment 5 — Analysis and resynthesis of a real timbre
blocks.brief: Choose one sustained instrumental or vocal note that you can record cleanly. Part A, analysis: measure the fundamental, the frequencies and levels of at least the first eight partials, and the deviation of each from an exact harmonic. Report the spectral centroid, computed from your measured values, and the attack time to 90% of peak amplitude. State your analysis window length and window function and justify both. Part B, resynthesis: rebuild the note additively (any DAW, synth or code) using your measured partial amplitudes and a matched amplitude envelope. Part C, evaluation: compare original and resynthesis level-matched and blind if possible, describe precisely what is missing, and then improve the resynthesis with one targeted addition (noise in the attack, partial-specific envelopes, or vibrato/jitter). Report what that addition changed.
items: A strong result justifies the analysis window length numerically against the fundamental frequency and the required resolution.
A strong result reports harmonic deviations in cents or hertz rather than describing them as "slightly off".
A strong result computes the spectral centroid from data and comments on whether it matches the perceived brightness.
A strong result identifies the attack transient as the largest missing element, and demonstrates the improvement from addressing it.
A strong result recognises that static partial amplitudes are the fundamental limitation, because real partials have individual envelopes.
A weak result presents a screenshot of an analyser without extracting numbers, or resynthesises with a preset and claims a match.

questions.q: A tone has a fundamental of 82.4 Hz (low E on a guitar). What is the frequency of its 7th harmonic?
questions.explain: 7 x 82.4 = 576.8 Hz. Harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental by definition; the 7th is 2 octaves and a minor seventh above, and it is about 31 cents flat of the equal-tempered pitch, which is why it is often described as a "blue" note.

questions.q: At a 48 kHz sample rate, what is the frequency resolution of a 2,048-point FFT?
questions.explain: 48,000 / 2,048 = 23.44 Hz per bin, over a window of 2,048/48,000 = 42.7 ms. At 50 Hz that resolution is nearly half an octave, which is why low-frequency measurement needs much longer windows.

questions.q: Two tones at 19 kHz and 20 kHz pass through a third-order nonlinearity. What is the frequency of the 2f1 - f2 intermodulation product?
questions.explain: 2 x 19,000 - 20,000 = 18,000 Hz. The other third-order product, 2f2 - f1, lands at 21,000 Hz. The CCIF twin-tone test uses exactly this pair because the second-order difference product at 1 kHz is squarely in the most audible region and cannot come from anything but distortion.

questions.q: Which statement about a linear system is correct?
options: It can attenuate frequencies but not amplify them
It cannot create frequencies that were not present at its input
It preserves phase exactly
It has zero distortion by definition of the word linear, including intermodulation
why: Linear systems can have any gain, positive or negative in dB.

Correct. Superposition guarantees that the output contains only frequencies present in the input, possibly with different amplitudes and phases. Creating new frequencies requires nonlinearity, or a time-varying system.
Linear systems routinely alter phase — every filter does — and a linear phase response is a special design case, not a definition.
This is nearly right but sloppy: a linear time-varying system (a tremolo, a ring modulator) also creates new frequencies without being nonlinear in the amplitude sense.
questions.explain: The "no new frequencies" test is the fastest way to classify a process. If you see harmonics appear that were not in the source, either the system is nonlinear or it is time-varying. Both possibilities are worth checking.

questions.q: Select every factor that contributes materially to the perceived timbre of an instrument.
options: The relative amplitudes of the harmonics
The attack transient
The absolute phase relationships between harmonics
Inharmonicity of the upper partials
How the spectrum changes with playing dynamics
why: True and obvious; the spectral envelope is the classic account of timbre.
True and under-appreciated. Removing the first 50 ms of a trumpet note substantially impairs identification (Risset and Wessel).

Largely false for steady tones. Ohm's acoustic law holds well enough that phase-scrambled versions with identical magnitude spectra are difficult to distinguish on loudspeakers, though large group delays and headphone listening are exceptions.
True. Piano stretch, bell partials and drum modal ratios are central to instrument identity.
True and often decisive. A loudly played trumpet has a spectral centroid an octave or more above a quiet one; it is not simply a louder version.
questions.explain: Timbre is a multidimensional, time-varying property. Any account that reduces it to "the harmonic content" fails to predict the backwards-piano result or the dynamics-dependence of brass.

questions.q: Order these waveforms by increasing spectral centroid (dullest to brightest) at equal fundamental and equal RMS level.
items: Sine
Triangle
Square
Sawtooth
Impulse train
questions.explain: A sine has all its energy at the fundamental. The triangle rolls off at 12 dB/octave, the square and sawtooth at 6 dB/octave (the sawtooth having twice as many partials), and an impulse train has a flat spectrum. Spectral centroid tracks this ordering and correlates strongly with perceived brightness.

questions.q: Match each spectral characteristic to its physical cause.
pairs: Only odd harmonics present
A tube or resonator closed at one end, or a symmetric nonlinearity
Partials progressively sharp of exact multiples
String bending stiffness (inharmonicity)
Fixed spectral peaks that do not move with pitch
Formants: resonances of the sound-producing body
Strong 2nd harmonic that grows with level
Asymmetric transfer characteristic
Sum and difference products unrelated to the source
Intermodulation distortion from a nonlinearity with two or more inputs
questions.explain: Every spectral feature has a mechanical or circuit cause. Being able to run the inference backwards, from spectrum to mechanism, is the diagnostic skill this module is training.

questions.stem: A mastering engineer receives a mix that measures 0.4% THD at 1 kHz, which the client considers unacceptably high. Analysis shows the distortion spectrum is dominated by the 2nd harmonic at -50 dB with the 3rd at -62 dB and nothing measurable above the 4th. A second version of the same mix measures 0.05% THD, but its distortion spectrum shows small products at the 7th, 9th and 11th harmonics, all around -70 dB, and a CCIF twin-tone test shows a 1 kHz difference product at -58 dB.

qs.q: Which version is more likely to sound cleaner, and why?
options: The 0.05% version, because lower THD always means cleaner
The 0.4% version, because its distortion is low-order and musically related while the other has high-order and intermodulation products
Neither; 0.4% and 0.05% are both inaudible
It cannot be determined from distortion measurements at all
why: THD as a single number is a poor predictor of audibility; the distribution across orders matters far more.

Correct. Second-harmonic distortion at -50 dB is an octave doubling and is frequently inaudible or even flattering; high-order products at -70 dB are dissonant, and a -58 dB intermodulation difference product is a strong indicator of an audible problem because it is unrelated to the source.
A -58 dB non-harmonic difference tone is well above threshold on many programme material and is not safely dismissed.
It can be determined reasonably well, provided you look at the spectrum rather than the single-number summary.
qs.explain: This is the practical case against THD as a headline specification, argued by Baxandall and others for fifty years. Order distribution and intermodulation behaviour predict audibility far better than the aggregate percentage.

qs.q: The 2nd harmonic sits at -50 dB relative to the fundamental. Expressed as a percentage of the fundamental amplitude, what is that?
qs.explain: 10^(-50/20) = 0.00316, i.e. 0.316%. Since the 3rd at -62 dB contributes only 0.079%, the RMS sum is sqrt(0.316^2 + 0.079^2) = 0.326%, close to the stated 0.4% once the 4th harmonic is included.

qs.q: The client insists on the 0.05% version anyway. Draft the technical argument you would make, and state what evidence would change your mind.
qs.model: The argument: a single THD percentage aggregates products of all orders into one number, weighting them only by amplitude and not by audibility. Auditory masking means a 2nd harmonic at -50 dB is close in frequency to the fundamental, falls within or near the same critical band region, and is an exact octave, so it is heavily masked and musically consonant; the ear tolerates it at levels an order of magnitude above what it tolerates for high-order products. The 7th, 9th and 11th harmonics are dissonant intervals that fall outside the masking skirt of the fundamental and are perceived as hardness or grain. Most decisively, the CCIF result: a 1 kHz difference product at -58 dB is not a harmonic of anything in the source, so it has no musical relationship to the programme, cannot be masked by an octave relationship, and appears whenever two strong partials coexist, which on real music is constantly. I would therefore recommend the 0.4% version on the evidence available. What would change my mind: a properly conducted level-matched blind comparison on the actual programme material showing a consistent preference for the 0.05% version; a demonstration that the 2nd-harmonic version has other problems the THD number is hiding, such as level-dependent behaviour that becomes gross at peaks; or a delivery context where the material will be further processed in ways that amplify low-order distortion, for example heavy downstream limiting or lossy encoding at a low bit rate. Measurements are evidence, not verdicts, and the correct next step is a listening test rather than an argument about numbers.
points: Explains that THD aggregates dissimilar products into one figure
Argues from masking and musical interval why low-order distortion is more tolerable
Identifies the intermodulation product as the decisive evidence and explains why it is worse
States specific evidence that would change the conclusion, including a level-matched blind test

questions.q: Why does zero-padding an FFT not improve frequency resolution?
options: Because it adds noise
Because resolution is set by the duration of actual signal observed, and padding adds no new observation
Because zeros bias the amplitude downward
Because the FFT requires a power-of-two length
why: Zeros add no noise; they are exactly zero.

Correct. Frequency resolution is fundamentally 1/T where T is the length of real data. Zero-padding interpolates between existing bins, producing a smoother-looking spectrum with more points, but it cannot separate two components that the observation length could not distinguish.
Padding does reduce the per-bin amplitude scaling, but that is a normalisation matter and not the reason resolution is unchanged.
Modern FFT implementations handle arbitrary lengths; and in any case that would be an implementation constraint, not a resolution argument.
questions.explain: The distinction between resolution (what you can separate) and interpolation (how finely you sample the display) trips up almost everyone at first. Zero-padding is useful for accurate peak-frequency estimation, and useless for separating close components.

questions.q: Explain, with reference to specific mechanisms, why transposing a vocal sample up a perfect fifth makes it sound like a smaller person, and describe how a formant-corrected pitch shifter avoids this.
questions.model: A vocal is well described by a source-filter model: the vocal folds produce a periodic, harmonically rich excitation whose fundamental is the pitch, and the vocal tract acts as a resonant filter imposing fixed peaks — formants — on the spectral envelope. The formant frequencies depend on the geometry of the tract, and tract length scales with body size, so listeners use formant positions as a cue to speaker size; a child's formants sit roughly 20-25% above an adult male's for the same vowel. Naive transposition, whether by varispeed or by a simple resampling shifter, multiplies every frequency in the signal by the same factor. That correctly moves the harmonics, which is what you wanted, but it also moves the formants by the same 1.5 ratio, which never happens when a real person sings higher: a singer changes fold tension, not tract length. The listener therefore infers a much shorter tract and hears a smaller speaker, the chipmunk effect. A formant-corrected shifter separates the two: it estimates the spectral envelope (by cepstral liftering, by linear prediction, or by channel vocoder analysis), removes it from the signal to obtain a flattened excitation, transposes only the excitation, and then reapplies the original envelope. The harmonics move; the formants stay. The practical limits are that envelope estimation is imperfect on breathy or noisy material, that transients are smeared by the analysis frames, and that the technique assumes source and filter are independent, which is only approximately true because the tract loads the folds and strongly influences their behaviour at high levels.
points: States the source-filter model explicitly
Explains that formants are fixed by tract geometry and are a size cue
Identifies that naive transposition scales formants with the pitch
Describes envelope estimation, transposition of the excitation, and re-application
Names at least one limitation of the technique

questions.q: A clarinet is often described as having a "hollow" tone. What is the physical basis?
options: Its bore is conical, producing only odd harmonics
It is a cylindrical tube effectively closed at the reed end, so it resonates predominantly at odd multiples of its quarter-wave frequency
Its reed vibrates at half the frequency of the air column
Its material absorbs even harmonics
why: A conical bore (oboe, saxophone) produces a full harmonic series; it is the cylindrical bore that produces odd-dominant spectra.

Correct. A cylinder closed at one end supports modes at c/4L, 3c/4L, 5c/4L and so on. The missing even harmonics remove the octave reinforcement, which the ear reports as hollowness, and it is also why the clarinet overblows a twelfth rather than an octave.
The reed is driven at the resonance of the air column, not at a subharmonic of it.
Materials have essentially no effect on the harmonic content of a wind instrument; the air column geometry does the work.
questions.explain: The same c/4L relation appears in three places in this course: the stopped pipe, the ear canal resonance near 3.4 kHz, and the quarter-wavelength boundary-cancellation rule. Recognising one physical relation in several disguises is most of what fluency in acoustics means.

modules.title: Room Acoustics
modules.tagline: Reflections, modes, reverberation and treatment. Why small rooms are harder than large ones, and what to fix first.
objectives: Able to compute axial, tangential and oblique room modes and identify which will cause audible problems.
Able to calculate reverberation time with the Sabine and Eyring equations and state where each fails.
Able to compute the Schroeder frequency and explain why a room behaves as two different acoustic systems either side of it.
Able to locate first-reflection points geometrically and justify absorption placement quantitatively.
Able to design a defensible treatment plan for a small room, in priority order, with a stated budget of absorption.

lessons.title: The Life of a Sound in a Room
glossary: Direct sound
The first arrival, travelling straight from source to receiver, carrying the localisation cue.
Early reflections
Reflections arriving within roughly the first 50-80 ms; fused with the direct sound but altering timbre and image.
Reverberant field
The statistically dense, diffuse later portion of the response, where individual reflections are no longer distinguishable.
Critical distance
The distance at which direct and reverberant sound are equal in level.
Direct-to-reverberant ratio
The energy ratio between direct sound and everything after it; the dominant cue for perceived distance.
Diffuse field
An idealised sound field in which energy arrives equally from all directions and energy density is uniform. Almost no real room fully achieves it.

blocks.html: Play a click in a room and a receiver records three things in succession: one direct arrival, a sparse set of discrete early reflections, and then a dense, decaying tail in which reflections arrive faster than the ear can separate them. These three regions are perceived quite differently, they are controlled by different treatment, and confusing them is the most common failure in room design.

blocks.caption: An energy-time curve. The direct sound gives localisation, the early reflections give timbre and apparent width, and the tail gives the sense of space. Treatment that shortens the tail does not fix an early-reflection problem.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 6
items: Master Handbook of Acoustics (6th ed.) — F. Alton Everest & Ken Pohlmann
Required. Chapters 9-13 (reverberation, modes, absorption, diffusion) and Chapter 20 on small-room design. This is the core text for the module; work the numerical examples.
Sound Reproduction (3rd ed.) — Floyd E. Toole

Required. Chapters 8-13 on rooms, reflections, and the evidence about what listeners actually prefer. Toole's position that early reflections are not universally harmful is the strongest challenge to conventional studio practice; read it as an argument, not as settled fact.
Acoustic Absorbers and Diffusers (3rd ed.) — Trevor J. Cox & Peter D'Antonio
Required. Chapters 5-6 on porous absorption and Chapters 9-10 on diffuser design. Read Chapter 6 specifically for why quarter-wavelength spacing matters and what it costs.
ISO 3382-1:2009, Acoustics — Measurement of room acoustic parameters, Part 1: Performance spaces
Required as reference. Read the definitions of T20, T30, EDT, C50, C80 and the measurement procedure. You should be able to say what each parameter is for.
Schroeder, M. R., "New Method of Measuring Reverberation Time", JASA 37, 1965, pp. 409-412
Required. Two pages. The backward-integration method that made reliable RT measurement possible, and still the basis of every measurement system you will use.
Sabine, W. C., Collected Papers on Acoustics (1922)
Optional. The founding document of architectural acoustics. Read the Fogg Lecture Room chapter for how the constant 0.161 was actually established.

blocks.label: Critical distance
blocks.caption: Q is the source directivity factor (1 for omnidirectional, 2 on a hard floor, 5-10 for a typical loudspeaker on-axis), R is the room constant in square metres, S the total surface area and alpha-bar the average absorption coefficient. Beyond Dc, moving further away no longer reduces the level.

blocks.html: Critical distance is the number that decides whether a room is "live" or "dead" in practice. In a treated 90 m<sup>3</sup> control room with average absorption around 0.25 and a monitor with Q about 6, R = 126 x 0.25 / 0.75 = 42 m<sup>2</sup> and D<sub>c</sub> = 0.141 √(6 x 42) = 2.2 m. Your listening position at 2 m is just inside it, meaning direct sound narrowly dominates. In an untreated bedroom with alpha-bar of 0.10, R falls to 14 m<sup>2</sup> and D<sub>c</sub> drops to 1.3 m — so at a normal 2 m listening distance you are hearing mostly room, which is exactly why untreated rooms sound "washy" and refuse to translate.

head: Arrival window
Perceptual role
Measured by
Controlled by
rows: Timbral colouration, comb filtering, image smear
Absorption at first-reflection points; desk and console geometry.
Apparent source width, loudness support, speech clarity
Side-wall treatment or deliberate lateral reflections.
Total absorption in the room; volume.

blocks.label: The small-room problem in one sentence
blocks.html: In a small room, the first reflections arrive so early (3-15 ms) that they fall inside the fusion window and colour the timbre instead of adding a sense of space, while the modal density at low frequencies is so sparse that individual modes dominate the response. Large halls have neither problem. Small rooms are not scaled-down halls; they are a different acoustic regime.

blocks.text: The genuine controversy: are early reflections bad?

blocks.html: Conventional studio practice since the 1980s has been to absorb first reflections heavily, following the "reflection-free zone" and LEDE (Live End Dead End) concepts of Davis and Davis. Floyd Toole, drawing on decades of controlled listening tests at the NRC and Harman, argues that this is largely wrong for listening rooms: listeners consistently prefer some lateral reflection energy, which increases apparent source width and envelopment, and the auditory system adapts to a room's signature within seconds. His position is that a loudspeaker with smooth off-axis response in a moderately reflective room outperforms a heavily deadened room.

The counter-argument is that mixing is not listening: an engineer needs to hear the recording's own spatial information, not the room's, and a room that flatters will cause decisions that do not translate. Both camps agree on more than they admit — everyone wants smooth loudspeaker directivity, controlled low frequencies, and no strong specular reflection within the first few milliseconds. What would settle it is a properly controlled study of mix outcomes, not listening preferences: take the same engineers, the same programme, and vary the room, then evaluate the resulting mixes blind on neutral systems. Nobody has done it at adequate scale. My own practice: absorb the very earliest reflections (under about 10 ms), treat the low end aggressively, and leave the rear of the room diffuse rather than dead.

blocks.q: A listener moves from 1 m to 4 m from a loudspeaker in a room whose critical distance is 1.5 m. What happens to the measured level?
options: It falls by 12 dB, following the inverse-square law
It falls by considerably less than 12 dB, because beyond the critical distance the reverberant field dominates
It stays exactly the same
It falls by 6 dB
blocks.explain: Inside the critical distance the direct field dominates and the 6 dB per doubling rule applies. Beyond it, the reverberant field is roughly uniform, so level flattens out. Moving 1 m to 4 m in this room might lose only 4-6 dB rather than 12. The consequence for measurement is important: any speaker sensitivity or frequency response measurement taken beyond Dc is measuring the room, not the loudspeaker.

lessons.title: Room Modes and the Small-Room Problem
glossary: Room mode
A standing wave supported by the room geometry, at which sound energy accumulates.
Axial mode
A mode involving one pair of parallel surfaces. The strongest type.
Tangential mode
A mode involving four surfaces; roughly 3 dB weaker than axial.
Oblique mode
A mode involving all six surfaces; roughly 6 dB weaker than axial.
Schroeder frequency
The frequency above which modes overlap enough that statistical (reverberant) behaviour takes over.
Modal ringing
The prolonged decay of energy at a modal frequency, heard as a pitched hangover on bass notes.
Speaker boundary interference response (SBIR)
The comb filtering caused by the reflection from the wall behind a loudspeaker, distinct from modal behaviour.

blocks.html: A pair of parallel rigid walls a distance L apart supports a standing wave whenever a half wavelength fits a whole number of times between them. Pressure is always maximum at a rigid boundary (particle velocity is zero there), so the modal pattern has pressure antinodes at the walls and nulls in between. The general expression for a rectangular room, due to Rayleigh, is worth memorising because every practical case is a special case of it.

blocks.label: Rayleigh mode equation for a rectangular room
blocks.caption: p, q, r are non-negative integers, not all zero. With two of them zero you get the axial modes f = nc/2L; with one zero, tangential; with none zero, oblique.

The first three axial modes between one pair of walls. Note the invariant: pressure is maximum at every rigid boundary for every mode. That is why corners excite and reinforce all modes, and why corners are where bass traps go.

head: Mode type
Surfaces involved
Relative energy
Example in a 6.4 x 4.8 x 2.9 m room

blocks.html: Below about 100 Hz in a small room there are only a handful of modes, widely spaced, and each one dominates its own frequency region. The result is a response with 15-25 dB peaks and nulls that changes completely if you move a metre. Above a certain frequency the modes become so numerous and so overlapped that the response becomes statistically smooth and the room behaves like a reverberant field. That crossover has a name and a formula.

blocks.label: Schroeder frequency
blocks.caption: T60 in seconds, V in cubic metres. Below fS, treat the room modally and think in terms of individual resonances; above it, treat it statistically and think in terms of reverberation and reflections.

blocks.html: For a typical 90 m3 project studio with an RT60 of 0.4 s, fS = 2000 √(0.4/90) = 133 Hz. For a 15,000 m3 concert hall with an RT60 of 2 s, fS = 2000 √(2/15000) = 23 Hz — below the audible range. This is the mathematical statement of why small rooms are hard. A concert hall has essentially no modal region within hearing; a bedroom studio has a modal region covering the entire bass range.

blocks.label: Three interventions that actually work below the Schroeder frequency
blocks.html: 1. Move the source or the listener. A mode cannot be excited from its own pressure null, and cannot be heard at one. Moving a subwoofer 60 cm can be worth 10 dB. 2. Add real absorption at the pressure maxima — corners, where all modes have an antinode. This requires depth: porous traps need to be a substantial fraction of a quarter wavelength, so 30-60 cm minimum, or use tuned membrane devices. 3. Use multiple subwoofers. Welti and Devantier (AES, 2006) showed that four subwoofers in a symmetric arrangement can flatten the seat-to-seat variation dramatically by cancelling the dominant modes. What does not work reliably: EQ. It can pull down a peak at one position, but it cannot fill a null (there is nothing there to boost) and the correction is only valid at the measurement point.

blocks.text: Room ratios: useful, oversold

blocks.html: Published "ideal" room ratios (Sepmeyer, Louden, Bolt's area, the 1:1.4:1.9 family) aim to spread the low modes as evenly as possible so that no two coincide and no large gaps appear. They are genuinely useful when you are designing a room from nothing. They are close to useless as an evaluation of an existing room, because you cannot change your walls, and because they say nothing about the two things that matter more: the absorption you provide and where you sit. A room with unremarkable ratios and 40 cm of corner absorption will outperform a golden-ratio room with bare walls every time.

Also distinguish modes from SBIR. The dip you almost always see between 50 and 150 Hz in a small room is usually not a mode at all: it is the cancellation from the reflection off the wall behind the loudspeaker, with the null at c/4d where d is the speaker-to-wall distance. A speaker 90 cm from the front wall produces a null at 343/3.6 = 95 Hz. The fix is geometric — flush-mount the speaker (d = 0), or pull it far enough out that the null falls below the speaker's useful range — and no amount of corner absorption will remove it.

blocks.q: A room is 3.6 m wide. What is the frequency of the first axial width mode, and where is its pressure null?
options: 47.6 Hz, null at the centre of the room
95.3 Hz, null at the walls
47.6 Hz, null at the walls
23.8 Hz, null at the centre
blocks.explain: f = c/2L = 343/7.2 = 47.6 Hz. The first axial mode has pressure maxima at both walls and a single pressure null exactly halfway between them. Sitting in the middle of the room widthwise therefore puts you in a null at 47.6 Hz — which is why the classic "sit in the exact centre" advice is bad advice for the width dimension, though centring for symmetry between the loudspeakers is still essential.

blocks.html: A room below its Schroeder frequency is like a wind instrument: a few strong, discrete resonances that determine everything. Above it, the room is like a bag of gravel: so many overlapping resonances that only the statistics matter. Treatment strategies that work on a wind instrument (change the geometry, damp specific resonances) are quite different from those that work on gravel (add absorption anywhere and it averages out).

lessons.title: Reverberation Time: Sabine, Eyring and Their Limits
glossary: RT60
The time for the sound level to decay by 60 dB after the source stops.
RT60 extrapolated from a 20 dB or 30 dB portion of the decay, since a full 60 dB is rarely measurable above the noise floor.
EDT
Early decay time: RT extrapolated from the first 10 dB. Correlates better with perceived reverberance than T30.
Sabin
The unit of absorption: one square metre of perfectly absorbing surface (metric sabin).
Absorption coefficient
Alpha: the fraction of incident energy not reflected, measured per octave or third-octave band in a reverberation chamber per ISO 354.
Clarity indices: the ratio of energy in the first 50 ms (speech) or 80 ms (music) to all later energy, in dB.

blocks.html: Wallace Clement Sabine measured reverberation in the Fogg Lecture Room at Harvard between 1895 and 1900, using an organ pipe, a stopwatch and his own ears, moving seat cushions in and out to vary absorption. He found that decay time was proportional to volume and inversely proportional to total absorption. The relation he derived is still the first calculation anyone does, and it is still the one most often misapplied.

blocks.label: Sabine equation (metric)
blocks.caption: V in cubic metres, A in metric sabins. The second sum covers discrete absorbers (people, chairs, bass traps) quoted in sabins rather than as coefficients. The constant 0.161 embeds the speed of sound; in imperial units it becomes 0.049.

blocks.html: A worked example. A control room 6.4 x 4.8 x 2.9 m has V = 89.1 m<sup>3</sup> and total surface S = 126.4 m<sup>2</sup>. Suppose the average absorption coefficient at 500 Hz is 0.20. Then A = 126.4 x 0.20 = 25.3 sabins and T<sub>60</sub> = 0.161 x 89.1 / 25.3 = 0.57 s. That is far too long for a small control room; the usual target is 0.20-0.35 s, reasonably uniform with frequency. To reach 0.30 s you need A = 0.161 x 89.1 / 0.30 = 47.8 sabins, so alpha-bar must rise to 0.38 — nearly double. In practice that means about 25-30 m<sup>2</sup> of effective broadband absorption, which is a great deal more than most people expect.

blocks.label: Eyring-Norris equation
blocks.caption: The logarithmic form is correct for highly absorbent rooms: as alpha-bar tends to 1, Eyring correctly gives T60 tending to zero, whereas Sabine gives a finite non-zero time. The 4mV term accounts for air absorption and matters above about 2 kHz in large volumes.

head: Average absorption
Sabine T60 (89 m3 room)
Eyring T60
Comment
rows: Untreated domestic room. Sabine is close enough.
Vocal booth. Sabine is nearly twice Eyring; use Eyring.

blocks.label: Five ways an RT60 calculation misleads you
blocks.html: 1. Both equations assume a diffuse field, which small rooms do not have. Below the Schroeder frequency the concept of RT60 is barely meaningful; you are measuring modal decay, not reverberation. 2. Both assume absorption is evenly distributed. A room with a dead front and a live back has a decay that is not a single exponential and no single RT60 describes it. 3. Published absorption coefficients come from ISO 354 reverberation-chamber tests and routinely exceed 1.0 because of edge diffraction; they are not physical fractions and they overstate performance in small patches. 4. RT60 says nothing about when energy arrives. Two rooms with identical RT60 can differ enormously in C50 and in early-reflection structure. 5. A single mid-band figure hides frequency dependence, and low-frequency RT is almost always much longer than mid-band RT in an untreated room.

blocks.title: Measuring RT60 properly
steps: Excite the room

A logarithmic swept sine (Farina's method) is preferred: it gives a high signal-to-noise ratio and separates harmonic distortion into a region of the impulse response you can discard. A balloon pop or starter pistol works but is not repeatable and is spectrally uneven.
Obtain the impulse response
Deconvolve the sweep. Check that the noise floor is at least 45 dB below the peak, or you cannot even measure T30.
Backward-integrate
Apply Schroeder integration: integrate the squared impulse response from the end backwards. This turns a noisy decay into a smooth curve and is why single-shot measurement became reliable in 1965.
Fit over a defined range
Fit a straight line from -5 to -25 dB (T20) or -5 to -35 dB (T30) and extrapolate to 60 dB. Report which you used. The -5 dB start avoids the direct sound.
Report per octave band
A single broadband number is nearly useless. Report at least 125 Hz to 4 kHz in octave bands, and inspect whether low-frequency decay is much longer.
Check for non-linearity
If the decay curve bends, the room has two decay rates (usually a dead upper region and a live low end, or coupled spaces). A single RT60 does not describe it and you should say so.

blocks.q: Why does the Eyring equation give a shorter RT60 than Sabine in absorbent rooms?
options: Because it includes air absorption
Because it models the decay as a sequence of discrete reflections, each losing a fraction of energy, which is correct when a single reflection removes a large fraction
Because it uses a different value for the speed of sound
Because it assumes a smaller room volume
blocks.explain: Sabine's form is effectively a first-order approximation valid when each reflection removes only a small fraction of the energy. Eyring uses -ln(1 - alpha-bar), the exact per-reflection energy loss, which diverges from alpha-bar as alpha-bar grows. At alpha-bar = 0.1 they agree within 5%; at 0.7 Eyring is nearly half. The air-absorption term 4mV is a separate refinement present in the Eyring form as usually quoted.

blocks.html: Opinion: for small rooms, stop leading with RT60. It is the wrong headline number. Report instead: the frequency response at the listening position with 1/6-octave smoothing, the early decay structure in the first 20 ms, the level and timing of the first three reflections, and the low-frequency decay per octave. Those four tell you what to do next. RT60 tells you a single averaged fact about a field your room does not actually have.

lessons.title: Treatment: Absorption, Diffusion, and What to Do First
glossary: Porous absorber
Mineral wool, fibreglass or open-cell foam; dissipates energy through viscous losses as air moves through the pores. Works on particle velocity.
Membrane (panel) absorber
A mass-spring resonator: a limp panel over a sealed air cavity, tuned to a low frequency.
Helmholtz resonator
A cavity with a neck, resonating at a frequency set by neck area, neck length and cavity volume. Narrowband unless damped.
Diffuser
A surface that scatters incident energy over a wide angle rather than absorbing it; QRD and PRD designs derive from Schroeder's number-theoretic sequences.
Gas flow resistivity
The property that determines how well a porous material absorbs. Typical useful range 5,000-15,000 Pa s/m2; denser is not better.
Reflection-free zone
A design goal in which no strong specular reflection reaches the listening position within a stated early window.

blocks.html: Absorption converts acoustic energy to heat. A porous absorber does this through viscous drag as air oscillates through the fibres, which means it works where particle velocity is high — and particle velocity is zero at a rigid boundary. This single fact determines almost everything about how to install absorption, and it is the fact most often ignored.

blocks.label: Quarter-wavelength rule for porous absorbers
blocks.caption: d is total depth including any air gap. Effective absorption starts roughly where the depth reaches a quarter wavelength. To work at 60 Hz you need about 1.43 m of total depth — which is why genuine bass absorption is a construction problem, not a shopping problem.

head: Total depth (material + gap)
Effective from about
Practical form
rows: Thin foam. Kills air, does nothing useful. Avoid.
Standard acoustic panel; only treats the top two octaves.
A reasonable minimum for first-reflection panels.
The single cheapest improvement available: mount the same panel on a 100 mm standoff.
A superchunk corner trap; the practical floor for most rooms.
Full soffit construction or a whole-wall absorber system.

blocks.label: The single most cost-effective acoustic decision
blocks.html: Mount your panels on a standoff. A 100 mm mineral-wool panel mounted flat on the wall is effective from about 860 Hz. The same panel on a 100 mm air gap is effective from about 430 Hz — a full octave lower, for the price of some timber battens. You are moving the absorber into the region where particle velocity is high rather than leaving it where velocity is zero.
