blocks.caption: Locating first-reflection points with a mirror. The technique is exact for specular reflection: the mirror image of the loudspeaker is the virtual source, so wherever you see the driver in the mirror is where the reflection reaches your ears.

blocks.text: Absorption versus diffusion

blocks.html: Absorption removes energy; diffusion redirects it. A diffuser scatters an incident wave over a wide range of angles, converting a strong specular reflection into many weak ones spread in time and direction. Manfred Schroeder's insight in the 1970s was that a well surface whose depths follow a quadratic-residue sequence produces near-uniform scattering over a designed bandwidth. The practical constraints are unforgiving: a diffuser only works above a frequency set by its total depth (the deepest well must be about a quarter wavelength), it needs to be several wavelengths wide to behave as designed, and it must be at least 2-3 m from the listener or you hear the individual well reflections as colouration.

head: Situation
Absorb
Diffuse
Reason
rows: Too close for a diffuser to work; the reflection arrives inside the fusion window.
Rear wall, 3 m or more behind listener
Diffusion preserves liveliness and envelopment without a strong specular return.
Rear wall, under 2 m behind listener
The diffuser is inside its own near field; you will hear well colouration.
All modes have a pressure antinode in corners. Diffusers do nothing below their design frequency.
You want energy retained but decorrelated; a dead drum room is very hard to make exciting.
Usually too low for a diffuser to be in its far field.

blocks.title: Treatment priority order for a small room
steps: 1. Fix the geometry first

Set up symmetrically. Get the speakers and listening position out of the exact centre of the length dimension, aim for the listener at roughly 38% of room length, and set an equilateral triangle. This costs nothing and often gains more than the first thousand pounds of panels.
2. Corners, floor to ceiling
Vertical corner traps as deep as you can tolerate — 30 cm minimum, 60 cm if possible. This addresses modal energy, which is the dominant problem and the hardest to fix later.
3. First reflection points
Side walls, ceiling, and the desk surface. 100 mm mineral wool on a 50-100 mm standoff. Verify with the mirror method rather than guessing.
4. Front wall behind the speakers
Treat or flush-mount to address SBIR. Absorption here must be deep to matter, since the null is usually between 60 and 150 Hz.
5. Rear wall
Absorption if the room is short, diffusion if you have 3 m or more. Do not leave a bare rear wall facing a bare front wall.
6. Measure, then consider EQ

Only after physical treatment. Apply correction above the Schroeder frequency sparingly, and below it only to reduce peaks, never to fill nulls. Correction that requires more than about 6 dB of boost is hiding a problem you should have fixed physically.

blocks.html: Two warnings about products. First, thin open-cell foam sold in wedge or pyramid shapes is close to useless below 1 kHz and yet is the most commonly bought treatment; a room covered in it has an unnaturally dead top end over an untreated bass response, which is arguably worse than doing nothing. Second, treat published absorption coefficients as optimistic: ISO 354 chamber tests measure large samples with exposed edges and routinely report coefficients above 1.0, which is physically impossible as a fraction. A coefficient of 1.15 does not mean 115% absorption; it means the test method over-reads.

blocks.q: You have 100 mm mineral wool panels and want them effective as low as possible. Which mounting gives the best result?
options: Flat against the wall, with a decorative fabric cover
On a 100 mm air gap from the wall
Two panels stacked flat against the wall (200 mm solid)
Angled at 45 degrees across a corner with no gap behind
blocks.explain: A corner-straddling panel is the best of these: it puts the absorber where all modes have a pressure antinode and creates a large triangular air cavity behind it, giving an effective depth well beyond 200 mm. Of the wall-mounted options, the 100 mm gap (effective from about 430 Hz) beats 200 mm of solid material (about 430 Hz too, but at twice the material cost) and both beat flat mounting (860 Hz). The general principle: depth from the boundary matters more than density of material.

blocks.title: Assignment 6 — A quantitative treatment plan
blocks.brief: Produce a treatment plan for a real room you have access to. Part A, analysis: measure the dimensions; compute all axial modes to 300 Hz and the tangential and oblique modes to 120 Hz; identify coincidences (modes within 5% of each other) and gaps (spacings greater than 25 Hz below 100 Hz); compute the Schroeder frequency using a measured or estimated RT60; compute the SBIR null frequency for your current loudspeaker-to-front-wall distance. Part B, target: state a target RT60 and compute, with the Sabine and Eyring equations, the total absorption in sabins required to reach it, and the resulting required average absorption coefficient. Part C, plan: specify actual panels — material, thickness, air gap, area, and location — with a computed absorption contribution per item at 125 Hz, 500 Hz and 2 kHz using published coefficients you cite. State the total achieved absorption per band and whether it meets the target. Part D, honesty: state what your plan will not fix and why.
items: A strong result computes modes with the full Rayleigh equation, not just axial modes, and identifies specific problem frequencies with reasoning.
A strong result computes the Schroeder frequency and uses it to divide the plan into modal and statistical strategies.
A strong result distinguishes SBIR from modal behaviour and proposes the correct (geometric) fix for it.
A strong result computes absorption per octave band, not a single broadband figure, and shows that low-frequency absorption is the binding constraint.
A strong result cites the source of every absorption coefficient used and notes that chamber-measured values overstate small-patch performance.
A strong result states explicitly what cannot be fixed (a null at the listening position, insufficient depth for the lowest mode) rather than claiming a complete solution.
A weak result lists products from a retailer without computing their contribution, or proposes EQ as a substitute for absorption below the Schroeder frequency.

questions.q: A room is 5.2 m long. What is the frequency of its first axial length mode? Use c = 343 m/s.
questions.explain: 343/(2 x 5.2) = 32.98 Hz. Its harmonics follow at 65.96, 98.94 Hz and so on. The pressure null of the first mode sits at the midpoint of the length, 2.6 m from each end wall.

questions.q: A studio has a volume of 120 m3, a total surface area of 160 m2, and an average absorption coefficient of 0.25. What is the Sabine RT60?
questions.hint: T60 = 0.161 V / A, with A = S x alpha
questions.explain: A = 160 x 0.25 = 40 sabins. T60 = 0.161 x 120 / 40 = 19.32/40 = 0.483 s. The Eyring value is 0.161 x 120 / (-160 x ln(0.75)) = 19.32 / 46.0 = 0.42 s, about 13% shorter, which is a fair indication of the error you accept by using Sabine at this absorption level.

questions.q: For the same room (V = 120 m3) with an RT60 of 0.48 s, what is the Schroeder frequency?
questions.explain: 2000 x sqrt(0.48/120) = 2000 x sqrt(0.004) = 2000 x 0.0632 = 126.5 Hz. Below this the room behaves modally and treatment must target specific resonances; above it, statistically, and broadband absorption plus reflection control is the right approach.

questions.q: A loudspeaker sits 1.1 m from the front wall. At what frequency does the speaker-boundary interference null occur?
questions.explain: f = c/4d = 343/(4 x 1.1) = 77.9 Hz. The extra path for the reflection is 2.2 m, half a wavelength at 78 Hz. Note that this is not a room mode: it depends only on the speaker-to-wall distance, moves when you move the speaker, and cannot be fixed by corner absorption. Flush-mounting eliminates it entirely.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true of porous absorbers.
options: They dissipate energy through viscous losses as air moves through the material
Mounting them on an air gap improves low-frequency performance
Denser material always absorbs better
They are ineffective at frequencies whose quarter wavelength greatly exceeds their total depth
Published absorption coefficients above 1.0 indicate a faulty product
why: True. The mechanism is viscous drag on oscillating air, which is why porous absorbers respond to particle velocity rather than pressure.
True, and it is the highest-value trick available: an air gap places the material where particle velocity is higher.
False. Beyond an optimum gas flow resistivity (roughly 5,000-15,000 Pa s/m2) the surface begins to reflect rather than admit the wave. Very dense material absorbs worse, not better.
True, and it is the reason 50 mm foam does essentially nothing at 100 Hz.
False. Coefficients above 1.0 are an artefact of the ISO 354 chamber method, principally edge diffraction on the test sample. They indicate a measurement convention, not a defect.
questions.explain: The unifying principle is that porous absorption is a velocity phenomenon requiring depth. Every practical rule — standoffs, corner traps, why thin foam fails — follows from it.

questions.q: Order these treatment interventions by priority for an untreated small room, highest value first.
items: Set up symmetrically and position the listener out of the modal null at about 38% of room length
Floor-to-ceiling corner absorption as deep as possible
Absorption at side-wall, ceiling and desk first-reflection points
Treat the front wall behind the loudspeakers or flush-mount them
Rear-wall absorption or diffusion depending on distance
Measurement-based EQ correction above the Schroeder frequency
questions.explain: Geometry is free and often decisive. Modal energy is the hardest problem and the most expensive to fix late. Reflection control is next. EQ comes last because it can only correct minimum-phase problems at a single position, and cannot fill a null.

questions.q: Match each acoustic problem to its correct primary remedy.
pairs: A deep null at 78 Hz that moves when the speaker moves
Flush-mount the speaker or change its distance from the front wall
Bass notes ringing on at 45 Hz regardless of position
Deep corner absorption and/or multiple subwoofers
Hollow colouration and smeared imaging
Absorption at first-reflection points
A long, splashy decay across the mid and high frequencies
Broadband absorption distributed around the room
Strong specular echo from a bare rear wall 4 m behind
Diffusion or absorption on the rear wall
questions.explain: Correct diagnosis determines the remedy. The single most common error is applying broadband mid-frequency absorption to a problem that is modal or geometric, which makes the room dull without fixing anything.

questions.stem: A client has a 4.2 x 3.4 x 2.4 m spare bedroom converted to a mix room. Measured RT60 at 500 Hz is 0.62 s. The response at the listening position shows a 14 dB peak at 41 Hz, a 12 dB null at 71 Hz, and a broadly even response above 250 Hz. The client has bought twelve 600 x 600 x 50 mm foam panels and mounted them flat on the side walls. The loudspeakers are 90 cm from the front wall.

qs.q: What is the first axial length mode of this room?
qs.explain: 343/(2 x 4.2) = 40.83 Hz, which matches the observed 41 Hz peak almost exactly. The width mode is 343/6.8 = 50.4 Hz and the height mode 343/4.8 = 71.5 Hz.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of the 71 Hz null?
options: The first axial height mode at 71.5 Hz
Speaker-boundary interference from the front wall at c/4d = 95 Hz
A tangential mode
The listener sitting in a pressure null of the height mode, or SBIR from the front wall
why: The height mode at 71.5 Hz is the right frequency, but a mode produces a peak at boundaries and a null only at its pressure null — so the explanation must include where the listener is sitting.
The SBIR null for 90 cm is at 343/3.6 = 95 Hz, not 71 Hz, so this alone does not fit.
The lowest tangential mode here is at about 65 Hz, plausible but weaker than axial and not the best single answer.

Correct. The 71.5 Hz height mode has a pressure null at half the room height, 1.2 m, which is very close to seated ear height. This is one of the most common and least recognised problems in small rooms.
qs.explain: The lesson is that a null is a position problem as much as a room problem. Raising or lowering the listening position, or the height of the room, changes it; absorption alone will not.

qs.q: Write the advice you would give this client, in priority order, with quantitative justification, and explain honestly what the foam they already bought can and cannot do.
qs.model: The foam is 50 mm thick and mounted flat, so it is effective only from about c/4d = 343/0.2 = 1.7 kHz upward. It is therefore doing nothing for either of the measured problems, both of which are below 100 Hz, and it is removing high-frequency energy from a region that measured evenly to begin with. Left as it is, the room will get duller without getting flatter. I would not remove it, but I would remount it on 50-100 mm standoffs, which drops its effective range to about 570-860 Hz, and I would move most of it to first-reflection points verified with a mirror rather than spreading it decoratively. Priority order. First, geometry, which is free: the 71 Hz null is very likely the height mode's pressure null at 1.2 m, close to seated ear height, so raise or lower the listening position by 20-30 cm and re-measure; also move the listening position along the length so it is not at the midpoint, aiming for roughly 38% of 4.2 m, about 1.6 m from the front wall. Second, the front-wall distance: at 90 cm the SBIR null is at 95 Hz; either flush-mount, or move the speakers to within about 25 cm of the wall so the null rises above 340 Hz where it can be handled, or well out into the room. Third, corner absorption: floor-to-ceiling superchunks in all four vertical corners, 40-60 cm across the diagonal, which is the only intervention that meaningfully addresses the 41 Hz mode. Fourth, ceiling and desk reflections. Honest limits: at 41 Hz a quarter wavelength is 2.1 m, so no absorber that fits in this room will fully damp that mode; expect to reduce the peak by perhaps 4-8 dB, not eliminate it. A single subwoofer plus position optimisation, or two subwoofers placed to cancel the length mode, will do more for the bottom octave than any panel. EQ may be used to pull down the 41 Hz peak because it is a resonance with energy present, but must not be used to fill the 71 Hz null, because there is nothing there to boost. Finally, an RT60 of 0.62 s in a 34 m3 room is roughly double a reasonable target of 0.25-0.30 s, and reaching that target requires about 18-20 sabins in a room with only 71 m2 of surface — an average alpha of 0.27, which twelve small foam tiles cannot deliver at any frequency that matters.
points: Identifies that 50 mm foam flat-mounted works only above roughly 1.7 kHz and does nothing below 100 Hz
Prioritises free geometric changes (listening height and position, speaker-to-wall distance) first, with the height-mode null explained
Specifies deep corner absorption as the modal remedy, with a realistic expectation of improvement
Distinguishes correctly between EQ-ing a peak and attempting to fill a null
Gives a quantitative target for total absorption or RT60 and shows the existing treatment is inadequate

questions.q: Why is pressure always at a maximum at a rigid room boundary?
options: Because the wall reflects sound back with a phase inversion
Because particle velocity must be zero at a rigid surface, and pressure and velocity are in quadrature in a standing wave
Because absorption is lowest at walls
Because the wall vibrates in sympathy
why: A rigid boundary reflects pressure with no inversion; a pressure-release boundary (an open end) is the case that inverts.

Correct. Air cannot move through a rigid wall, so particle velocity is forced to zero; in a standing wave pressure and velocity are 90 degrees apart in space, so a velocity null coincides with a pressure antinode.
Absorption varies with material, and the boundary condition holds regardless.
A vibrating wall is a non-rigid boundary, which is a different case and reduces the effect.
questions.explain: This is the single most useful fact in practical room acoustics. It explains why corners are the best place for bass traps (three boundaries meeting means maximum pressure for every mode), why porous absorbers need depth, and why a pressure microphone at a wall reads high at low frequencies.

questions.q: Two rooms have identical measured RT60 at every octave band. What can you conclude about how they will sound?
options: They will sound the same
Very little: RT60 says nothing about the timing and direction of early reflections, which dominate perceived timbre and imaging
One must be larger than the other
They must have the same volume
why: RT60 is an average decay rate. Two rooms can share it while differing entirely in their early-reflection structure, which is what the ear uses first.
Correct. C50, C80, early decay time, the lateral energy fraction, and the level and timing of the first few reflections all vary independently of RT60, and all of them matter more in a small room.
Volume and absorption trade off in the Sabine equation, so equal RT60 tells you only about the ratio V/A.
Same reason: only the ratio is constrained, not the volume.
questions.explain: This is why ISO 3382 defines a family of parameters rather than one. In small rooms, RT60 is arguably the least informative member of that family, and reporting it alone is the commonest way to make a room measurement look rigorous while saying nothing.

questions.q: A client wants to "fix the room with DSP correction instead of panels, because it is cheaper". Give a technically honest response.
questions.model: DSP correction can genuinely help, and refusing it outright is as unserious as relying on it entirely. What it does well: it corrects minimum-phase problems, meaning peaks caused by resonances where energy is genuinely present, and it can compensate broad tonal tilts and loudspeaker anomalies. Below the Schroeder frequency, modal peaks are largely minimum phase, so pulling them down is legitimate and effective. What it cannot do: it cannot fill a null. A null is a cancellation, so there is little or no energy at that frequency at that point; boosting raises noise and drives the loudspeaker hard for no audible benefit, and can cost 10-20 dB of headroom. It cannot fix time-domain problems: a mode that rings for 800 ms still rings after you flatten its amplitude, because you have corrected the steady-state magnitude and not the decay. It cannot fix a problem that varies with position, and correction is exact only at the measurement point or points; move 40 cm and the correction is wrong, sometimes worse than no correction. And it cannot improve the direct-to-reverberant ratio at all, because it processes the signal identically for the direct sound and every reflection. Absorption does all four of those things, which no filter can. The honest recommendation is a hybrid, in this order: geometry first (free), then physical absorption concentrated at corners and first-reflection points, then measurement, then modest DSP correction limited to cuts below the Schroeder frequency and gentle broad shaping above it. If any correction filter requires more than about 6 dB of boost, that is a diagnostic that a physical problem has not been addressed rather than a setting to accept. On cost: a modest amount of mineral wool and timber is usually cheaper than a good correction system, and it also lowers the noise floor and improves the room for recording, which DSP does not.
points: Concedes that DSP genuinely corrects minimum-phase peaks and broad tonal errors
States clearly that it cannot fill nulls and explains why, with the headroom consequence
Notes that it does not shorten modal decay time or improve the direct-to-reverberant ratio
Notes that correction is position-specific
Gives a concrete hybrid recommendation with a threshold that signals an unaddressed physical problem

questions.q: A porous absorber assembly must be effective from 150 Hz upward. What minimum total depth (material plus air gap) does the quarter-wavelength rule require?
questions.explain: d = c/(4f) = 343/(4 x 150) = 0.572 m, about 57 cm. This is why a genuinely broadband corner trap is enormous, and why claims that a 10 cm panel provides "full-range absorption" should be treated as marketing rather than physics.

modules.title: Digital Audio
modules.tagline: Sampling, Nyquist, aliasing, quantisation, dither, jitter and latency — what the numbers in the file actually mean.
objectives: Able to state the Nyquist-Shannon theorem precisely, including its assumptions, and compute alias frequencies.
Able to derive the 6.02n + 1.76 dB dynamic range relation and explain what limits it in practice.
Able to explain why dither is necessary, choose a dither type, and say when noise shaping helps and when it does not.
Able to quantify the audible consequences of jitter and to distinguish clock problems from other faults.
Able to defend a specific choice of sample rate and bit depth for a stated project on evidence rather than habit.

lessons.title: Sampling and the Nyquist-Shannon Theorem
glossary: Sampling
Measuring a continuous signal at regular instants. The result is a sequence of numbers, not a staircase.
Sample rate
The number of samples per second, in hertz. 44,100 Hz for CD, 48,000 Hz for video and most professional work.
Nyquist frequency
Half the sample rate: the highest frequency that can be represented unambiguously.
Bandlimited
Containing no energy above a stated frequency. The theorem's central assumption.
Sinc function
sin(pi x)/(pi x): the ideal interpolation kernel implied by the sampling theorem.
Oversampling
Sampling well above the required rate, then filtering and decimating in the digital domain.

blocks.html: Harry Nyquist established the bandwidth requirement for telegraph signalling in 1928; Claude Shannon gave the modern statement in 1949; Vladimir Kotelnikov had published an equivalent result in the Soviet Union in 1933 and E. T. Whittaker had the interpolation formula in 1915. The theorem states that a signal containing no frequencies at or above B can be exactly reconstructed from samples taken at any rate greater than 2B. Not approximately. Exactly.

blocks.label: The sampling theorem and its reconstruction formula
blocks.caption: The second line is the part usually omitted. Reconstruction is not "joining the dots": each sample is replaced by a sinc function scaled by its value, and the sum is the unique bandlimited signal passing through every sample.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 7
items: Principles of Digital Audio (6th ed.) — Ken C. Pohlmann
Required. Chapters 2-4 on sampling, quantisation and dither, and Chapter 16 on jitter and clocking. This is the standard reference and it is unusually careful with the mathematics.
Lipshitz, S. P., Wannamaker, R. A. & Vanderkooy, J., "Quantization and Dither: A Theoretical Survey", JAES 40(5), 1992, pp. 355-375
Required. The paper that settled how dither actually works and why TPDF at 2 LSB peak-to-peak is the right default. Read the sections on the statistics of the total error signal.
Shannon, C. E., "Communication in the Presence of Noise", Proc. IRE 37(1), 1949, pp. 10-21
Required. Read Sections I-II for the sampling theorem in the original. It is remarkably readable and makes the bandlimiting assumption explicit in a way that most textbook restatements do not.
Lavry, D., "Sampling Theory for Digital Audio" (Lavry Engineering white paper, 2004)
Required. The clearest available argument that very high sample rates trade converter accuracy for bandwidth nobody can hear. Read it as one side of a live argument.
Meyer, E. B. & Moran, D. R., "Audibility of a CD-Standard A/D/A Loop Inserted into High-Resolution Audio Playback", JAES 55(9), 2007, pp. 775-779
Required. The most-cited negative result on high-resolution audibility, and its published criticisms. Read the method section carefully and decide for yourself what it does and does not establish.
Mastering Audio (3rd ed.) — Bob Katz
Required. Chapters on dither, word length reduction and delivery. Katz is opinionated and states when he is being opinionated, which is exactly the right register for this material.

blocks.label: The staircase picture is wrong
blocks.html: Every popular explanation of digital audio shows a staircase and asks you to imagine the "steps" being smoothed away, with the implication that higher sample rates give a "smoother" waveform. This is a serious misunderstanding. The samples are point measurements; the reconstruction filter produces the unique bandlimited waveform through them, and there are no steps in the analogue output of a correctly designed converter. Sample rate determines bandwidth, not resolution or smoothness. Bit depth determines the noise floor. They are orthogonal.

blocks.caption: Undersampling. Seven cycles sampled eight times per window produce exactly the same sample values as one cycle. Nothing downstream can undo this, which is why the anti-alias filter must precede the sampler.

blocks.label: Where an out-of-band component lands
blocks.caption: A 30 kHz tone sampled at 44.1 kHz folds to |30,000 - 44,100| = 14,100 Hz. A 25 kHz tone at 48 kHz folds to 23 kHz. The alias is not a distortion of the original; it is a perfectly good tone at the wrong frequency.

head: Sample rate
Nyquist
Common use
Honest assessment
rows: Chosen to fit PCM on a video recorder in 1979; entirely adequate for delivery.
The sensible default. Integer relationship with video frame rates.
Tracking, mixing with heavy nonlinear processing
Defensible: gives filter designers room and reduces aliasing in nonlinear plug-ins.
Marketing, some archival, sound design for extreme pitch shifting
Doubles storage and CPU for content no one has demonstrated hearing. Genuinely useful for material you will pitch down by an octave or more.
A different architecture entirely; excellent noise floor in-band, enormous ultrasonic noise, awkward to edit.

blocks.text: The high-sample-rate argument, honestly presented

blocks.html: For higher rates: anti-alias and reconstruction filters at 44.1 kHz must transition from passband to stopband between roughly 20 and 22 kHz, which demands a steep filter with either significant passband ripple or long pre-ringing. At 96 kHz the filter can be gentle. Separately — and this is the strongest argument — nonlinear processes (saturation, distortion, compression with fast detectors, and most guitar amp simulations) generate harmonics above Nyquist that fold back as inharmonic aliases. Running such processing at a higher rate, or oversampling internally, genuinely reduces audible artefacts.

Against: the ear's upper limit is around 20 kHz in youth and 12-16 kHz in most working adults; there is no established mechanism for perceiving content above that. Higher rates halve the time available per conversion, which in practice worsens converter linearity and jitter sensitivity. Ultrasonic content can also cause intermodulation in downstream analogue equipment, creating audible artefacts that would not otherwise exist. Meyer and Moran (2007) found listeners could not distinguish a 16/44.1 loop inserted into high-resolution playback, though critics correctly note their programme material may not have contained much ultrasonic content and their statistical power was limited.

My position, marked as opinion: record and mix at 48 kHz (or 96 kHz if your session is dominated by nonlinear processing that does not oversample internally), deliver at whatever the platform wants, and spend the saved CPU on better plug-ins and the saved money on acoustic treatment. The differences that survive a level-matched blind test at these rates are small compared with a 3 dB error in your room's bass response.

blocks.q: A 21 kHz tone is sampled at 32 kHz with no anti-alias filter. Where does it appear?
options: 21 kHz
11 kHz
16 kHz
It disappears
blocks.explain: |21,000 - 32,000| = 11,000 Hz. Because 21 kHz exceeds the 16 kHz Nyquist frequency, it folds down to 11 kHz, where it is squarely audible and completely inseparable from real signal. This is why every converter has a steep analogue filter before the sampler, and why software that generates harmonics must oversample.

lessons.title: Quantisation, Bit Depth and Dither
glossary: Quantisation
Rounding each sample to the nearest available level. Distinct from sampling, which is discretisation in time.
LSB
Least significant bit: the size of one quantisation step.
Quantisation error
The difference between the true and quantised value, bounded by half an LSB.
Dither
Noise added deliberately before quantisation to decorrelate the error from the signal.
TPDF
Triangular probability density function dither, 2 LSB peak-to-peak: the standard correct choice for word-length reduction.
Noise shaping
Feeding quantisation error back through a filter so the resulting noise is redistributed to less audible frequencies.

blocks.html: Quantisation is where digital audio actually loses information. Sampling, given bandlimiting, loses nothing. Quantisation replaces a continuum of possible values with a finite set, and the difference between the true value and the stored one is an error you cannot recover. The size of that error relative to full scale gives the theoretical dynamic range.

blocks.label: Signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio for an ideal converter
blocks.caption: n is the number of bits. The 6.02 comes from 20 log10(2): each bit doubles the number of levels and therefore halves the step size. The 1.76 dB is 10 log10(3/2), the difference between the RMS of a full-scale sine and the RMS of uniformly distributed error.

blocks.html: The derivation is worth following once. An n-bit converter has 2<sup>n</sup> levels. If the step size is q, the quantisation error is uniformly distributed between -q/2 and +q/2, with RMS value q/√12. A full-scale sine has peak-to-peak amplitude 2<sup>n</sup>q, so amplitude 2<sup>n</sup>q/2 and RMS 2<sup>n</sup>q/(2√2). The ratio is 2<sup>n</sup>√12/(2√2) = 2<sup>n</sup>√(3/2), and 20 log<sub>10</sub> of that is 6.02n + 1.76 dB. Every term in that expression has a physical meaning; none of it is a fudge factor.

blocks.caption: Theoretical dynamic range by bit depth, with two reality checks marked. Note that 24-bit theoretical range exceeds by 20 dB anything any converter has ever achieved, and by 55 dB the range of any real acoustic environment.

head: Bit depth
Levels
Theoretical dynamic range
Reality
rows: CD. Adequate for delivery with proper dither; marginal for tracking.
Around the ceiling of real converter performance.
The recording standard. The bottom 25 bits are buried in analogue noise; the point is headroom, not resolution.
Internal DAW summing and some field recorders. Cannot clip in the arithmetic; can still clip at the converter.

blocks.text: Why dither is not optional

blocks.html: If you simply round to the nearest level, the error is correlated with the signal. That makes it distortion, not noise, and distortion of a particularly unpleasant kind: on a fading reverb tail or a quiet passage, the error tracks the waveform and produces harmonics and, worse, granular artefacts as the signal crosses level boundaries. The quiet parts of your music develop a gritty, chirping quality. This is quantisation distortion, and it is audible far above the theoretical noise floor.

blocks.caption: The error waveform beneath is periodic and phase-locked to the signal. Anything periodic and signal-locked is distortion; the ear detects it at levels 20 dB or more below where it would detect equivalent random noise.

blocks.html: Dither fixes this by adding a small amount of random noise before quantisation. Lipshitz, Wannamaker and Vanderkooy showed in 1992 that TPDF dither with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 2 LSB renders both the mean and the variance of the total error independent of the signal — that is, it makes the error a true noise, statistically unrelated to what you recorded. The price is a rise in the noise floor of about 4.77 dB relative to undithered quantisation. The gain is that signals well below one LSB remain audible and undistorted, which is not a metaphor: a properly dithered system can reproduce a sine wave 20 dB below the quantisation step.

head: Dither type
Character
Noise penalty
When to use
rows: Eliminates first-order distortion but leaves noise modulation
Not recommended; TPDF costs little more and is fully correct.
Fully decorrelated error, no noise modulation
The default and correct choice for word-length reduction.
Same total noise power, redistributed away from 2-5 kHz
Total power higher, perceived level 8-18 dB lower
Final 16-bit delivery masters, once, at the very end.
Very low perceived noise, large ultrasonic energy
Use with caution: it can misbehave through lossy codecs and cascaded processing.

blocks.label: Dither rules that matter in practice
blocks.html: Dither once, at the end. Every word-length reduction needs dither, but repeated dithering accumulates noise floor. If your DAW mixes in 32-bit float and you export at 24-bit, the dither is essentially inconsequential; if you export at 16-bit, dither there and only there. Do not noise-shape twice. Cascaded shapers can produce audible ultrasonic build-up. Do not dither into a lossy codec at very low bit rates — the codec's own noise floor is far above the dither and the shaping can confuse its psychoacoustic model. And note that if you are exporting 24-bit from a 32-bit float session, the theoretical benefit of dither is real but the practical benefit is nil, because the analogue noise floor of the recording is 40 dB above the 24-bit LSB.

blocks.q: Why does dither allow a signal below one LSB to be reproduced?
options: Because it increases the number of quantisation levels
Because the added noise causes the quantiser output to switch between levels at a rate proportional to the sub-LSB signal, encoding it in the statistics of the output
Because it filters out the quantisation error
Because it raises the signal above the LSB threshold
blocks.explain: Without dither, a signal below half an LSB quantises to a constant and vanishes entirely. With dither, the sum of signal and noise crosses the decision threshold more often when the signal is high and less often when it is low, so the average of the output tracks the signal even though no single sample can represent it. Information is carried in the density of transitions rather than in individual sample values — the same idea that underlies delta-sigma conversion.

lessons.title: Clocks, Jitter and Latency
glossary: Word clock
The timing reference defining when samples are taken. In a multi-device system exactly one device must be master.
Jitter
Timing deviation of the sampling instants from their ideal positions, measured in picoseconds RMS or as a spectrum.
Sampling jitter
Jitter at the actual conversion instant. The only kind that directly damages the signal.
Interface jitter
Timing variation on a digital transmission link (AES3, S/PDIF, ADAT). Harmful only insofar as it propagates to the conversion clock.
Latency
The delay through a signal path, from the buffer, converter filters, and any look-ahead processing.
Round-trip latency
Input converter + buffer + processing + output converter, which is what a performer monitoring through the computer actually experiences.

blocks.html: The sampling theorem assumes samples are taken at exactly regular intervals. Real clocks wobble. If the sampling instant is displaced by an amount Δt, the sampled value is wrong by the signal's slew rate times Δt — and slew rate is proportional to frequency and amplitude. Jitter therefore produces an error that grows with frequency and with level, appearing as sidebands around every component rather than as a broadband noise floor.

blocks.label: Jitter-induced error level relative to a full-scale sine
blocks.caption: At 20 kHz, 1 ns of RMS jitter gives 2 pi x 20,000 x 1e-9 = 1.26e-4, i.e. -78 dB. 100 ps gives -98 dB, and 10 ps gives -118 dB. At 100 Hz the same 1 ns gives -104 dB.

blocks.html: Two consequences follow immediately. First, jitter matters most at high frequencies and high levels, which is the opposite of where most listeners expect converter problems. Second, the numbers put the issue in perspective: a competent modern converter has sampling jitter well under 100 ps, giving worst-case artefacts around -98 dB at 20 kHz — below the noise floor of any recording made in a real room. Jitter was a genuine practical problem in the 1990s and is largely a solved problem in equipment designed after about 2005, because asynchronous sample-rate conversion and local reclocking became standard.

blocks.label: What still matters about clocking
blocks.html: Not audio quality in the abstract, but synchronisation: in a multi-device digital system, exactly one device must be clock master and everything else must slave to it, or you will get periodic clicks as buffers slip. Choose the master by which device is doing the conversion that matters most, not by price. External "audiophile" master clocks generally make measured jitter worse than a converter's internal clock, because the converter must then use a PLL to recover timing from an external signal rather than using its own local crystal directly. This is the opposite of the marketing, and it is well documented in AES literature.

blocks.text: Latency, and how to budget it

blocks.label: Buffer latency
blocks.caption: A 128-sample buffer at 48 kHz is 2.67 ms. Round trip is typically twice that plus converter filter delay (0.5-1.5 ms) plus any look-ahead processing.

head: Buffer (samples)
At 44.1 kHz
At 48 kHz
At 96 kHz
Practical use
rows: Very low latency tracking; heavy CPU load.
The usual tracking compromise; round trip about 7-9 ms.
Mixing with heavy plug-in counts; unusable for performance.

blocks.html: Perceptual thresholds: musicians generally tolerate round-trip latency up to about 10 ms without complaint; above roughly 15-20 ms most performers begin to adjust their timing and drummers and vocalists are the most sensitive. For context, 10 ms is the acoustic delay from standing 3.4 m from your amplifier — which is why the complaint is not really about the absolute delay but about the fact that a headphone monitor mixes a delayed electronic path with the undelayed bone-conducted and acoustic path, producing comb filtering that the brain finds much more disturbing than delay alone.

items: Look-ahead processing (limiters, transient designers, some pitch correction) adds latency that the DAW must compensate. Delay compensation only works when the plug-in reports its latency correctly; hardware inserts often cannot be compensated automatically.

Linear-phase EQ is a latency device by construction: a symmetric FIR filter of length N has N/2 samples of delay. A linear-phase EQ working to 20 Hz needs a very long filter and can add tens of milliseconds.
Oversampling plug-ins add the latency of their internal up- and down-sampling filters, often 1-4 ms each.
Analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue converters add 0.3-1.5 ms each from their decimation and interpolation filters. Slow-roll-off filter modes have less delay and less pre-ringing.
Networked audio (Dante, AVB) adds a configurable transport latency, typically 0.25-5 ms, on top of everything else.

blocks.q: A converter has 200 ps of RMS sampling jitter. What is the artefact level at 10 kHz relative to a full-scale sine?
options: About -78 dB
About -98 dB
About -118 dB
About -60 dB
blocks.explain: 2 pi x 10,000 x 200e-12 = 1.257e-5, and 20 log10(1.257e-5) = -98.0 dB. That is below the noise floor of essentially any recording made in a real acoustic space. Note also that the same jitter at 100 Hz gives -138 dB: jitter artefacts scale directly with signal frequency, so they are a high-frequency problem or no problem at all.

lessons.title: Choosing a Format, and What the Numbers Cannot Tell You
glossary: PCM
Pulse code modulation: the linear representation used by WAV, AIFF, FLAC and CD.
Lossless compression
FLAC, ALAC, WavPack: bit-exact reduction in file size, typically 40-60% of the original.
Lossy compression
MP3, AAC, Opus, Vorbis: perceptual coding that discards information under a masking threshold.
Sample rate conversion
Resampling between rates. Quality varies enormously between implementations; test yours.
Delta-sigma
The converter architecture used by essentially all modern audio converters: 1-bit or few-bit quantisation at a very high rate with aggressive noise shaping.
Bit-transparency
The property of a signal path that delivers samples unaltered end to end. Easy to break with volume controls, mixers and OS resamplers.

blocks.html: Almost every converter you will ever use is a delta-sigma design. It samples at a very high rate (typically 64 to 256 times the output rate) with only a few bits of resolution, uses aggressive noise shaping to push quantisation noise into the megahertz region, and then digitally filters and decimates to the output rate. This architecture is why a 24-bit converter can work at all: no one builds a 24-bit ladder DAC with the required component matching. It also explains why the analogue anti-alias filter can be gentle (the effective initial sample rate is enormous) and why almost all of the filtering is digital.

blocks.title: What actually happens between the microphone and the file
steps: Analogue gain
Preamp raises microphone level to converter input level. This stage sets your real noise floor; nothing downstream can improve it.
Gentle anti-alias filter
Because the modulator runs at, say, 6.144 MHz, the analogue filter only needs to reject above about 3 MHz. This is why modern converters have no audible passband ripple.
Delta-sigma modulation
A few-bit quantiser in a feedback loop pushes quantisation noise out of the audio band. The output is a very high-rate, low-resolution stream.
Digital decimation filter

A steep FIR filter removes everything above the target Nyquist frequency, then the rate is reduced. This filter is where pre-ringing and passband ripple live, and where "filter character" options come from.
Word length and storage
Truncate or dither to 24 bits and write to file. At this point the analogue noise floor is far above the LSB.
Playback: interpolation filter
The reverse process. A steep digital filter interpolates up, the modulator drives the output stage, and a gentle analogue filter removes what is left.

head: Decision
Defensible answer
Why
rows: 48 kHz, or 96 kHz if the session leans heavily on non-oversampling nonlinear plug-ins
Bandwidth is not the constraint; aliasing in processing sometimes is.
It costs 50% more storage and buys 48 dB of headroom insurance. There is no argument against it.
Preserves headroom for transients and keeps the converter input out of its distortion region.
Cannot clip in the arithmetic; intermediate overs are recoverable by pulling down the master.
24-bit at the session rate, plus a 16/44.1 with TPDF or shaped dither if required
Give the mastering engineer the unaltered file, not a pre-dithered one.
Whatever the platform specifies, at -1 dBTP or lower
Codec overshoot is real; loudness is normalised anyway.
24-bit PCM (WAV or BWF) plus FLAC, with checksums and documented metadata
Lossless, open, and readable in thirty years. Do not archive in a proprietary session format alone.

blocks.label: The mistake that actually costs you quality
blocks.html: Not sample rate. Not bit depth. Not jitter. It is gain staging and conversion count: a signal that passes through five sample-rate conversions, three lossy encodes, and a preamp set 20 dB too hot has been damaged in ways no format choice can repair. Count the conversions in your chain and eliminate the ones that do not need to be there. This is the bridge to Module 8.

blocks.text: What measurement cannot settle

blocks.html: Everything in this module is measurable, and most disputes about digital audio would be settled quickly if people insisted on level-matched blind comparison. But two genuine open questions remain. First: the audibility of the pre-ringing produced by steep linear-phase decimation filters. Pre-ringing at 22 kHz is inaudible in itself, but there is a live argument about whether the associated impulse-response smearing is detectable on transients; converter makers now routinely offer minimum-phase and apodising filter options, which is a tacit admission that some listeners prefer them, though preference is not the same as audibility of an artefact.

Second: whether high-resolution formats provide any benefit that is not attributable to better mastering. Much "high-resolution" catalogue is remastered from the same tapes with less compression, so listeners comparing a hi-res release with a loud CD master are comparing masters, not formats. A meta-analysis by Reiss (JAES, 2016) found a small but statistically significant ability to discriminate high-resolution content, especially among trained listeners, though the effect sizes were small and the included studies varied greatly in rigour. The honest summary is that the effect, if it exists, is far smaller than the effect of your room, your monitors, and your mastering decisions.

blocks.q: A 32-bit float file shows samples above 0 dBFS on the meter but sounds undistorted. What is happening?
options: The meter is faulty
Floating-point representation has no hard ceiling, so values above full scale are stored accurately and can be recovered by lowering the gain before conversion
The file is corrupt
The signal is clipping but the distortion is masked
blocks.explain: A 32-bit float has an exponent as well as a mantissa, so it represents values far above and below the fixed-point full-scale range with constant relative precision. Nothing clips in the arithmetic. The clipping happens only when the signal reaches a fixed-point converter or file format, so pulling the master fader down before that point recovers the signal exactly. This is why 32-bit float field recorders can be run without setting gain, and why it is a convenience rather than a quality improvement.

blocks.title: Assignment 7 — Measure your own digital chain
blocks.brief: Produce a measurement report on the digital path you actually use. Part A, aliasing: generate a sine sweep from 15 kHz to just below Nyquist, pass it through three nonlinear plug-ins (a saturator, a distortion, a fast limiter) at a rate of 44.1 or 48 kHz, and record the spectra. Identify aliased components and give their frequencies, showing the |f - n fs| arithmetic that predicts each one. Repeat with the plug-ins oversampled or with the session at 96 kHz and quantify the reduction in dB. Part B, dither: take a fade-to-silence of a real recording, reduce it to 8-bit with and without TPDF dither, and describe the difference; then compute the theoretical noise floors and check them against measurement. Part C, latency: measure your actual round-trip latency by looping an output to an input and recording an impulse, and compare with the value your DAW reports. Explain any discrepancy. Part D: state which of these three effects you could hear, under what conditions, and how confident you are.
items: A strong result predicts alias frequencies arithmetically before measuring, and matches predictions to observed spectral lines.
A strong result quantifies the improvement from oversampling in dB at specific frequencies rather than describing it as "cleaner".
A strong result computes theoretical noise floors from 6.02n + 1.76 and compares them with measurement, explaining any gap.
A strong result measures round-trip latency empirically and accounts for the difference from the reported figure using converter filter delay.
A strong result reports honestly on audibility, including cases where the measured artefact was inaudible.
A weak result relies on plug-in GUI meters, omits the arithmetic, or claims audible differences without a level-matched comparison.

questions.q: What is the Nyquist frequency for a 88.2 kHz sample rate?
questions.explain: 88,200 / 2 = 44,100 Hz. Nyquist is always exactly half the sample rate; the theorem requires the signal to contain nothing at or above it.

questions.q: A 26 kHz tone reaches a sampler running at 44.1 kHz with a failed anti-alias filter. At what frequency does it appear in the digital signal?
questions.explain: |26,000 - 44,100| = 18,100 Hz. It is now indistinguishable from a genuine 18.1 kHz component and no later processing can remove it. This is why nonlinear plug-ins that do not oversample can produce inharmonic grit on bright material.

questions.q: What is the theoretical dynamic range of a 20-bit converter?
questions.explain: 6.02 x 20 + 1.76 = 120.4 + 1.76 = 122.16 dB. This is close to the practical ceiling of real converter performance, which is why moving from 20-bit to 24-bit buys arithmetic headroom rather than measurable noise performance.

questions.q: A DAW is set to a 256-sample buffer at 96 kHz. What is the one-way buffer latency in milliseconds?
questions.explain: 256 / 96,000 = 0.002667 s = 2.67 ms. Round trip is roughly twice this plus converter filter delay, so expect about 6-7 ms in practice. Note that doubling the sample rate halves the latency for the same buffer size, which is a legitimate reason to track at 96 kHz on a fast machine.

questions.q: A converter has 50 ps RMS sampling jitter. What is the jitter artefact level at 15 kHz, relative to a full-scale sine?
questions.explain: 2 pi x 15,000 x 50e-12 = 4.712e-6. 20 log10(4.712e-6) = -106.5 dB. Far below the noise floor of any recording made in a real acoustic space, which is the honest context for most modern arguments about clocking.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about the sampling theorem.
options: It requires the signal to be bandlimited below the Nyquist frequency
Reconstruction is exact, not approximate, when the conditions are met
Higher sample rates give higher resolution within the audio band
The reconstruction formula uses sinc interpolation, not straight-line joining of samples
Aliased components can be removed by filtering after sampling
why: True, and it is the assumption most often forgotten. Without bandlimiting, the theorem says nothing.
True. Given bandlimiting and ideal reconstruction, the original continuous waveform is recovered exactly.
False. Sample rate sets bandwidth; bit depth sets the noise floor. They are independent axes.
True. Each sample contributes a scaled sinc function; the sum is the unique bandlimited waveform through all samples.
False. Once folded down, an alias occupies a legitimate in-band frequency and is indistinguishable from real signal. Prevention before sampling is the only remedy.
questions.explain: The theorem is exact and its assumptions are strict. Most popular confusion about digital audio comes from treating sample rate as a resolution parameter, which it is not.

questions.q: Order the stages a signal passes through in a modern delta-sigma analogue-to-digital converter.
items: Analogue gain stage
Gentle analogue anti-alias filter
Delta-sigma modulator at a high oversampled rate
Digital decimation filter
Rate reduction to the target sample rate
Word length reduction and file write
questions.explain: The key architectural insight is that oversampling moves the hard filtering from the analogue domain to the digital domain, where it can be made steep and repeatable. It also means the "anti-alias filter" people worry about is a digital FIR filter, and its pre-ringing behaviour is a design choice rather than a physical constraint.

questions.q: Match each digital audio problem to its cause.
pairs: Inharmonic grit on bright material through a saturator
Aliasing from harmonics generated above Nyquist
Gritty, chirping quality on quiet reverb tails
Undithered word length reduction
Periodic clicks in a multi-device digital setup
More than one device acting as clock master
Sidebands around high-frequency tones that grow with level
Sampling jitter
Clipping only after AAC encoding
Inter-sample peaks exceeding full scale on reconstruction
questions.explain: Each of these has a distinct signature and a distinct fix. Aliasing is fixed by oversampling, quantisation distortion by dither, clocking by choosing one master, jitter by better converter design, and codec clipping by a true-peak ceiling.

questions.stem: An engineer records a session at 44.1 kHz, 24-bit, with peaks at -1 dBFS. The session uses a guitar amp simulator without oversampling, a fast digital limiter on the drum bus, and a linear-phase EQ on the mix bus. The mix is exported to 16-bit with truncation (no dither) and then encoded to 256 kbps AAC. The client reports harshness on cymbals, grit in the fade-outs, and occasional distortion on the loudest sections.

qs.q: Which decisions in this chain are plausibly responsible for the reported problems? Select all that apply.
options: Recording at 44.1 kHz with a non-oversampling amp simulator
Recording peaks at -1 dBFS
Exporting to 16-bit with truncation
Using a linear-phase EQ on the mix bus
Encoding to AAC from a file that peaks near full scale
why: Correct. A distortion model generates harmonics well above 22.05 kHz; without oversampling they fold back as inharmonic components, heard as harshness on cymbals and bright guitars.
Correct. -1 dBFS leaves no headroom for transients, pushes the converter analogue stage toward its distortion limit, and guarantees inter-sample overs downstream.
Correct. Truncation leaves signal-correlated quantisation error, which is exactly the gritty, granular quality reported in fades.
Not a cause of any of the reported symptoms. Linear-phase EQ adds latency and pre-ringing, which could smear transients, but produces neither harshness of this kind nor grit in fades.
Correct. AAC encoding of near-full-scale material routinely overshoots by 1-2 dB true peak, producing the occasional distortion on loud sections.
qs.explain: Four independent faults, each with a distinct mechanism and a distinct fix: oversample the nonlinear plug-in, track at -12 to -18 dBFS, dither the word-length reduction, and set a -1 dBTP ceiling before encoding.

qs.q: The amp simulator generates a 3rd harmonic of a 9 kHz input. Where does that harmonic land after aliasing at 44.1 kHz?
qs.explain: The 3rd harmonic is at 27 kHz, above the 22.05 kHz Nyquist. |27,000 - 44,100| = 17,100 Hz. Note that this is not a harmonic of anything in the source: 17,100 is not an integer multiple of 9,000, which is precisely why aliasing sounds harsh rather than merely bright.

qs.q: Rewrite the chain, specifying each change and the mechanism it addresses. Say which change you expect to make the largest audible difference and why.
qs.model: Changes, in order of the chain. (1) Track at 24-bit with peaks around -12 to -18 dBFS rather than -1 dBFS. Mechanism: preserves converter headroom and keeps the analogue input stage out of its distortion region; the noise cost is nil because the recording noise floor is set by the room and the preamp, not by the LSB. (2) Enable oversampling on the amp simulator, or run the session at 88.2 or 96 kHz. Mechanism: harmonics generated above Nyquist are removed by the internal decimation filter instead of folding back as inharmonic aliases. This addresses the cymbal harshness directly. (3) Check the drum-bus limiter for oversampled or true-peak detection; a fast limiter is also a nonlinearity and will alias if it is not oversampled. (4) Keep the linear-phase EQ if it is doing something useful, but be aware it adds latency and pre-ringing; on a mix bus with mostly gentle moves a minimum-phase EQ is usually the better default. (5) Export the master at 24-bit at the session rate for archival and for mastering, undithered word length reduction not being required from a 32-bit float bus to 24-bit in any audible sense. (6) For the 16-bit deliverable, apply TPDF or a moderate noise-shaped dither once, at the final word-length reduction, and nowhere else. Mechanism: decorrelates the quantisation error so it becomes noise rather than signal-locked distortion, which is the direct cause of the grit in fades. (7) Set a true-peak ceiling of -1 dBTP (or -1.5 for heavily limited material) before AAC encoding. Mechanism: absorbs codec overshoot so the decoder does not clip. Largest audible difference: the oversampling change. Aliasing produces inharmonic components that are not masked by the source, sit in the most sensitive region of hearing, and are present whenever the material is bright and loud; the other faults are either level-dependent or confined to quiet passages. I would expect the truncation fix to be second, because signal-correlated distortion in fades is very noticeable once you know what to listen for.
points: Addresses aliasing with oversampling or a higher session rate and explains the mechanism
Addresses tracking level with a specific target and correctly argues the noise cost is negligible
Specifies dither once at final word-length reduction, with the decorrelation mechanism
Specifies a true-peak ceiling before lossy encoding
Ranks the changes by expected audibility with a reason

questions.q: Why must the anti-alias filter be placed before the sampler rather than after it?
options: Because digital filters cannot be made steep enough
Because once a component has aliased it occupies a legitimate in-band frequency and is indistinguishable from real signal
Because analogue filters have lower noise
Because the sampler adds noise above Nyquist
why: Digital filters can be made far steeper than analogue ones; steepness is not the issue.

Correct. Aliasing is a many-to-one mapping: a 26 kHz component and an 18.1 kHz component at 44.1 kHz produce identical samples. No filter can separate them afterwards because the information distinguishing them no longer exists.
Noise is not the relevant property; the ordering constraint is informational.
The sampler does not add noise above Nyquist; by construction nothing above Nyquist exists in the sampled representation.
questions.explain: The general principle is that aliasing destroys information irreversibly, so it must be prevented, never corrected. This is also why plug-ins that create harmonics must oversample internally: they are effectively re-sampling the signal at their own operating rate.

questions.q: A client insists on delivering a 192 kHz, 32-bit master "for maximum quality". Give a technically grounded response that neither dismisses nor endorses the request.
questions.model: Start with what is true. Bit depth beyond 24 provides no audible benefit for a delivered file: 24-bit gives 146 dB of theoretical dynamic range, the best converters manage about 120-125 dB, and no acoustic environment on Earth spans more than about 120 dB. 32-bit float is genuinely valuable as an internal working format and on field recorders because it cannot clip in the arithmetic, but as a delivery format it doubles file size for headroom that no longer has anywhere to go. Sample rate is a more interesting argument. There is a real case for high rates during production: nonlinear processing generates harmonics above Nyquist that fold back as inharmonic aliases, and working at 96 kHz reduces that. There is also a real case for archival capture of analogue sources where you cannot go back. But for delivery, the case is weak: the ear's upper limit is around 20 kHz at best, no mechanism for perceiving higher frequencies has been established, ultrasonic content can cause intermodulation in downstream analogue equipment, and converters running at 192 kHz have half the settling time per sample, which typically worsens rather than improves linearity. Meyer and Moran found no discrimination of a 16/44.1 loop in high-resolution playback; Reiss's 2016 meta-analysis found a small significant effect concentrated in trained listeners. Neither result licenses a strong claim in either direction, and both effects are far smaller than the difference a competent mastering decision makes. So the recommendation: deliver 24-bit at the production rate, which for most work should be 48 or 96 kHz; supply 32-bit float only if the client has a specific downstream workflow that benefits; and if the client wants a high-resolution product for marketing reasons, say so plainly and deliver it, because that is a commercial decision and not a technical one. I would also point out where the same budget buys more: room treatment, better monitoring, and more time on the mix.
points: Explains why bit depth beyond 24 gives no audible delivery benefit, with numbers
Distinguishes the production case for high sample rates (aliasing in nonlinear processing) from the delivery case
Cites specific evidence on both sides and characterises its strength honestly
Gives a concrete recommendation and concedes the commercial dimension
Redirects to interventions with larger effect sizes

questions.q: What does TPDF dither at 2 LSB peak-to-peak achieve that RPDF dither at 1 LSB does not?
options: A lower noise floor
It eliminates noise modulation, making the variance of the total error independent of the signal
It allows a higher sample rate
It removes the need for an anti-alias filter
why: TPDF has a higher noise floor than RPDF (+4.77 dB versus +3.0 dB relative to undithered). Lower noise is not the benefit.

Correct. Lipshitz, Wannamaker and Vanderkooy showed that RPDF renders the first moment of the error signal-independent but leaves the second moment (variance) modulated by the signal, which is audible as a noise floor that breathes with the programme. TPDF makes both moments independent.
Dither has no relationship to sample rate.
Dither addresses quantisation, not sampling; the anti-alias filter is a separate requirement.
questions.explain: The practical statement is: TPDF costs 1.8 dB more noise than RPDF and buys complete statistical independence of the error. That trade is almost always worth it, which is why TPDF is the default in every competent implementation.

modules.title: Gain Staging and Level Discipline
modules.tagline: The capstone: one continuous level budget from air pressure to delivered file, and the discipline that keeps it honest.
objectives: Able to construct a complete noise and headroom budget for a signal chain and identify the stage that limits it.
Able to apply the Friis cascade relation to decide where gain belongs and where it does not.
Able to reason correctly about impedance bridging, loading and their effect on level and tone.
Able to design a gain structure for a fixed-point or floating-point digital system and justify every level choice.
Able to calibrate a monitoring chain and specify a metering strategy tied to a delivery specification.
Able to audit an existing chain end to end and produce a prioritised list of corrections with quantified benefits.

lessons.title: The Chain as a Noise and Headroom Budget
glossary: Headroom
The margin in dB between nominal operating level and the point of unacceptable distortion or clipping.
Noise floor
The level of unwanted residual signal with no programme present, referred to a stated point in the chain.
Dynamic range
The span between the noise floor and the clipping point of a system, in dB.
EIN
Equivalent input noise: a preamplifier's output noise referred back to its input, allowing comparison independent of gain.
Noise figure
The degradation in signal-to-noise ratio caused by a stage, in dB, relative to the thermal noise of its source.
Thermal (Johnson) noise
The irreducible noise of a resistance, with RMS voltage sqrt(4kTRB).

blocks.html: Everything in the previous seven modules converges here. A signal chain has a ceiling set by clipping and a floor set by noise, and every stage moves the signal within that window. Gain staging is the discipline of keeping the signal high enough above the floor and far enough below the ceiling at every stage, given that no single stage can repair what another has destroyed. The window is finite, the constraints are quantifiable, and most of what passes for gain-staging folklore dissolves once you compute the budget.

blocks.title: Assigned reading — Module 8
items: Modern Recording Techniques (9th ed.) — Huber & Runstein

Required. The chapters on the recording console, signal flow and the digital audio workstation. Read specifically for signal-flow diagrams; treat the level advice as dated and check it against this module.
Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science (3rd ed.) — Bob Katz

Required. Chapters 14-16 on metering, monitoring calibration and the K-System, and the chapters on the loudness war. This is the clearest published argument for monitor calibration as a professional obligation.
Small Signal Audio Design (3rd ed.) — Douglas Self
Required. Chapters 1-3 on noise, gain structure and impedance. Self is exact where most audio writing is vague, and the noise calculations here are the ones this lesson uses.
Handbook for Sound Engineers (5th ed., ed. Glen Ballou)
Optional reference. The chapters on grounding, interfacing and levels. Use it to look things up rather than to read through.
ITU-R BS.1770-5 and EBU R 128 (revisited)
Required. Re-read them now that you can compute everything in them. Note in particular how R 128 makes level a delivery contract rather than an aesthetic decision.
AES-6id-2006, "AES information document for digital audio — Personal computer audio quality measurements"
Optional. Useful for how to measure a chain you did not design.

blocks.label: Thermal noise of a source resistance
blocks.caption: k is Boltzmann's constant 1.38e-23 J/K, T absolute temperature, R resistance, B bandwidth. For a 150 ohm microphone at 293 K over a 20 kHz bandwidth this gives 0.22 microvolts, or -130.9 dBu. That is the floor no preamplifier can beat.

blocks.html: A good microphone preamplifier has an EIN of about -128 to -129 dBu with a 150 ohm source. Compare that with the -130.9 dBu thermal floor and you find a noise figure of roughly 2-3 dB: the preamp adds only 2-3 dB of noise to what physics already guarantees. That is close enough to perfect that arguing about preamp noise is usually a waste of time — unless your source is a very quiet dynamic or ribbon microphone needing 60-70 dB of gain, in which case those 2-3 dB are audible and preamp choice genuinely matters.

blocks.label: Friis cascade formula for noise
blocks.caption: F and G are linear power ratios, not decibels. The message is stark: the first stage dominates, and every subsequent stage's noise contribution is divided by all the gain preceding it.

blocks.label: The single most important gain-staging principle
blocks.html: Apply your gain as early as possible, at the first stage that can supply it cleanly. A signal amplified 40 dB at the preamp and then attenuated 20 dB later has a far better signal-to-noise ratio than the same signal amplified 20 dB at the preamp and 20 dB at the end, because the later gain amplifies all the noise picked up in between. This is the Friis formula stated in words, and it is why "turn the preamp down and make it up in the box" is bad advice whenever the preamp is not being driven into distortion.

blocks.text: Where noise actually comes from

head: Source
Typical contribution
Can you improve it?
rows: 20-35 dBA in a treated studio; 40+ dBA in a bedroom
Yes, and it is usually the dominant term. HVAC, computers, traffic.
7 dBA (very quiet capacitor) to 25 dBA (cheap capacitor)
Yes, by microphone choice. Dynamics have no self-noise but need more gain.
Yes, but the improvement is only audible at high gain settings.
Marginal. Almost never the limiting factor.
Irrelevant. It is 30-40 dB below everything else.
Yes, by not leaving unused channels open and by not over-gaining early stages.

blocks.html: Read that table as a ranking. The noise you can hear on a typical recording is, in order: the room, the microphone, the preamp, and then a very long gap before anything digital. Engineers who agonise over converter noise while recording in a room with a 42 dBA HVAC floor have mis-identified their problem by about 60 dB. This is the most common quantitative error in the field.

blocks.caption: A realistic budget. Most of a 16-bit format's range is not used for programme at all: it is transient headroom above and unusable margin below the analogue noise floor.

blocks.q: A summing bus carries 32 channels, each with an identical uncorrelated noise floor. How much higher is the bus noise than a single channel?
options: +3 dB
+15 dB
+30 dB
+32 dB
blocks.explain: 10 log10(32) = 15.05 dB. Noise from independent channels adds in power, not in pressure. This is why muting or removing unused channels matters, and why a large analogue console has a measurably worse noise floor than a small one at the same gain settings. Note that if the noise were correlated — a shared power-supply hum, for instance — it would add at 20 log10(32) = 30 dB instead, which is why hum problems scale so much worse than hiss.

lessons.title: Analogue Gain Staging: Preamps, Impedance and Consoles
glossary: Voltage bridging
The modern interface convention: a low output impedance (typically 50-200 ohms) driving a high input impedance (10 k or more), transferring voltage rather than power.
Impedance matching
Equal source and load impedance, maximising power transfer. Correct for RF and legacy telephony, wrong for modern audio.
Pad
A fixed attenuator, typically -10 or -20 dB, placed before a stage to prevent overload.
Insert point
A break in the signal path allowing external processing, typically at line level after the preamp.
Unity gain
A setting at which a stage neither amplifies nor attenuates. The reference position for a fader.
Ground loop
A circulating current in a signal ground path caused by a potential difference between two grounded points, heard as hum at the mains frequency and its harmonics.

blocks.html: Modern audio interfaces transfer voltage, not power. Outputs are designed with a low source impedance and inputs with a much higher load impedance, typically a ratio of at least 10:1. Under those conditions the load draws almost no current and the transferred voltage is nearly the full open-circuit output. This is called voltage bridging, and it replaced 600 ohm impedance matching in the 1970s. Almost every impedance question in the studio is answered by remembering that fact.

blocks.label: Voltage transferred across an interface
blocks.caption: With Zout = 100 ohms and Zin = 10 kohms, the loss is 20 log(10000/10100) = 0.09 dB. With Zin = 600 ohms it becomes 1.34 dB, and the source may also distort. This is why plugging a modern output into a legacy 600 ohm input can change both level and tone.

head: Interface
Typical source Z
Typical load Z
Notes
rows: The 5-10x rule. Some preamps offer variable input impedance, which measurably changes the frequency response of dynamic and ribbon microphones by loading their transformers.
Ribbons are the most impedance-sensitive microphones; a 1.2 kohm input can audibly dull them.
Essentially lossless. Long cable runs add capacitance, which matters over 30 m or so.
Guitar pickup to amp or DI
A 10 kohm input loads a passive pickup badly, cutting highs and level. This is what a DI box exists to fix.
A high output impedance interacts with the headphone's impedance curve and changes its frequency response.

blocks.text: Setting a preamp properly

blocks.title: The order of operations that actually works
steps: Choose the microphone and its position first
Position changes tone by 10-20 dB in specific bands; no amount of gain fixes a bad position. Get this right before touching a knob.
Engage the pad only if you need it
A pad before the preamp costs you signal-to-noise but protects against overload. A pad on a loud source (kick drum, trumpet) is correct; a pad plus high gain on a quiet source is self-defeating.
Set gain for peaks around -12 to -18 dBFS
This corresponds to roughly +6 to 0 dBu on a system aligned at 0 dBu = -18 dBFS. It leaves 12-18 dB for transients you have not heard yet.
Check with the loudest thing the performer will do
Not the soundcheck level. Ask for the chorus, the fill, the shout. Most clipping happens on material that was never checked.
Leave the fader at unity while setting gain
A fader at -20 dB hides an over-hot preamp; a fader at +10 dB hides an under-set one. Unity is the reference position that lets you see the truth.
Then, and only then, insert processing
Every compressor, EQ and saturator has an assumed operating level. Feeding one 15 dB hot changes its behaviour, not just its output level.

blocks.label: The "record it hot" myth and where it came from
blocks.html: On analogue tape, recording hot was correct: tape hiss is a fixed floor and the medium saturates gracefully, so pushing level improved signal-to-noise and added pleasant compression. On early 16-bit digital it was also arguably correct, because 16 bits gave 98 dB and converters were poor. On a modern 24-bit converter it is wrong: the noise floor is 40 dB below anything acoustic, converters distort before they clip, and the practice destroys headroom for no benefit. The advice survives because it was right for twenty years, and a generation of engineers learned it as a principle rather than as a response to a specific medium.

A related point about consoles. Analogue mixers have a defined nominal operating level, usually +4 dBu, and a maximum before clipping usually 18-24 dB above it. Every stage — input, insert, EQ, bus, master — has its own headroom. Overdriving an early stage and pulling it back later produces distortion you cannot remove; underdriving early and boosting later produces noise you cannot remove. The channel meter usually shows only one point in the chain, so "the meter looks fine" is not evidence that the EQ section is not clipping. On a console with EQ in circuit and 12 dB of boost engaged, the EQ output can be clipping while the post-fader meter reads nominal.

blocks.text: Grounding and hum: a level problem in disguise

items: Balanced connections reject common-mode interference by subtracting the two conductors; anything picked up equally on both cancels. Common-mode rejection of 60-90 dB is typical, and it degrades if source impedances on the two legs are unequal.

Ground loops arise when two pieces of equipment are grounded at different points with a potential difference between them, and a signal cable completes the circuit. The current flows in the cable shield and appears as hum.

Fixes in order of preference: power everything from one distribution point; break the shield at one end of the offending cable (pin 1 lift at the receiving end only); use a transformer isolator. Never lift a mains safety earth. It is a lethal shortcut and it is the reason performers have died on stage.

Hum diagnosis by frequency: a fundamental at the mains frequency (50 or 60 Hz) with weak harmonics usually indicates magnetic induction into a cable or transformer; strong harmonic content (100/120 Hz and above) usually indicates a ground loop or a power supply problem.

blocks.q: A ribbon microphone sounds dull and lacks output on a particular preamp. What is the most likely cause?
options: The preamp has too much gain
The preamp input impedance is too low, loading the ribbon's output transformer
The microphone needs phantom power
The cable is unbalanced
blocks.explain: A ribbon element has a very low source impedance and relies on a step-up transformer. Loading that transformer with a low input impedance (say 1.2 kohms) damps its high-frequency resonance and reduces output. Ribbons generally want 5-10 times their rated impedance, so 3-10 kohms. Note also that most passive ribbons must NOT receive phantom power, and that a miswired cable plus phantom can destroy the ribbon instantly.

lessons.title: Digital Gain Staging: Fixed Point, Floating Point and Plug-in Behaviour
glossary: Fixed point
Integer representation with a hard maximum. 16- and 24-bit files, and most converters and hardware DSP.
Floating point
Representation with a mantissa and exponent. 32-bit float has effectively no clipping point in the arithmetic.
Intersample peak
A peak in the reconstructed waveform exceeding the largest sample value.
Plug-in sweet spot
The input level at which a modelled analogue plug-in behaves as its hardware original did, usually referenced to -18 dBFS.
Gain compensation
Automatic adjustment of output gain to match input gain, so that a process can be evaluated without loudness bias.
Pan law
The attenuation applied to a signal panned centre so that its level is consistent across the stereo field; commonly -3, -4.5 or -6 dB.

blocks.html: Inside a modern DAW the mix bus is 32-bit float or better, so intermediate levels cannot clip in the arithmetic. This is genuinely liberating and widely misunderstood. It does not mean levels do not matter. Three things still constrain you: fixed-point boundaries at the converter and at the file, plug-ins that model nonlinear hardware and therefore respond to absolute level, and your own ability to judge a mix when every fader is at an arbitrary position.

head: Location
Format
Can it clip?
What to do
rows: Levels here are a matter of convenience and plug-in behaviour, not of damage.
Feed it around -18 dBFS RMS unless the manual says otherwise.
A fixed-point hardware insert or DSP card
Respect its stated nominal and maximum levels.
True-peak ceiling at -1 dBTP; dither on word-length reduction.
A float mix that peaks at +6 dBFS will clip the D/A even though the file is fine.

blocks.html: The plug-in point deserves elaboration because it is where most modern gain-staging confusion lives. A linear digital EQ does not care what level you feed it: attenuating by 10 dB before and boosting 10 dB after produces a bit-identical result. A modelled compressor, tape machine, console channel or preamp does care, because its nonlinearity is calibrated to an assumed operating level. Most such plug-ins are designed around 0 VU = -18 dBFS (EBU alignment). Feed one a signal peaking at -0.5 dBFS and you are driving the modelled circuit 17 dB past its design point; it will behave like the hardware would with 17 dB of extra input, which may be what you want but is rarely what you intended.
