blocks.caption: One alignment decision links the three domains. Once you fix 0 dBu = -18 dBFS and calibrate the monitor gain, a level in one domain has an unambiguous meaning in all three.

blocks.label: A practical working standard
blocks.html: Track so peaks land near -15 dBFS and typical RMS near -20 dBFS. Set clip gain (not the fader) so each channel reads roughly -18 dBFS RMS before processing. Keep faders near unity so you can see relative balance at a glance. Mix into a master bus that peaks around -6 dBFS, leaving room for a mastering stage. None of these numbers is sacred; the discipline of having consistent numbers is what pays.

blocks.text: Pan law, summing and the myths around them

blocks.html: When a mono source is panned centre it appears in both channels. If the two channels are summed acoustically at a listening position they add coherently (+6 dB), but if they are summed electrically to mono they also add coherently while decorrelated stereo material adds at +3 dB. Pan law is the compensation applied at centre to keep perceived level constant as a source is panned. Common values are -3 dB (correct for uncorrelated summation), -6 dB (correct for coherent summation) and -4.5 dB (a compromise, and the most common default). The practical consequence: a session imported between DAWs with different pan laws will have different centre balances, which is a real and frequently mysterious source of mix changes.

The other myth worth killing: "analogue summing sounds better than digital summing". Digital summing in 32-bit float is arithmetically exact; there is nothing to improve. What analogue summing boxes actually contribute is crosstalk, transformer and amplifier nonlinearity, slight channel-to-channel level and phase differences, and a different gain structure that usually results in different processing decisions. Those may well sound better to you. They are colouration, not accuracy, and they should be evaluated level-matched and blind like anything else.

blocks.q: A mix bus in 32-bit float peaks at +4 dBFS. The exported 24-bit WAV is clipped. What happened?
options: 32-bit float files always clip on export
The float bus cannot clip, but the fixed-point export format has a hard ceiling at 0 dBFS, so everything above it was truncated
The dither caused clipping
The master fader was set incorrectly, which cannot be undone
blocks.explain: Float arithmetic has no ceiling, so the internal signal was intact; converting to fixed-point 24-bit clamps everything above full scale. The fix is trivial and lossless: pull the master fader down by more than 4 dB and export again. The signal was never damaged, which is exactly the benefit of a float bus — but only if you notice before the fixed-point conversion.

blocks.html: An opinion, defended: gain-staging advice has become superstitious in the float era. You will read that you must hit -18 dBFS on every channel or the mix will "sound worse". In a fully linear chain that is false and demonstrably so — the null test proves it. What is true is narrower and still important: nonlinear processes are level-dependent, fixed-point boundaries are real, and consistent levels make you a faster and more consistent engineer. Argue for the discipline on those grounds and you will be right; argue for it as a law of digital audio and someone will null-test you.

lessons.title: End-to-End Level Discipline: Calibration, Metering and Delivery
glossary: Monitor calibration
Setting a known acoustic level for a known electrical level, so that monitoring gain is repeatable.
K-System
Katz's proposal linking meter scale and monitor gain: K-20, K-14, K-12, with 0 on the meter corresponding to 83 dB SPL per channel.
Reference level
The agreed acoustic level at the listening position for a stated electrical level, e.g. -20 dBFS pink noise reading 83 dBC.
Dialogue-gated loudness
A loudness measurement restricted to speech, used by Netflix and in some broadcast specifications.
Delivery specification
The contractual set of technical requirements for a deliverable: format, loudness, true peak, channel order, metadata.
Null test
Summing two signals with one inverted; a residual of nothing proves bit-identity, and the residual level quantifies any difference.

blocks.html: The final piece of level discipline is the one most studios skip: making the acoustic level in the room a known, repeatable quantity. Without it, every equal-loudness effect from Module 3 operates on your decisions uncontrolled, and every comparison you make is confounded by level. Calibration takes under an hour and is the highest return on time available in this entire course.

blocks.title: Calibrating a monitoring chain
steps: Generate the reference signal
Band-limited pink noise (500 Hz to 2 kHz for film work per SMPTE ST 202, or full-band for music) at -20 dBFS RMS, or -18 dBFS if you are working to EBU alignment. State which you used.
Position the meter
At the listening position, at ear height, microphone pointing up or forward per the meter's calibration, away from your body.
Set one channel at a time

Play the noise through the left speaker only, adjust the monitor controller or the amplifier trim until the meter reads your target, then repeat for the right. Adjust the speaker's own trim, not the monitor controller, so the controller stays at a marked reference position.
Choose a defensible target

85 dBC slow per channel for a large film dubbing stage; 79 dBC for a small music control room (Katz's recommendation for near-field work); 83 dBC as a common compromise. Two channels together will read about 3 dB higher.
Mark the controller
Physically mark the reference position. That mark is now the meaning of "reference level" in your room.
Verify with programme

Play a known commercial reference at its native level and confirm the result is comfortable and matches your expectation. If reference level is uncomfortably loud, your room is too reverberant or too small for that target; choose a lower one and document it.

blocks.html: The Katz K-System deserves a mention because it is the most coherent attempt to link metering and monitoring. K-20 places 0 on the meter 20 dB below full scale and calibrates that to 83 dB SPL per channel, giving 20 dB of headroom above the reference point — appropriate for wide-dynamic-range music and film. K-14 gives 14 dB, for pop and rock. K-12 gives 12 dB, for broadcast. The scheme largely lost to LUFS-based normalisation, but its central insight survives intact: a meter reading means nothing unless the monitoring gain it implies is fixed.

blocks.text: A metering strategy, not a meter

head: Question
Meter
Target
rows: Peaks at -12 to -18 dBFS while tracking.
Am I driving this modelled plug-in correctly?
RMS or VU, calibrated to -18 dBFS = 0 VU
Around 0 VU on the plug-in's own meter.
How loud does this section feel?
Compare sections against each other, not against an absolute.
What will the platform do to this?
Know the number; do not chase it.
Will this clip a codec or a consumer D/A?
-1 dBTP, or -1.5 for heavily limited material.
Correlation meter plus an actual mono listen
Sustained readings below zero warrant investigation.
How much dynamic range is left?
No target; use it to detect over-compression relative to references.

blocks.label: The three-number delivery habit
blocks.html: Before you send anything, state three numbers to yourself: integrated loudness, true peak, and sample rate/bit depth. If you cannot state all three from measurement, you are not ready to deliver. Add a fourth for broadcast and streaming work: the specification you are meeting, by name and version. "Around -14, peaks are fine" is how deliverables get rejected.

One last technique that resolves more arguments than any other: the null test. Take two versions of a signal, invert one, sum them, and listen to and measure the residual. If the residual is digital silence, the two are bit-identical and any perceived difference is imagination or a level mismatch. If the residual is non-zero, its level and spectrum tell you exactly what the difference is. Null testing settles disputes about summing engines, about plug-in bypass, about whether a gain change is truly transparent, and about whether an "upgrade" changed anything at all. It requires sample-accurate alignment and exact level matching, which is itself a useful discipline.

blocks.q: You calibrate each monitor separately to 79 dBC with -20 dBFS pink noise. Playing the same noise through both channels, what should the meter read?
options: 79 dBC
82 dBC
85 dBC
158 dBC
blocks.explain: Two loudspeakers playing the same signal at a point equidistant from both sum coherently at low frequencies and incoherently at high frequencies, and with band-limited pink noise in a real room the measured result is close to +3 dB. So expect about 82 dBC. Some standards specify per-channel calibration precisely to avoid this ambiguity, which is why you must always state whether a monitoring reference is per channel or for both.

blocks.title: Capstone Assignment — A full level audit and calibration report
blocks.brief: Produce a professional-grade technical report on a complete signal chain you control, from acoustic source to delivered file. Part A, calibration: calibrate your monitoring to a stated reference and document the procedure, the meter used, the weighting and time constant, the achieved level per channel and for both, and the marked controller position. Part B, chain budget: for one real recording, tabulate the level at every stage in the correct unit (dB SPL, mV or dBV, dBu, dBFS), using your interface's documented full-scale input voltage. Include the noise floor at each stage and identify which stage limits your dynamic range, with the arithmetic. Part C, headroom: state the crest factor of your source material measured from real takes, and justify your tracking level from it. Part D, delivery: produce a deliverable meeting a named real specification (EBU R 128, or a named streaming platform, or a named broadcaster), and report integrated loudness, loudness range, true peak, sample rate and bit depth, with screenshots or logged values. Part E, verification: perform at least one null test relevant to your chain and report the residual level in dBFS. Part F, critique: identify the three weakest points in your chain, quantify the improvement available from fixing each, and rank them by benefit per unit cost. Be honest where the answer is "this makes no measurable difference".
items: A strong result applies the Friis principle explicitly, identifying the first stage as dominant and showing the arithmetic for at least one cascade.

A strong result identifies the limiting noise source correctly, which in almost every real studio is the acoustic environment rather than any electronic stage, and resists the temptation to blame the converter.
A strong result measures crest factor from actual takes rather than assuming a figure, and derives the tracking level from it rather than from habit.
A strong result meets a named specification exactly, quotes its version, and reports all required numbers rather than approximations.
A strong result includes a null test with a numerical residual and draws the correct conclusion from it, including the conclusion that a difference is imaginary if the residual is silence.
A strong result ranks improvements by benefit per cost and states clearly where an expensive upgrade would deliver no measurable benefit.

A weak result reports levels without units or references, omits the acoustic noise floor, treats 24-bit dynamic range as if it were achievable, or recommends equipment purchases that the measured budget does not justify.

questions.q: Sixteen channels of identical uncorrelated noise are summed to one bus. By how many decibels does the bus noise exceed one channel?
questions.explain: 10 log10(16) = 12.04 dB. Uncorrelated noise adds in power. Had the noise been correlated (a shared hum, for instance) it would add in voltage: 20 log10(16) = 24.08 dB, which is why hum problems escalate so much faster than hiss.

questions.q: What is the thermal noise voltage of a 200 ohm source over a 20 kHz bandwidth at 293 K? Give the answer in microvolts. Use vn = sqrt(4kTRB) with k = 1.38e-23.
questions.explain: 4 x 1.38e-23 x 293 x 200 x 20,000 = 6.47e-14; the square root is 2.544e-7 V = 0.254 microvolts, or -129.7 dBu. No preamplifier can do better than this with a 200 ohm source; the best achieve within 2-3 dB of it.

questions.q: A system is aligned so that 0 dBu = -18 dBFS. A signal measures +6 dBu at the console output. What is its level in dBFS?
questions.explain: +6 dBu is 6 dB above the 0 dBu reference, so it is 6 dB above -18 dBFS, i.e. -12 dBFS. Alignment maps are simple offsets; the difficulty is only ever remembering which alignment your facility uses.

questions.q: A microphone with a sensitivity of 12 mV/Pa is placed where the peak sound pressure is 8 Pa. What peak voltage does it produce, in millivolts?
questions.explain: 12 mV/Pa x 8 Pa = 96 mV peak, which is -20.4 dBV or -18.2 dBu. To reach -12 dBFS peak in a system aligned at 0 dBu = -18 dBFS you need the peak at +6 dBu, so you need 24.2 dB of preamp gain. Being able to run this calculation is what lets you predict a gain setting before you touch the knob.

questions.q: Where in a signal chain should gain preferentially be applied, and why?
options: As late as possible, to preserve headroom throughout
As early as possible, at the first stage that can supply it cleanly, because later stages' noise is divided by all preceding gain
Evenly distributed across all stages
It makes no difference in a linear system
why: Late gain amplifies everything picked up along the way, including all intermediate noise. It preserves headroom at the cost of signal-to-noise.
Correct. This is the Friis cascade formula: the noise contribution of stage k is divided by the product of all gains before it. The first stage dominates the total noise figure.
Even distribution is a compromise that is optimal for neither noise nor headroom.
It makes a large difference to noise even in a perfectly linear system, because noise is added at each stage regardless of linearity.
questions.explain: The qualifier "cleanly" is doing real work: early gain is right only up to the point where the stage begins to distort. Beyond that, a pad plus lower gain is correct. Gain staging is the search for that boundary at every stage.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about levels in a 32-bit floating point DAW.
options: The mix bus cannot clip in the arithmetic
Channel levels are irrelevant to modelled analogue plug-ins
Exporting to a fixed-point format will clip anything above 0 dBFS
A linear digital EQ produces a bit-identical result whether fed at -30 or -6 dBFS, given matching output gain
The converter output can still clip even though the file does not
why: True. The exponent gives an enormous representable range; nothing clips in float arithmetic.
False. Modelled nonlinear processors are calibrated to an operating level, typically 0 VU = -18 dBFS, and respond to absolute level by design.
True, and it is the most common way a float session ends up with a clipped deliverable.
True, and the null test proves it. This is why blanket claims that channel levels must sit at -18 dBFS for linear processing are false.
True. The D/A is fixed point; a float mix peaking above full scale clips at the monitor output even if the file is never rendered.
questions.explain: The nuance to hold: float removes the arithmetic constraint but not the boundaries. Levels matter at every fixed-point boundary and inside every nonlinear process, and nowhere else.

questions.q: Order these gain-staging actions in the sequence a competent engineer performs them.
items: Choose the microphone and set its position
Engage a pad if the source will overload the preamp input
Set preamp gain with the fader at unity, checking the loudest passage
Confirm peaks land around -12 to -18 dBFS
Insert processing calibrated to the resulting operating level
Set the monitoring level to the calibrated reference before making tonal judgements
questions.explain: The ordering matters because each step constrains the next. Setting gain before choosing microphone position wastes the setting; inserting a modelled compressor before establishing operating level makes its behaviour arbitrary; judging tone before calibrating monitoring makes every decision level-dependent.

questions.q: Match each symptom to its most probable cause.
pairs: Hiss that rises when a channel fader is raised, with nothing playing
Preamp gain set too high and compensated by fader attenuation
Distortion audible only on loud passages, present in the recorded file
Converter input driven too close to full scale
A modelled compressor behaving far more aggressively than expected
Channel level well above the plug-in's assumed 0 VU = -18 dBFS
Mains-frequency hum that appears only when two devices are connected
Ground loop between differently grounded chassis
Clipping that appears only after AAC encoding
Insufficient true-peak headroom before the codec
Centre-panned sources changing level after moving a session between DAWs
Different pan law settings
questions.explain: Every one of these is a level or interface problem with a specific mechanism and a specific fix. Diagnosis in this domain is largely about locating the stage at which the level went wrong, which is why a chain budget is worth writing down.

questions.stem: You inherit a project studio. Measurements: acoustic noise floor 41 dBA at the listening position with the HVAC running (33 dBA with it off); a capacitor microphone with 14 dBA self-noise; a preamp with -125 dBu EIN; a 24-bit converter with 116 dB A-weighted dynamic range; monitors uncalibrated, with the controller marked only "loud" and "quiet". Recent mixes have been rejected twice for being over the true-peak limit, and the engineer reports that "mixes sound bass-heavy on other systems".

qs.q: Which single limitation dominates the achievable signal-to-noise ratio of a quiet acoustic recording in this room?
options: The converter's 116 dB dynamic range
The preamp's -125 dBu EIN
The 41 dBA acoustic noise floor with HVAC running
The microphone's 14 dBA self-noise
why: 116 dB of converter range is 40-50 dB better than anything else in the chain and is nowhere near limiting.
-125 dBu EIN is within about 6 dB of the thermal floor and is inaudible behind a 41 dBA room.
Correct. A 41 dBA room floor swamps a 14 dBA microphone by 27 dB. Turning the HVAC off during takes recovers 8 dB immediately at no cost, and further acoustic isolation work would recover more.
14 dBA is 27 dB below the room and therefore not the binding constraint, though it would become relevant after the room was fixed.
qs.explain: The ranking is nearly always: room, then microphone, then preamp, then everything digital. Engineers routinely invert it and spend money at the wrong end of the chain by 40 dB or more.

qs.q: With the HVAC off (33 dBA) and a peak level of 105 dB SPL at the microphone, what is the achievable acoustic signal-to-noise ratio in dB, ignoring all electronic contributions?
qs.explain: 105 - 33 = 72 dB. That is the ceiling imposed by the room, and it is 44 dB below the converter's capability. Note that this is also comfortably within 16-bit range, which is a useful reality check on format anxiety.

qs.q: Write a prioritised remediation plan, quantifying the benefit of each step, and explain which of the reported symptoms each step addresses.
qs.model: Priority 1, monitoring calibration, cost near zero. The "bass-heavy on other systems" complaint is the classic signature of mixing at a level that is either uncalibrated or too high, since the equal-loudness contours flatten with level and a mix balanced loud will carry too much low end when played quietly. Generate -20 dBFS pink noise, set each monitor separately to a documented target (79 dBC slow per channel is appropriate for a small room), mark the controller, and make all tonal decisions there. Expected benefit: eliminates a systematic, repeatable error worth several decibels of low-frequency balance; also makes every future comparison level-consistent. Priority 2, delivery metering, cost near zero. The true-peak rejections are a specification problem, not a quality problem: install a true-peak meter with at least 4x oversampling, set a -1 dBTP ceiling (-1.5 dBTP if the master is heavily limited), and adopt the habit of stating integrated loudness, true peak and format before sending anything. Expected benefit: eliminates the rejections entirely. Priority 3, HVAC discipline, cost near zero. Switching the HVAC off during takes recovers 8 dB of noise floor immediately, from 41 to 33 dBA. Expected benefit: 8 dB of signal-to-noise on every quiet source, which is larger than the difference between any two preamps on the market. Priority 4, acoustic treatment, moderate cost. The bass-heavy complaint is likely to have a room-response component as well as a monitoring-level one; measure the response at the listening position, compute the modal frequencies and the SBIR null, and treat corners and first reflections. Expected benefit: the largest remaining improvement in decision quality, though it cannot be quantified in a single number before measurement. Priority 5, further noise reduction below 33 dBA, high cost. This requires isolation construction and would only be justified for very quiet acoustic work. What I would not do: replace the converter or the preamp. The converter is 44 dB better than the room and the preamp is within 6 dB of the thermal limit; neither is audible behind a 33 dBA noise floor, and money spent there buys nothing measurable.
points: Puts monitor calibration first and connects it explicitly to the equal-loudness contours and the bass-heavy symptom
Addresses the true-peak rejections with a specific metering change and a numerical ceiling
Quantifies the HVAC benefit as 8 dB and notes it exceeds any equipment upgrade available
Explicitly declines to upgrade converter or preamp, with a numerical justification
Ranks by benefit per cost rather than by equipment appeal

questions.q: Why is "record it as hot as possible" bad advice on a modern 24-bit converter?
options: Because 24-bit converters have a lower noise floor at high levels
Because the analogue noise floor of the source and preamp is 40 dB or more above the 24-bit LSB, so the extra level buys no audible signal-to-noise while destroying headroom
Because 24-bit files cannot represent high levels accurately
Because dither becomes ineffective at high levels
why: Converter noise is essentially level-independent; the premise is false.

Correct. The theoretical 146 dB range of 24 bits is unreachable; real converters manage 115-125 dB and the acoustic environment rarely offers more than 70-80 dB. Recording 15 dB hotter therefore adds nothing audible and removes 15 dB of transient headroom, while pushing the converter's analogue front end toward its distortion region.
Fixed-point representation is uniformly accurate across its range; there is no high-level penalty in the arithmetic.
Dither is applied at word-length reduction and is unrelated to tracking level.
questions.explain: The advice was correct for analogue tape and defensible for early 16-bit digital. It is a fossil of those media. The relevant question now is always: what is my actual noise floor, and is it set by the room, the microphone, or the electronics?

questions.q: A colleague claims their new analogue summing box "opens up the mix in a way digital summing cannot". Design the test that would settle this, and state what each possible outcome would mean.
questions.model: Design. Render the same multitrack twice: once summed in the DAW, once through the analogue box and back in, with identical fader positions and no processing on the master. Then: (1) Time-align the two files sample-accurately, since the analogue path adds converter latency; use a transient or a click track for alignment. (2) Level-match to within 0.1 dB using integrated loudness or an RMS measurement over the whole file, since the analogue path will not have exactly unity gain and a small level difference will drive any preference judgement on its own. (3) Perform a null test: invert one and sum. Record the residual level in dBFS and its spectrum. (4) Conduct a blind ABX with fast switching, a pre-declared trial count (16 or more), and a pre-declared significance threshold, using several excerpts including dense and sparse material. Outcomes and their meaning. If the null residual is at digital silence, the two paths are bit-identical and any perceived difference is imagination or an artefact of the comparison; this outcome is essentially impossible for an analogue path, which is worth saying up front. More realistically the residual will be non-zero, and its level and spectrum tell you what the box does: a residual dominated by low-order harmonics indicates nonlinearity; a residual that scales with level indicates distortion rather than noise; a residual concentrated at high frequencies with a comb structure indicates small time or phase differences; a broadband residual at a constant low level is simply added noise. A non-zero residual proves a difference exists but not that it is audible or preferable, which is what the ABX establishes. If ABX is significant, the difference is audible and the residual spectrum explains why; the remaining question, preference, requires a separate level-matched paired-comparison test, because audible is not the same as better. If ABX is not significant with adequate trials, report that honestly along with the statistical power, and note that this does not prove no difference exists, only that it was not detected under these conditions. My expectation, stated as a prior rather than a conclusion: there will be a measurable residual dominated by low-order distortion and small level and phase differences, and it may well be audible and preferred on some material. That is a legitimate reason to own the box. It is not evidence that digital summing is arithmetically deficient, which it is not.
points: Specifies sample-accurate time alignment and explains why it is necessary
Specifies level matching to a stated tolerance before any listening
Includes a null test and explains how to interpret the residual level and spectrum
Specifies a blind ABX with pre-declared trial count and significance threshold
Distinguishes audibility from preference and treats a null result honestly

questions.q: A modelled analogue compressor is fed a signal peaking at -1 dBFS. Assuming the plug-in follows the common convention of 0 VU = -18 dBFS, what is the consequence?
options: No consequence; digital plug-ins are level-independent
The modelled circuit is being driven roughly 17 dB above its design operating point, so its distortion and detector behaviour will differ substantially from the hardware at nominal level
The plug-in will clip and produce digital distortion
The output will simply be louder by 17 dB
why: Level independence holds for linear processes only. A modelled compressor is deliberately nonlinear.

Correct. The model reproduces the hardware's behaviour as a function of absolute internal level, so feeding it 17 dB hot reproduces what the hardware would do with 17 dB more input: more distortion, faster and deeper gain reduction, and a different attack character.
It is running in floating point, so it will not clip in the arithmetic, though the modelled circuit may well be modelled as clipping.
A compressor is not a gain stage; the output level depends on the gain reduction and the makeup, not simply on input level.
questions.explain: This is the one genuine, mechanism-based case for gain staging inside a float DAW. It applies to modelled preamps, tape, consoles, saturators and compressors — and not to clean digital EQ, delay, gain or panning.

questions.q: A preamp has an EIN of -127 dBu with a 150 ohm source. The thermal floor for that source over a 20 kHz bandwidth is -130.9 dBu. What is the preamp's noise figure, in dB?
questions.explain: -127 - (-130.9) = 3.9 dB. The preamp adds 3.9 dB to the noise that physics already guarantees. Excellent designs achieve 1-2 dB; below about 6 dB the choice is rarely audible unless you are using 65 dB or more of gain on a very quiet source.

questions.q: Which quantity does the reference 20 micropascals define?
options: 0 dBu
0 dBFS
0 dB SPL
0 VU
why: 0 dBu is 0.7746 V RMS, an electrical reference.
0 dBFS is digital full scale, a numerical reference.
Correct. 20 micropascals is the reference pressure for sound pressure level, chosen as the approximate threshold of hearing for a 1 kHz tone.
0 VU is a meter calibration point, conventionally +4 dBu in professional analogue use.
questions.explain: Six references recur throughout this course. Confusing them is the single most common source of nonsense in audio specifications.

questions.q: What is the wavelength of a 55 Hz tone in air at 20 degrees Celsius? Use c = 343 m/s.
questions.explain: 343/55 = 6.236 m. A quarter of that is 1.56 m, which is the total depth a porous absorber would need to be effective at this frequency — a good illustration of why low-frequency absorption is a construction problem.

questions.q: A point source measures 96 dB SPL at 1.5 m outdoors. Ignoring air absorption, what is the level at 18 m?
questions.explain: 20 log10(18/1.5) = 20 log10(12) = 21.58 dB of loss. 96 - 21.58 = 74.4 dB SPL. The inverse-square rule applies only in a free field to a source small compared with the distance.

questions.q: An amplifier is changed from 120 W to 600 W into the same loudspeaker. What is the level increase in dB?
questions.explain: 10 log10(600/120) = 10 log10(5) = 6.99 dB. Five times the amplifier for 7 dB. A loudspeaker 7 dB more sensitive would give the same result on the original amplifier, which is why sensitivity is usually the better place to spend money.

questions.q: Convert +12 dBu to RMS volts.
questions.explain: 0.7746 x 10^(12/20) = 0.7746 x 3.981 = 3.084 V RMS. Knowing that 0 dBu is 0.775 V and that every 6 dB doubles the voltage gets you close without a calculator: +12 dBu is roughly four times 0.775, i.e. about 3.1 V.

questions.q: Three uncorrelated sources measure 82, 82 and 76 dB SPL. What is their combined level?
questions.explain: 10^8.2 + 10^8.2 + 10^7.6 = 1.585e8 + 1.585e8 + 3.981e7 = 3.568e8, and 10 log10(3.568e8) = 85.5 dB. Two equal sources give +3 dB (85 dB), and the third adds a further 0.5 dB. Decibels never add arithmetically.

questions.q: Two microphones are placed on one source, one 30 cm further away than the other, and summed. What happens?
options: A polarity inversion will correct the resulting cancellation
A comb filter with notches at 572 Hz, 1,716 Hz, 2,860 Hz and so on
Nothing, because the signals are correlated
A 6 dB level increase at all frequencies
why: Polarity inversion moves the notch frequencies; it does not remove them, because the relationship is a delay rather than a sign.
Correct. 30 cm is 0.875 ms of delay, so the first notch is at 1/(2 x 0.000875) = 572 Hz and the spacing is 1/tau = 1,143 Hz.
Correlation is precisely why they comb; uncorrelated signals would simply add in power.
+6 dB occurs only where the two are in phase, which for a delayed pair is only at the comb peaks.
questions.explain: The comb-filter relations f_notch = (2n-1)/2tau and delta-f = 1/tau, combined with tau = d/c, connect a physical distance to a frequency response in two steps. This is the most-used calculation in practical microphone work.

questions.q: A measurement shows comb notches spaced 250 Hz apart. What is the corresponding path-length difference in metres? Use c = 343 m/s.
questions.explain: tau = 1/250 = 4 ms; path difference = c x tau = 343 x 0.004 = 1.372 m. Two steps: spacing to delay, delay to distance. Then look for a surface that creates that extra path.

questions.q: A room is 7.1 m long. What is the frequency of its second axial length mode (n = 2)?
questions.explain: f = nc/2L = 2 x 343 / (2 x 7.1) = 343/7.1 = 48.3 Hz. The first is at 24.2 Hz. Note that the second axial mode has two pressure nulls, at one quarter and three quarters of the room length.

questions.q: A hall has a volume of 4,200 m3, a surface area of 1,850 m2 and an average absorption coefficient of 0.16. What is the Sabine RT60?
questions.explain: A = 1,850 x 0.16 = 296 sabins. T60 = 0.161 x 4,200 / 296 = 676.2/296 = 2.28 s. That is a long reverberation time, appropriate for romantic orchestral repertoire and far too long for speech.

questions.q: For a 4,200 m3 hall with an RT60 of 2.28 s, what is the Schroeder frequency?
questions.explain: 2000 x sqrt(2.28/4200) = 2000 x sqrt(5.43e-4) = 2000 x 0.0233 = 46.6 Hz. Below 47 Hz the hall behaves modally; above it, statistically. Compare with a 90 m3 control room, where the Schroeder frequency is around 130 Hz and the entire bass range is modal.

questions.q: What is the Nyquist frequency for a 176.4 kHz sample rate?
questions.explain: 176,400/2 = 88,200 Hz. Nyquist is always exactly half the sample rate.

questions.q: A 33 kHz component reaches a sampler running at 48 kHz with no anti-alias filtering. Where does it appear?
questions.explain: |33,000 - 48,000| = 15,000 Hz, squarely audible and inseparable from real signal. This is exactly what happens inside a non-oversampling distortion plug-in fed bright material.

questions.q: What is the theoretical dynamic range of a 16-bit system?
questions.explain: 6.02 x 16 + 1.76 = 96.32 + 1.76 = 98.08 dB. Adequate for delivery of virtually all real acoustic material, because no realistic acoustic environment offers more than about 80 dB of usable range.

questions.q: How many decibels of dynamic range do you gain by moving from 16-bit to 24-bit?
questions.explain: 6.02 x 8 = 48.16 dB, since each bit is worth 6.02 dB. The gain is real arithmetically and inaudible in practice, because both figures exceed the noise floor of any recording environment; the true benefit is headroom insurance while tracking.

questions.q: Using the NIOSH criterion (85 dBA for 8 hours, 3 dB exchange rate), what is the permitted daily exposure time at 94 dBA, in minutes?
questions.explain: 8 h / 2^((94-85)/3) = 8/2^3 = 1 hour. A single loud rehearsal exhausts the daily allowance. Under the US OSHA 5 dB rule the same level permits about 4.6 hours, a policy difference not supported by the physiology.

questions.q: Using ERB = 24.7(4.37 f/1000 + 1), what is the equivalent rectangular bandwidth at 500 Hz?
questions.explain: 24.7 x (4.37 x 0.5 + 1) = 24.7 x 3.185 = 78.7 Hz. Two components within about 79 Hz of each other at 500 Hz fall in one auditory filter and cannot be separated by equalisation.

questions.q: A 32-sample buffer runs at 44.1 kHz. What is the one-way buffer latency in milliseconds?
questions.explain: 32/44,100 = 0.000726 s = 0.73 ms. Round trip will be roughly twice this plus converter filter delay, so about 2.5-3.5 ms in practice — comfortably below the threshold at which performers notice.

questions.q: A master measures -9.2 LUFS integrated. A streaming service normalises to -14 LUFS. How much gain will be applied?
questions.explain: -14 - (-9.2) = -4.8 dB of attenuation. Since 1 LU equals 1 dB by construction, loudness offsets are simple subtraction. Any dynamic range sacrificed to reach -9.2 LUFS is given away for nothing on a normalising platform.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true.
options: Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air
Doubling the distance from a point source in a free field reduces SPL by 6 dB
Doubling amplifier power increases SPL by 6 dB
A polarity inversion is equivalent to a 180 degree phase shift at all frequencies
Air absorption attenuates high frequencies more than low frequencies
why: True. c is approximately 331.3 + 0.606 theta, so about 0.6 m/s per degree Celsius.
True in a free field for a source small compared with the distance: 20 log10(2) = 6.02 dB.
False. Doubling power is 10 log10(2) = 3.01 dB. Doubling voltage or pressure gives 6 dB.
False for broadband signals. Inversion is a sign change, frequency-independent; a 180 degree phase shift is defined only at one frequency. They coincide only for a single sinusoid.
True. Air absorption is strongly frequency-dependent, which is why distant thunder rumbles.
questions.explain: These five statements between them cover the most common confusions in the first half of the course: temperature dependence, the two decibel formulas, and the polarity-versus-phase distinction.

questions.q: Select every intervention that will genuinely reduce a modal problem at 42 Hz in a small room.
options: Moving the subwoofer to a different position
Moving the listening position
Adding 50 mm foam panels to the side walls
Deep floor-to-ceiling corner absorption
Using multiple subwoofers placed to cancel the dominant mode
Applying a narrow parametric boost at 42 Hz to fill the null
why: True. A mode cannot be excited from its own pressure null; moving the source can reduce excitation substantially.
True. Level at a modal frequency varies enormously with position, and moving out of a null or off a peak is free.
False. 50 mm foam is effective only above roughly 1.7 kHz; it does nothing whatever at 42 Hz.
True. Corners are pressure antinodes for every mode, and depth is what makes low-frequency absorption work.
True. Welti and Devantier showed that multiple, correctly placed subwoofers can substantially flatten low-frequency response across seats.
False. A null is a cancellation with little energy present; boosting raises noise and consumes headroom without filling it.
questions.explain: Below the Schroeder frequency, geometry and deep absorption work; thin absorption and corrective boost do not. Getting this ranking right saves both money and disappointment.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about dither.
options: It should be applied at every word-length reduction in a chain
TPDF at 2 LSB peak-to-peak makes the error statistically independent of the signal
It raises the noise floor slightly compared with undithered truncation
Noise shaping reduces total noise power
It allows signals below one LSB to be reproduced
why: False as stated. Dither is required at word-length reduction, but the correct practice is to reduce word length once, at the end; repeated dithering accumulates noise.
True. This is the central result of Lipshitz, Wannamaker and Vanderkooy (1992): both the mean and the variance of the total error become signal-independent.
True, by about 4.77 dB for TPDF, which is the price paid for eliminating signal-correlated distortion.
False. Noise shaping redistributes noise in frequency, and in fact increases total power; it lowers perceived loudness by moving energy away from the ear's most sensitive region.
True. The dither causes the quantiser to switch between levels at a rate that encodes the sub-LSB signal in the statistics of the output.
questions.explain: The unifying idea is that dither trades a small amount of noise for the elimination of correlated distortion, which the ear detects at levels far below where it detects equivalent noise.

questions.q: Order the stages of the auditory pathway from outside inward.
items: Pinna
Ear canal
Tympanic membrane
Ossicles
Cochlea
Inner hair cells
Auditory nerve
questions.explain: The canal contributes a quarter-wave resonance near 3.4 kHz, the ossicles provide impedance matching, and the cochlea performs the frequency analysis. Each stage has a specific and quantifiable role.

questions.q: Order these by increasing wavelength.
items: 15 kHz
4 kHz
1 kHz
250 Hz
63 Hz
25 Hz
questions.explain: Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency: 2.3 cm, 8.6 cm, 34.3 cm, 1.37 m, 5.44 m and 13.7 m respectively. The ability to make this conversion instantly is the highest-leverage skill in practical acoustics.

questions.q: Order these treatment and setup steps for an untreated small control room, highest value first.
items: Establish symmetry and choose listening position and speaker distance to avoid the worst modal nulls
Calibrate monitoring to a documented reference level
Deep floor-to-ceiling corner absorption
Absorption at side-wall, ceiling and desk first-reflection points
Address speaker-boundary interference from the front wall
Measurement-guided EQ correction, cuts only below the Schroeder frequency
questions.explain: The ordering runs from free and decisive to expensive and marginal. Calibration is placed second because it costs almost nothing and eliminates a systematic error in every judgement made thereafter.

questions.q: Match each formula to what it computes.
pairs: c / 2L
The fundamental axial room mode of a dimension L
c / 4d
The first boundary-cancellation frequency for a surface at distance d
The first comb-filter notch for a delay tau
Theoretical dynamic range of an n-bit system in dB
Sabine reverberation time
2000 sqrt(T60/V)
Schroeder frequency
questions.explain: Six relations account for most quantitative work in this course. Notice that the first three are all quarter- and half-wavelength arguments in different clothing.

questions.q: Match each measurement to the question it answers.
pairs: True peak (dBTP)
Will this clip a converter or a lossy codec?
Integrated LUFS
How loud will a platform judge this programme to be?
How clear will speech be in this room?
ERB
Will these two components fall in one auditory filter?
Crest factor
How much headroom do the transients need?
Noise figure
How much noise does this stage add above the thermal floor?
questions.explain: Choosing the right measurement is most of the skill. A meter reading is only meaningful in the context of the question that prompted it.

questions.q: Why do porous absorbers need to be spaced away from a wall or made very deep to work at low frequencies?
options: Because the air gap adds mass to the system
Because they dissipate energy through particle velocity, which is zero at a rigid boundary and maximal a quarter wavelength away
Because low frequencies contain more energy
Because the gap allows the panel to resonate
why: An air gap adds compliance, not mass. Mass-spring behaviour is the mechanism of membrane absorbers.
Correct. Viscous dissipation requires air movement, and air cannot move at a rigid boundary. A quarter wavelength out is where velocity peaks.
Energy content depends on the source, and is irrelevant to the mechanism.
Porous absorbers are deliberately non-resonant; resonance is the mechanism of tuned devices.
questions.explain: This one fact explains the failure of thin foam at low frequencies, the value of standoffs, and why corner traps must be deep. It is the same boundary condition that puts pressure maxima at walls.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between sample rate and bit depth?
options: Higher sample rates give higher resolution within the audio band
Sample rate sets bandwidth; bit depth sets the noise floor. They are independent
Bit depth determines the highest frequency that can be recorded
Both determine the smoothness of the reconstructed waveform
why: This is the staircase misconception. Given bandlimiting, reconstruction is exact at any sufficient rate; extra rate buys bandwidth, not in-band accuracy.
Correct, and it is the single most important conceptual point in digital audio.
Bit depth has no relationship to bandwidth.
There is no "smoothness" parameter; the reconstruction filter produces the unique bandlimited waveform through the samples.
questions.explain: Almost every popular misunderstanding of digital audio traces to conflating these two axes. Keeping them separate makes the format arguments much shorter.

questions.q: A live engineer sets a delay ring to arrive at exactly the same time as the main array. What will listeners under the ring experience?
options: Perfect coherence and improved clarity
The image will localise to the nearby ring, and severe comb filtering will occur
A distinct echo
Total cancellation of the main system
why: Perfect coherence at one point is unachievable across an audience area, and even at one point the level difference decides localisation.

Correct. With no relative delay, localisation follows level, and the closer ring is louder, so the show appears overhead. The two correlated arrivals also comb-filter across the seating area as the path difference varies.
An echo requires a delay beyond the fusion threshold, roughly 30-50 ms for speech.
Cancellation requires opposite polarity or a half-wavelength path difference at a specific frequency, not simultaneous arrival.
questions.explain: The correct practice is to delay the fill by the propagation time plus 5-15 ms, so that the main system remains the first wavefront and the precedence effect locks the image on stage.

questions.q: What does the C-minus-A difference in a sound level measurement tell you?
options: Whether the meter is calibrated
How much low-frequency energy is present, since A-weighting discounts it heavily
The crest factor of the signal
The measurement uncertainty
why: Calibration is checked with an acoustic calibrator, not by comparing weightings.

Correct. A-weighting is 39 dB down at 31.5 Hz while C-weighting is only 3 dB down, so a large difference indicates strong low-frequency content. Differences above about 10 dB are common in dance venues and are a recognised indicator that A-weighted limits under-represent the exposure.
Crest factor is a peak-to-RMS ratio and is unrelated to frequency weighting.
Uncertainty is a property of the instrument and procedure.
questions.explain: Two weightings for the price of one measurement is a cheap spectral diagnostic, which is why many modern noise conditions specify both LAeq and LCeq.

questions.stem: You are commissioned to fix a 5.6 x 4.1 x 2.7 m project studio and its workflow. Measurements: room temperature 22 degrees C; acoustic noise floor 38 dBA; measured RT60 at 500 Hz of 0.55 s; a broad 13 dB peak at 30-32 Hz, a 10 dB null at 63 Hz at the seated listening position; response reasonably smooth above 300 Hz. Loudspeakers sit 80 cm from the front wall. The engineer tracks with peaks at -0.8 dBFS, mixes at whatever level feels right, exports 16-bit with truncation, and has had two deliverables rejected for exceeding -1 dBTP.

qs.q: What is the first axial length mode of this room? Use c = 331.3 + 0.606 x 22.
qs.explain: c = 331.3 + 13.33 = 344.6 m/s. f = c/2L = 344.6/11.2 = 30.77 Hz, which matches the observed 30-32 Hz peak. Using 343 m/s gives 30.6 Hz, close enough for diagnosis but worth doing properly when the temperature is known.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of the 63 Hz null at the seated listening position?
options: The second axial length mode
Speaker-boundary interference from the front wall
Air absorption
The first axial height mode, whose pressure null falls at seated ear height
why: The second axial length mode sits at 344.6/5.6 = 61.5 Hz, close in frequency, but its two pressure nulls fall at one quarter and three quarters of the room length, not at the stated listening position; and axial length modes are usually excited strongly by front-wall loudspeakers.
The SBIR null for an 80 cm speaker-to-wall spacing is at c/4d = 344.6/3.2 = 107.7 Hz, nowhere near 63 Hz. This distractor is only plausible if you do not do the arithmetic.
Air absorption at 63 Hz over a few metres is a fraction of a decibel and cannot produce a 10 dB null.

Correct. The first axial height mode is at c/2H = 344.6/5.4 = 63.8 Hz, and its single pressure null sits at half the room height, 1.35 m — essentially seated ear height. This is one of the most common and least recognised faults in small rooms.
qs.explain: Two candidate mechanisms both predict a dip near 63 Hz until you compute them: the height mode lands at 63.8 Hz with its null exactly where the listener sits, while SBIR at 80 cm lands at 108 Hz. The general lesson is to compute every candidate and let the arithmetic choose, rather than accepting the first plausible story. The fix here is free: change the listening height.

qs.q: What is the Schroeder frequency of this room? Volume is 61.99 m3 and RT60 is 0.55 s.
qs.explain: 2000 x sqrt(0.55/62.0) = 2000 x sqrt(0.008871) = 2000 x 0.09419 = 188.4 Hz. Everything below 188 Hz in this room must be treated as a modal problem, which is a large fraction of the musically important bass range.

qs.q: Write the full remediation plan covering both the room and the workflow, in priority order, with quantitative justification for each item and an honest statement of what will remain unfixed.
qs.model: Workflow first, because it costs nothing and fixes the rejections immediately. (1) Tracking level: move peaks from -0.8 dBFS to -12 to -18 dBFS. With a 38 dBA room floor and a 24-bit converter, the noise cost is precisely zero — the acoustic floor is more than 60 dB above the LSB — while the benefit is 12-17 dB of transient headroom and keeping the converter input stage out of its distortion region. (2) Word-length reduction: apply TPDF or a moderate noise-shaped dither once at the final 16-bit reduction, and never truncate. Truncation leaves signal-correlated error, which is distortion rather than noise and is audible on fades far above the theoretical floor. (3) True peak: meter with at least 4x oversampling and set a -1 dBTP ceiling, -1.5 dBTP if the master is heavily limited, before any lossy encode. This eliminates the rejections by construction. (4) Monitor calibration: play -20 dBFS pink noise, set each speaker separately to a documented target such as 79 dBC slow, mark the controller, and make all tonal judgements at that mark. Without this, the equal-loudness contours make every low-frequency decision level-dependent. Room next. (5) Geometry, free: the 63 Hz null is very likely the first axial height mode at 63.8 Hz, whose pressure null is at 1.35 m, essentially seated ear height. Raise or lower the listening position by 20-25 cm and re-measure. Also check the position along the length; aim for roughly 38% of 5.6 m, about 2.1 m from the front wall, and confirm symmetry left to right. (6) Deep corner absorption, floor to ceiling, in all four vertical corners, 40-60 cm across the diagonal. The 30.8 Hz mode has a wavelength of 11.2 m, so a quarter wavelength is 2.8 m and no absorber that fits will fully damp it; expect 4-8 dB of peak reduction and a useful shortening of the decay, not elimination. (7) First reflections at side walls, ceiling and desk, using 100 mm mineral wool on a 100 mm standoff, which is effective from about 430 Hz. Verify positions with a mirror rather than guessing. (8) RT60: at 0.55 s in a 62 m3 room the target should be about 0.25 s, which requires raising total absorption from about 20 sabins to about 40 sabins; the treatment above should approach that, and it should be re-measured rather than assumed. (9) Only then, EQ: cuts only, below 188 Hz, at the measured peak frequencies, never boosts to fill the 63 Hz null, since there is little energy there to raise and any boost costs headroom and is valid at one position only. What will remain unfixed: the 30.8 Hz mode will still be audible as a peak and as a longer decay; the room is too small for the wavelengths involved. The response will remain position-dependent below 188 Hz, so mix-position discipline matters. And a 38 dBA noise floor limits very quiet acoustic recording regardless of any electronic upgrade, which is a construction problem rather than an equipment problem.
points: Fixes tracking level and justifies the zero noise cost with reference to the actual acoustic floor
Specifies dither once at final word-length reduction and a -1 dBTP ceiling, addressing the rejections
Includes monitor calibration and links it to the equal-loudness contours
Identifies the height-mode null and prescribes a free geometric fix
Prescribes deep corner absorption with a realistic, quantified expectation of improvement
Restricts EQ to cuts below the Schroeder frequency and explains why nulls cannot be filled
States honestly what will remain unfixed and why

questions.stem: A mastering client sends two candidate masters. Master A: -6.8 LUFS integrated, LRA 2 LU, sample peak -0.1 dBFS, true peak +1.4 dBTP. Master B: -12.5 LUFS integrated, LRA 8 LU, sample peak -1.6 dBFS, true peak -1.2 dBTP. The release will go to streaming platforms that normalise to approximately -14 LUFS, and to a vinyl cut. The client prefers A in unlevel-matched comparison.

qs.q: After normalisation to -14 LUFS, how many dB louder or quieter will Master A be than Master B?
qs.explain: Both are normalised to the same integrated loudness, so they play back at the same loudness. A is attenuated by 7.2 dB and B by 1.5 dB. The client's preference for A therefore reflects the unmatched comparison, not any advantage that survives playback.

qs.q: Which master is the more serious problem for the vinyl cut, and why?
options: Master B, because its lower level requires more groove excursion
Master A, because heavy limiting raises average level and high-frequency energy, forcing the cutting engineer to reduce level or apply elliptical filtering
Neither; vinyl cutting is unaffected by digital loudness
Master B, because its wider loudness range causes tracking errors
why: Lower average level generally makes cutting easier, not harder; groove excursion is driven by low-frequency energy and level.

Correct. A dense, limited master with high average level and strong high-frequency content forces reduced cutting level, de-essing, elliptical filtering of low-frequency stereo content, or shorter sides. Cutting engineers routinely request a less limited master for exactly this reason.
Vinyl cutting is strongly affected: the medium has mechanical limits on excursion, velocity and acceleration.
A wide loudness range is generally welcome on vinyl and does not cause tracking errors by itself.
qs.explain: Different media impose different constraints. This is why the correct deliverable is often a set of masters rather than one, and why a single loudness target is a poor artistic goal.

qs.q: Master A true-peaks at +1.4 dBTP while sample-peaking at -0.1 dBFS. What does that tell you?
options: The meter is faulty
The reconstructed waveform exceeds full scale between samples, so it will clip in the D/A or after lossy encoding
The file contains DC offset
The file is 32-bit float
why: A discrepancy between sample peak and true peak is expected on limited material and is not a fault.

Correct. Inter-sample peaks arise because the continuous waveform through the samples can exceed the largest sample value. Heavily limited material routinely overshoots by 1-2 dB, and lossy codecs add more.
DC offset would show as an asymmetric waveform and a non-zero mean, not as a true-peak excess.
Bit depth is unrelated to inter-sample behaviour.
qs.explain: Sample peak measures the numbers; true peak estimates the waveform. Delivery specifications are written in dBTP for exactly this reason.

qs.q: Write the message you would send the client. Make the technical case, propose a concrete course of action, and acknowledge honestly what is a matter of taste rather than fact.
qs.model: The facts first. Both masters will play at the same loudness on every normalising platform: A will be turned down by 7.2 dB and B by 1.5 dB, so the loudness advantage the client hears in the studio does not survive delivery. What does survive is the difference in crest factor and loudness range: A has 2 LU of range against B's 8 LU, meaning transients and dynamic contrast have been removed to buy a level increase that the platform gives back for free. A also true-peaks at +1.4 dBTP, which will clip in consumer D/A converters and after AAC or Ogg encoding; that is not a matter of preference but a defect against every current delivery specification, all of which require -1 dBTP or lower. For vinyl, A will force the cutting engineer to reduce level, filter low-frequency stereo content and possibly de-ess further, so the vinyl will be quieter and duller than it needs to be. Proposed course of action: adopt B as the streaming and vinyl master, with a true-peak ceiling of -1 dBTP confirmed by an oversampled meter. If the client wants additional density, produce an intermediate at around -10 LUFS with the same ceiling and compare it with B level-matched to within 0.2 LU and blind; that is the only comparison that carries information. Keep A only if there is a specific non-normalising outlet, such as a DJ or club deliverable, where absolute level is genuinely useful. What is taste and not fact: how much limiting a record should have is an artistic decision, and dense, aggressive mastering is a legitimate aesthetic with a long history. I am not claiming B is more musical. I am claiming that the specific level difference between them buys nothing on the intended platforms and costs a measurable amount, and that the true-peak figure on A is a technical defect regardless of taste. If after a level-matched blind comparison the client still prefers the denser master, that is a real preference and I will deliver it, with the peak ceiling corrected.
points: States that normalisation removes the loudness advantage, with the specific dB figures
Identifies the +1.4 dBTP as a technical defect against delivery specifications, not a preference
Explains the vinyl consequence concretely
Proposes a level-matched blind comparison as the decision procedure
Separates the technical claim from the aesthetic one, and concedes the aesthetic point

questions.q: Explain why a mix balanced at 90 dB SPL will typically sound bass-light when played at 60 dB SPL, and describe two defensible professional responses.
questions.model: The equal-loudness contours (ISO 226) show that the ear's frequency response is level-dependent: at low loudness levels the contours are steeply tilted, requiring far more sound pressure at low frequencies to achieve the same loudness as a midrange tone, and they flatten progressively as level rises. Between the 20-phon and 90-phon contours the tilt from 31.5 Hz to 1 kHz falls from roughly 51 dB to roughly 25 dB. Consequently, reducing playback level by 30 dB costs perceived low-frequency loudness far more than it costs midrange loudness, so a mix whose low end was judged correct at 90 dB SPL sounds thin at 60 dB SPL. Nothing about the signal changed; the transfer function of the listener did. Two professional responses. First, calibrate and standardise the monitoring level: measure with a sound level meter using pink noise at a defined electrical level, set a documented reference such as 79 dBC per channel for a small room, mark the control, and make all tonal-balance judgements there. This does not remove the physics but it removes the variance, so that a decision made today matches one made last week and the engineer builds a stable internal reference. Second, check deliberately at multiple levels as part of the process: make balance and arrangement decisions quietly, where the midrange dominates and masking problems are exposed, and return to the calibrated reference for any low-frequency judgement. A third, more limited response is level-dependent loudness compensation at playback, which is technically correct but only when tied to a known absolute level; the historical implementations failed because they were not. The honest limitation is that no mix is correct at all playback levels, so the engineer is choosing which level to be correct at, and should choose the one the audience will most often use.
points: States that the equal-loudness contours flatten with increasing level
Quantifies the effect with specific tilts or frequencies
Recommends calibrated monitoring with a specific procedure and target
Recommends deliberate multi-level checking with a rationale for each level
Acknowledges that no single mix is correct at every playback level

questions.q: A colleague proposes to record an entire album at 192 kHz, 32-bit float, arguing that "more data means more quality". Give a rigorous response covering sampling theory, converter behaviour, and where the effort would be better spent.
questions.model: Bit depth first, because it is the clearer case. 24-bit gives 6.02 x 24 + 1.76 = 146 dB of theoretical dynamic range. No converter achieves it; the best manage 120-125 dB, limited by analogue circuitry. No acoustic environment offers more: a very quiet studio at 15-20 dBA with peaks at 120 dB SPL provides about 100-105 dB. 32-bit float is genuinely useful as an internal DAW format and on field recorders where it removes the need to set gain, because it cannot clip in the arithmetic; as a capture and storage format for a studio session with a properly set preamp it doubles storage for headroom that has nowhere to go. Sample rate is more nuanced. The sampling theorem says a signal bandlimited below Nyquist is reconstructed exactly, so 48 kHz already covers the entire audible band with margin; higher rates buy bandwidth, not in-band resolution, and the staircase intuition that suggests otherwise is simply wrong. There are two real arguments for higher rates: anti-alias and reconstruction filters can be gentler, and more importantly, nonlinear processing that does not oversample internally will fold harmonics back into the audible band as inharmonic aliases, which a higher session rate reduces. Both are arguments for 88.2 or 96 kHz, not for 192 kHz. Against 192 kHz specifically: it halves the time available per conversion, which typically worsens converter linearity and jitter sensitivity; it doubles storage and CPU relative to 96 kHz; and ultrasonic content can intermodulate in downstream analogue equipment, creating audible artefacts that would not otherwise exist. The evidence on audibility is genuinely mixed — Meyer and Moran (2007) found no discrimination of a 16/44.1 loop, while Reiss's 2016 meta-analysis found a small significant effect concentrated in trained listeners — but every reported effect is far smaller than the effect of the room, the monitors, the microphone position or the arrangement. Recommendation: 24-bit at 48 or 96 kHz, chosen by whether the session leans on non-oversampling nonlinear plug-ins. Spend the saved storage and CPU on acoustic treatment, on a better room, and on more takes.
points: Shows that 24-bit theoretical range already exceeds converter and acoustic limits, with numbers
Explains that sample rate sets bandwidth rather than in-band resolution, and rejects the staircase intuition
Gives the legitimate arguments for higher rates (filter design, aliasing in nonlinear processing) and limits them to 88.2/96 kHz
Names the costs of 192 kHz specifically, including reduced conversion time and ultrasonic intermodulation
Cites evidence on both sides and redirects effort to higher-impact interventions

questions.q: Which of the following will most reliably improve the signal-to-noise ratio of a quiet acoustic recording in a typical project studio?
options: Upgrading from a 116 dB converter to a 124 dB converter
Upgrading from a preamp with -122 dBu EIN to one with -128 dBu EIN
Turning off the HVAC and reducing the room noise floor from 41 to 33 dBA
Recording at 32-bit float instead of 24-bit
why: Converter dynamic range is already 40-50 dB better than the acoustic environment; 8 dB more changes nothing audible.
A 6 dB EIN improvement is real but audible only at very high gain settings with quiet sources, and it is still far below the room floor.
Correct. An 8 dB reduction in the dominant noise source is 8 dB of real improvement in the recorded signal-to-noise ratio, and it costs nothing.
Float format changes headroom behaviour, not noise; the noise floor is set by the acoustics and the analogue chain.
questions.explain: The ranking of noise sources is nearly always: room, microphone, preamp, then everything digital. Money and attention are routinely spent at the wrong end of that list by a margin of 40 dB or more.

questions.q: A vocal is masked by an electric bass. Which intervention addresses the mechanism most directly?
options: Boost the vocal in the masked region
Reduce the bass energy in the region overlapping the vocal
Compress the vocal more heavily
High-pass the bass at 100 Hz
why: Boosting the masked source raises overall level while improving the masker-to-target ratio only proportionally; it usually makes the mix louder rather than clearer.
Correct. Masking is determined by the masker within the shared auditory filter, so removing masker energy in that band improves the ratio directly and lowers overall level at the same time.
Compression raises average level and reduces dynamic contrast; it does not change the spectral overlap.
High-passing at 100 Hz removes energy well below the overlap region and does not touch the masker in the band that matters.
questions.explain: Critical-band theory gives a clear ranking of interventions, and it is also the theoretical basis for sidechained dynamic EQ, which removes masker energy only while the target is present.

questions.q: What is the primary reason a linear system cannot produce harmonic distortion?
options: Because it has no gain
Because superposition guarantees the output contains only frequencies present at the input
Because it is always minimum phase
Because harmonics require a time-varying process
why: Linear systems can have any gain.
Correct. Linearity plus time-invariance means a sinusoidal input produces a sinusoidal output at the same frequency, possibly scaled and phase-shifted. New frequencies require nonlinearity.
Linearity and minimum phase are independent properties; all-pass filters are linear and not minimum phase.
Time variation is a separate route to new frequencies (tremolo, ring modulation), but it is not what harmonic distortion is.
questions.explain: The "no new frequencies" test classifies any process in one step. If harmonics appear that were not in the source, the system is either nonlinear or time-varying, and the two cases are distinguishable by whether the new components are harmonically related to the input.

questions.q: A colleague reports that version A of a mix "sounds wider and more open" than version B. Measurement shows A is 1.1 LU louder, with otherwise near-identical spectra. What is the correct next step?
options: Accept the judgement, since trained ears detect things measurement cannot
Level-match A to B within about 0.2 dB and repeat the comparison blind
Increase the difference by boosting A further to confirm
Measure the phase correlation
why: Trained listeners are as susceptible to loudness bias as anyone; the effect is one of the most robust in audio perception.
Correct. A 1.1 LU difference is far more than enough to produce a consistent preference on its own. Any comparison not level-matched to roughly 0.1-0.2 dB and blinded is uninterpretable.
Amplifying the confound cannot resolve it.
Correlation is worth checking eventually, but it cannot be interpreted while a 1.1 dB level difference is present.
questions.explain: Level matching and blinding are the minimum standard of evidence for any audio comparison. They cost minutes and they resolve most studio disputes, including a great many that would otherwise result in equipment purchases.

questions.q: A microphone is 40 cm from a hard reflective surface, with the source far away. At what frequency is the first boundary-cancellation null?
questions.explain: 343/(4 x 0.4) = 214.4 Hz, with further nulls at 643 Hz and 1,072 Hz. The two safe strategies are flush-mounting, which pushes the null above the audio band, and getting far enough away that the reflection is weak and late.

questions.q: A porous absorber assembly must be effective from 90 Hz upward. What total depth does the quarter-wavelength rule require, in metres?
questions.explain: d = c/4f = 343/360 = 0.953 m. Nearly a metre. This is why genuine low-frequency absorption means soffits, whole-wall systems or very large corner traps, and why claims of full-range absorption from a 10 cm panel should be disregarded.
